knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak-Solution Recovery for the Three-Dimensional Filtration Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The pair defined by (6.2) and (6.3) satisfies the stated weak formulation and boundary data of Problem 5.1.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((u,\varphi)\) be defined by \((6.2)\) and \((6.3)\). Then \((u,\varphi)\) is a weak solution of Problem \(5.1\). Namely, for every \(\zeta\in H^1(M)\) vanishing near \(G_1\cup G_2\cup G_2^{++}\), \[\int_\Omega u_{x_i}\zeta_{x_i}\,dx=0,\] and \[u=H\text{ on }G_1,\qquad u=h\text{ on }G_2,\qquad u=x_3\text{ on }G_2^{++}\cap\overline\Omega,\qquad u=x_3\text{ on }\Gamma.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pair (u, phi) defined by (6.2) and (6.3) is a weak solution of Problem 5.1: it satisfies the stated integral identity for every admissible test function and the prescribed boundary values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (u,\varphi)\text{ is a weak solution of Problem }5.1;\quad \forall\zeta\in H^1(M)\text{ vanishing near }G_1\cup G_2\cup G_2^{++},\ \int_\Omega u_{x_i}\zeta_{x_i}\,dx=0;\quad u|_{G_1}=H,\ u|_{G_2}=h,\ u|_{G_2^{++}\cap\overline\Omega}=x_3,\ u|_\Gamma=x_3.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variational Inequality Associated with a Convex Function and a Maximally Monotone Operator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a Hilbert-space variational inequality generated by a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function and a set-valued maximally monotone operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a Hilbert space, let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), and let \(B:\mathcal H\to2^{\mathcal H}\) be maximally monotone. The associated variational inequality is to find \(x\in\mathcal H\) such that \((\exists u\in Bx)(\forall y\in\mathcal H)\;\langle x-y,u\rangle+f(x)\leq f(y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function f and a maximally monotone operator B on a Hilbert space, find x and some u in Bx such that the inner product of x−y with u plus f(x) is at most f(y) for every y in the space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Sol}=\{x\in\mathcal H\mid(\exists u\in Bx)(\forall y\in\mathcal H),\ \langle x-y,u\rangle+f(x)\leq f(y)\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: OPQVIC Model and QVI Formulation of an Optimistic SLMFG
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines optimization with a parametric QVI constraint and records the operator and feasible-set map used for an optimistic single-leader multi-follower game.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An OPQVIC has the form \(\min_{x,y}F(x,y)\) subject to \(x\in X\) and \(y\in\operatorname{QVI}(T(x,\cdot),K(x,\cdot))\), where \(y\in K(x,y)\) and \(\langle T(x,y),y-z\rangle\ge 0\) for every \(z\in K(x,y)\). For the stated optimistic SLMFG formulation, \(T(x,y)=(\nabla_{y_j}f_j(x,y))_{j=1}^M\) and \(K(x,y)=\prod_{j=1}^M Y_j(x,y_{-j})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An OPQVIC minimizes an upper-level objective subject to a point solving a quasi-variational inequality whose feasible set may depend on that point. For the stated multi-follower game formulation, the QVI operator concatenates the followers' partial gradients and its feasible-set map is the product of their parameterized feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x,y}\left\{F(x,y):x\in X,\ y\in K(x,y),\ \langle T(x,y),y-z\rangle\ge0\ \forall z\in K(x,y)\right\},\quad T=(\nabla_{y_j}f_j)_{j=1}^M,\quad K=\prod_{j=1}^M Y_j(x,y_{-j}).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hölder continuity of the mixed-boundary variational-inequality solution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global Hölder regularity under the hypotheses of Theorem 9.1.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u\in\mathbb K\) solve the mixed-boundary variational inequality (9.1), under the assumptions of Theorem 9.1: \(\psi\in L^\infty(\Omega)\cap H^1(\Omega)\) with \(\psi\le0\) on \(\partial_1\Omega\), \(f_0\in L^{p/2}(\Omega)\), \(f_j\in L^p(\Omega)\) for \(j=1,\ldots,N\) with \(p>N\), and \(g\in L^q(\partial_2\Omega)\) with \(q>N-1\). Then \(u\in C^{0,\lambda}(\overline\Omega)\) for some \(0<\lambda<1\), where \(\lambda\) depends only on \(\Omega,N,p,q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the preceding obstacle and data assumptions, the solution is Hölder continuous on the closure of the domain, with an exponent depending only on the domain, dimension, and integrability exponents.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u\in C^{0,\lambda}(\overline\Omega)\text{ for some }0<\lambda<1\text{ depending only on }\Omega,N,p,q

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Parameter monotonicity and pointwise error bound for obstacle penalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded result; hypothesis (2.2), variational inequality (2.1), penalized problem (2.7), and penalty function (2.8) retain their source-local meanings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume (2.2). Let \(u\) solve the variational inequality (2.1), and for every \(\varepsilon>0\) let \(u_\varepsilon\) solve the penalized problem (2.7), with \(\vartheta_\varepsilon\) defined by (2.8). The family is nondecreasing with respect to \(\varepsilon\), and for every \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(x\in\Omega\), \[u(x)\leq u_\varepsilon(x)\leq u(x)+\varepsilon.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under hypothesis (2.2), the penalized solutions are nondecreasing as the penalty parameter ε increases and approximate the obstacle variational-inequality solution pointwise from above with error at most ε.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0<\varepsilon_1\leq\varepsilon_2\Longrightarrow u_{\varepsilon_1}\leq u_{\varepsilon_2},\qquad \forall\varepsilon>0\ \forall x\in\Omega:\ u(x)\leq u_\varepsilon(x)\leq u(x)+\varepsilon

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unique Solution and Regularity for the Filtration Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the source-defined domain \(R\), datum \(g\) from (3.11), Problem 3.1, definition (4.7), and region \(\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathbb K=\{v\in H^1(R):v\geq 0\text{ in }R,\ v=g\text{ on }\partial R\}\), where \(g\) is defined in (3.11), and let \(w\in\mathbb K\) satisfy
\[
\int_R\left[w_x(v-w)_x+w_y(v-w)_y\right]dx\,dy\geq-\int_R(v-w)dx\,dy\qquad\text{for all }v\in\mathbb K.
\]
Set \(u=y-w_y\), and define \(\varphi(x)\), \(0<x<a\), by (4.7). Then Problem 3.1 admits the unique solution pair \(\{u,\varphi\}\). Moreover, \(u\in C^{0,\lambda}(\overline\Omega)\), and the curve \(y=\varphi(x)\), \(0<x<a\), admits an analytic parametrization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let w solve the stated variational inequality with the source-defined boundary datum. Reconstruct u as y minus the y-derivative of w and define the free boundary by the source formula. The resulting pair is the unique solution of Problem 3.1; u is Hölder continuous on the closed region, and the free-boundary curve admits an analytic parametrization.
assumptions_latex: \mathbb K=\{v\in H^1(R):v\geq 0\text{ in }R,\ v=g\text{ on }\partial R\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{u,\varphi\}\text{ is the unique solution pair of Problem 3.1},\quad u\in C^{0,\lambda}(\overline\Omega),\quad y=\varphi(x)\text{ admits an analytic parametrization}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniqueness and Limit Convergence of Penalized Bilevel-VI Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence theorem for problem (4.33); the unexpanded condition and referenced problem systems are retained exactly by number.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the lower-level mapping \(h\) be continuous and monotone on \(X\), assume that condition \((4.22)\) holds, and let the upper-level mapping \(H\) be continuous and strictly monotone on \(X\). Then, for every sufficiently small \(\varepsilon>0\), problem \((4.33)\) has a unique solution \(x_\varepsilon\). Moreover, \(x_\varepsilon\to z^*\) as \(\varepsilon\to0\), where \(z^*\) is the solution of the LVI specified by \((4.24)\), \((4.25)\), and \((4.31)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the lower-level mapping is continuous and monotone, condition (4.22) holds, and the upper-level mapping is continuous and strictly monotone, then problem (4.33) has a unique solution for every sufficiently small positive parameter, and those solutions converge to the solution of the referenced LVI as the parameter tends to zero.
assumptions_latex: h\text{ is continuous and monotone on }X
H\text{ is continuous and strictly monotone on }X
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\,\bar\varepsilon>0\ \forall\varepsilon\in(0,\bar\varepsilon):\ \operatorname{SOL}(4.33)=\{x_\varepsilon\},\qquad \lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}x_\varepsilon=z^*

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent formulations of a multifunction variational inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the multifunction VI and its normal-cone formulation; the projection, normal-map, and fixed-point formulations require a nonempty closed convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\Omega:C\rightrightarrows\mathbf E\), \(\operatorname{VI}(\Omega,C)\) seeks \(x_0\in C\) and \(y_0\in\Omega(x_0)\) such that \(\langle y_0,x-x_0\rangle\ge 0\) for every \(x\in C\), equivalently \(0\in\Omega(x_0)+N_C(x_0)\). If \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, this is also equivalent to \(x_0\in P_C(x_0-\Omega(x_0))\). Defining \(\Omega_C(\bar x)=\Omega(P_C\bar x)+\bar x-P_C\bar x\), a zero \(0\in\Omega_C(\bar x)\) yields the VI solution \(x_0=P_C\bar x\); equivalently, \(\bar x\in (I-\Omega)(P_C\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifunction variational inequality asks for a feasible point and one of its operator values whose inner product with every feasible displacement is nonnegative. It is equivalently a normal-cone inclusion. For a nonempty closed convex set it also has projection, normal-map zero, and fixed-point formulations.
assumptions_latex: For the projection-based formulations, \(C\subseteq\mathbf E\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variational-inequality representation of porous-medium filtration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transforms a sufficiently regular solution of Problem 3.1 into a variational-inequality solution and recovers the filtration region as its positivity set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{\varphi,u\}\) solve Problem 3.1 with \(u\in H^1(\Omega)\cap C^0(\overline\Omega)\) and smooth \(\varphi\). Let \(w\) solve \(w_y=y-u\) in \(\Omega\), with \(w=0\) on \(\Gamma=\{(x,y):y=\varphi(x),\ 0<x<a\}\), and define \(\widetilde w=w\) in \(\Omega\) and \(\widetilde w=0\) in \(R\setminus\Omega\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated regularity, the zero extension of the auxiliary Cauchy solution belongs to K and satisfies the extracted variational inequality for every competitor in K; the filtration domain is exactly the positivity set of w.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variational inequality of the second kind and its tangent condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition, principal special cases, and the directionally differentiable necessary condition stated in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), \(\varphi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), and let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty. The problem is to find \(x\in K\) such that \[a(x,y-x)+\varphi(y)-\varphi(x)\geq0\qquad\forall y\in K.\] It specializes to a standard VI when \(a(u,v)=v^TF(u)\) and \(\varphi\equiv0\), and to minimization of \(\varphi\) over \(K\) when \(a\equiv0\). If \(a(u,\cdot)\) is linear for every \(u\) and \(\varphi\) is directionally differentiable, every solution also satisfies \[a(x,d)+\varphi'(x;d)\geq0\qquad\forall d\in\mathcal T(x;K).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variational inequality of the second kind seeks a point in a nonempty set for which a bifunction term plus the change in a scalar function is nonnegative against every feasible comparison point. It includes ordinary variational inequalities and constrained minimization as special cases. Under linearity in the bifunction's second argument and directional differentiability of the scalar function, every solution satisfies the corresponding inequality in every tangent direction.
assumptions_latex: a(u,\cdot)\text{ is linear for every }u\text{ and }\varphi\text{ is directionally differentiable for the tangent condition}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in K,\quad a(x,y-x)+\varphi(y)-\varphi(x)\geq0\ \forall y\in K;\quad a(x,d)+\varphi'(x;d)\geq0\ \forall d\in\mathcal T(x;K)\text{ under the additional assumptions}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First-order condition for a reduced PDE-control problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary variational inequality under differentiable control-to-state reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $U,Y,Z$ be Banach spaces, let $U_{\mathrm{ad}}\subset U$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and suppose $J:Y\times U\to\mathbb R$ and $e:Y\times U\to Z$ are continuously Fréchet differentiable. Assume that on a neighborhood of $U_{\mathrm{ad}}$ the state equation $e(y,u)=0$ has a unique solution $y(u)$ and $e_y(y(u),u)$ is boundedly invertible. Define $\widehat J(u)=J(y(u),u)$. If $\bar u$ is a local minimizer of the reduced problem over $U_{\mathrm{ad}}$, then
$$\bar u\in U_{\mathrm{ad}},\qquad \langle\widehat J'(\bar u),u-\bar u\rangle_{U^*,U}\ge0\quad\forall u\in U_{\mathrm{ad}}.$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under differentiable and locally well-posed state reduction, every local minimizer of the reduced PDE-control problem satisfies the reduced-gradient variational inequality over the admissible control set.
assumptions_latex: \varnothing\ne U_{\mathrm{ad}}\subset U\text{ is closed and convex}
J\in C^1(Y\times U;\mathbb R),\quad e\in C^1(Y\times U;Z)
e_y(y(u),u)\text{ is boundedly invertible for all }u\in V
\bar u\text{ is a local minimizer of }\widehat J\text{ over }U_{\mathrm{ad}}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar u\in U_{\mathrm{ad}}\quad\text{and}\quad\langle\widehat J'(\bar u),u-\bar u\rangle_{U^*,U}\ge0\quad\forall u\in U_{\mathrm{ad}}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection fixed-point representation of a convex variational inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between a constant-field variational inequality and a metric-projection equation in Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $W$ be a Hilbert space, let $\varnothing\ne\mathcal C\subset W$ be closed and convex, and let $P_{\mathcal C}$ be its metric projection. For every $w,y\in W$ and every $\gamma>0$, $$w\in\mathcal C\ \text{and}\ (y,v-w)_W\ge0\quad\forall v\in\mathcal C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad w=P_{\mathcal C}(w-\gamma y).$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any positive step size, a point satisfies the convex-set variational inequality for the vector y exactly when projecting the point after a step in direction minus y returns the same point.
assumptions_latex: \varnothing\ne\mathcal C\subset W\text{ is closed and convex}
P_{\mathcal C}\text{ is the metric projection onto }\mathcal C
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[w\in\mathcal C\ \land\ (y,v-w)_W\ge0\ \forall v\in\mathcal C\right]\iff w-P_{\mathcal C}(w-\gamma y)=0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence of solutions for coercive noncompact cusco variational inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence theorem replacing compactness of the feasible set with the stated coercivity condition on the multifunction-plus-normal-cone mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbf E\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(\Omega:C\rightrightarrows\mathbf E\) be cusco. If \[\liminf_{\substack{\|x\|\to\infty\\x\in C}}\inf_{z\in\Omega(x)+N_C(x)}\langle x,z\rangle>0,\] then there exist \(x_0\in C\) and \(y_0\in\Omega(x_0)\) such that \(\langle y_0,x-x_0\rangle\ge 0\) for every \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cusco multifunction on a nonempty closed convex set has a variational-inequality solution when the stated normal-cone coercivity condition holds at infinity.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbf E\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x_0\in C\;\exists y_0\in\Omega(x_0)\;\forall x\in C:\ \langle y_0,x-x_0\rangle\ge 0.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projected-gradient representation of first-order constrained optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space variational optimality represented as a metric-projection fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $W$ be a Hilbert space, let $\varnothing\ne\mathcal C\subset W$ be closed and convex, and let $J$ be defined on an open neighborhood of $\mathcal C$. If $\bar w$ is a local minimizer and $J$ is Gâteaux differentiable at $\bar w$, then for every $\gamma>0$, $$\bar w=P_{\mathcal C}\bigl(\bar w-\gamma\nabla J(\bar w)\bigr).$$ More generally, this fixed-point equation is equivalent to $$\bar w\in\mathcal C,\qquad \langle J'(\bar w),w-\bar w\rangle_{W^*,W}\ge0\quad\forall w\in\mathcal C.$$ Consequently, under the additional convexity, strict-convexity, or reflexive-space coercivity hypotheses of the corresponding variational-inequality theorem, the fixed-point equation respectively yields global sufficiency, uniqueness, or existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differentiable local minimizer over a nonempty closed convex set is a projected-gradient fixed point for every positive step size. The fixed-point equation is equivalent to the first-order variational inequality and therefore has the same stated convex optimality consequences.
assumptions_latex: \varnothing\ne\mathcal C\subset W\text{ is closed and convex}
J\text{ is defined on an open neighborhood of }\mathcal C
J\text{ is Gâteaux differentiable at }\bar w
\nabla J(\bar w)\text{ is the Riesz representative of }J'(\bar w)
\text{For necessity: }\bar w\text{ is a local minimizer over }\mathcal C
\text{For the additional conclusions: the corresponding convexity, strict-convexity, or reflexive coercivity hypotheses hold}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar w=P_{\mathcal C}(\bar w-\gamma\nabla J(\bar w))\iff\left[\bar w\in\mathcal C\ \land\ \langle J'(\bar w),w-\bar w\rangle_{W^*,W}\ge0\ \forall w\in\mathcal C\right].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Essential bound for a mixed-boundary obstacle variational inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A priori bound for a solution of the mixed-boundary variational inequality (9.1).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u\in\mathbb K\) solve the mixed-boundary variational inequality (9.1). If \(\psi\in L^\infty(\Omega)\cap H^1(\Omega)\) with \(\psi\le 0\) on \(\partial_1\Omega\), \(f_0\in L^{p/2}(\Omega)\), \(f_j\in L^p(\Omega)\) for \(j=1,\ldots,N\), where \(p>N\), and \(g\in L^q(\partial_2\Omega)\), where \(q>N-1\), then for a suitable constant \(C\), almost everywhere in \(\Omega\), \[\psi(x)\le u(x)\le \max\{\max_\Omega\psi,0\}+C\left(\|f_0\|_{L^{p/2}(\Omega)}+\sum_{i=1}^N\|f_i\|_{L^p(\Omega)}+\|g\|_{L^q(\partial_2\Omega)}\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The solution is bounded below by the obstacle and bounded above almost everywhere by the nonnegative obstacle maximum plus a constant times the stated volume-force and boundary-data norms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \psi(x)\le u(x)\le \max\{\max_\Omega\psi,0\}+C\left(\|f_0\|_{L^{p/2}(\Omega)}+\sum_{i=1}^N\|f_i\|_{L^p(\Omega)}+\|g\|_{L^q(\partial_2\Omega)}\right)\quad\text{a.e. in }\Omega

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear variational inequality induced by a bilinear form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bilinear-form variational inequality on a closed convex subset of a Hilbert space; excludes the extract's unsupported projection interpretation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $V$ be a Hilbert space, let $K\subset V$ be closed and convex, let $a:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ be a continuous bilinear form, and let $F\in V'$. The associated linear variational inequality is to find $w\in K$ such that
\[
a(w,v-w)\ge F(v-w)\qquad\text{for every }v\in K.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a closed convex set, a continuous bilinear form, and a continuous linear functional, the linear variational inequality seeks a point w in the set satisfying the variational inequality for every feasible comparison point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded-Truncation Criterion for Monotone Variational Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An equivalence between global solvability and the existence of an interior solution on some norm-bounded truncation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathbb K\subset X\) be closed and convex, and let \(A:\mathbb K\to X'\) be monotone and continuous on finite-dimensional subspaces. Define \(\mathbb K_R=\mathbb K\cap\{v\in X:\|v\|\le R\}\). The variational inequality \(u\in\mathbb K\), \(\langle Au,v-u\rangle\ge0\) for every \(v\in\mathbb K\), has a solution if and only if there exist \(R>0\) and a solution \(u_R\in\mathbb K_R\) of \(\langle Au_R,v-u_R\rangle\ge0\) for every \(v\in\mathbb K_R\) such that \(\|u_R\|<R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a monotone operator continuous on finite-dimensional subspaces, the variational inequality on a closed convex set is solvable exactly when some bounded truncation has a solution lying strictly inside its truncating ball.
assumptions_latex: \mathbb K\subset X\text{ is closed and convex}
A:\mathbb K\to X'\text{ is monotone and continuous on finite-dimensional subspaces}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists u\in\mathbb K\ \forall v\in\mathbb K:\langle Au,v-u\rangle\ge0\iff\exists R>0\ \exists u_R\in\mathbb K_R:\bigl[\forall v\in\mathbb K_R,\ \langle Au_R,v-u_R\rangle\ge0\bigr]\land\|u_R\|<R

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variational-inequality characterization of constrained minimizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order necessity for Gâteaux-differentiable minimization on a convex set, with convexity providing sufficiency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a real Banach space \(U\), and let \(f\) be real-valued and Gâteaux differentiable on an open set containing \(C\). If \(\bar u\in C\) minimizes \(f\) over \(C\), then \(f'(\bar u)(u-\bar u)\ge 0\) for all \(u\in C\). Conversely, if \(\bar u\in C\) satisfies this inequality and \(f\) is convex, then \(\bar u\) minimizes \(f\) over \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every constrained minimizer satisfies the derivative variational inequality. For a convex objective, the same inequality is sufficient for global optimality.
assumptions_latex: U\text{ is a real Banach space}
f\text{ is real-valued and Gâteaux differentiable on an open set containing }C
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar u\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in C}f(u)\Rightarrow f'(\bar u)(u-\bar u)\ge0\ \forall u\in C;\quad f\text{ convex and }f'(\bar u)(u-\bar u)\ge0\ \forall u\in C\Rightarrow\bar u\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in C}f(u)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support and density conditions from a first variation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary optimality condition for a regular minimizer of a functional on probability measures, with separate continuous and measurable first-variation cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathcal P(\Omega)\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), and suppose \(\rho_0\) minimizes \(F\), is regular for \(F\), and admits a first variation \(g=\frac{\delta F}{\delta\rho}(\rho_0)\). Set \(\ell=\operatorname*{ess\,inf}g\). If \(g\in C_0(\Omega)\), then \(g\ge \ell\) everywhere and \(\operatorname{spt}(\rho_0)\subseteq\operatorname{argmin}g=\{g=\ell\}\). If instead \(g\) is measurable and \(\rho_0\ll\mathcal L^d\), then \(g\ge\ell\) almost everywhere and \(g=\ell\) almost everywhere on \(\{\rho_0>0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a regular minimizing probability measure with an existing first variation, the first variation cannot fall below its essential infimum. When it is continuous and vanishes at infinity, the minimizer is supported on its minimizers; when it is merely measurable and the minimizing measure has a Lebesgue density, it equals its essential infimum almost everywhere wherever that density is positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g\in C_0(\Omega)\Rightarrow\bigl[g\ge\ell\ \text{everywhere and }\operatorname{spt}(\rho_0)\subseteq\{g=\ell\}=\operatorname{argmin}g\bigr];\quad \bigl[g\text{ measurable and }\rho_0\ll\mathcal L^d\bigr]\Rightarrow\bigl[g\ge\ell\ \text{a.e. and }g=\ell\ \text{a.e. on }\{\rho_0>0\}\bigr].

knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Correspondence Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotone, segment-hemicontinuous Hilbert-space correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(C\subseteq H\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(F:C\to H\). Assume that \(\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle\ge 0\) for every \(x,y\in C\), and that for every \(x,y\in C\) the map \(t\mapsto\langle F(x+t(y-x)),y-x\rangle\), defined for \(t\in[0,1]\), is right-continuous at \(t=0\). Then, for every \(x^*\in C\),
\[x^*\in\operatorname{SOL}_S(F,C)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x^*\in\operatorname{SOL}_M(F,C).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a monotone operator that is right-continuous along feasible segments, the Stampacchia and Minty solution sets coincide.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(C\subseteq H\) is nonempty and convex.
\(F:C\to H\) is monotone and right-continuous at the initial point of every segment in \(C\) in the stated scalar-pairing sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{SOL}_S(F,C)=\operatorname{SOL}_M(F,C)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Pseudomonotone Correspondence Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise pseudomonotonicity with segment hemicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(C\subseteq H\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(F:C\to H\). Assume that, for every \(x,y\in C\),
\[\langle F(x),y-x\rangle\ge0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\langle F(y),y-x\rangle\ge0,\]
and that the map \(t\mapsto\langle F(x+t(y-x)),y-x\rangle\), defined for \(t\in[0,1]\), is right-continuous at \(t=0\). Then, for every \(x^*\in C\),
\[x^*\in\operatorname{SOL}_S(F,C)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x^*\in\operatorname{SOL}_M(F,C).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a pointwise pseudomonotone operator that is right-continuous along feasible segments, the Stampacchia and Minty solution sets coincide.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(C\subseteq H\) is nonempty and convex.
\(F:C\to H\) satisfies the displayed pointwise pseudomonotonicity implication and segment right-continuity condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{SOL}_S(F,C)=\operatorname{SOL}_M(F,C)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(C=[0,1]\) and \(F(x)=1-2x\), direct evaluation of
\[F(x^*)(y-x^*)\ge0\qquad(y\in C)\]
gives \(\operatorname{SOL}_S(F,C)=\{0,\tfrac12,1\}\). In contrast, the Minty inequalities \(F(y)(y-x^*)\ge0\) force \(x^*\le0\) from \(y<\tfrac12\) and \(x^*\ge1\) from \(y>\tfrac12\), with incompatible endpoint inequalities; thus \(\operatorname{SOL}_M(F,C)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decreasing affine operator on an interval has three Stampacchia solutions but no Minty solution, showing that nonmonotonicity can separate the concepts.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(N_C(x)=\{v\in H:\langle v,y-x\rangle\le0\text{ for every }y\in C\}\) for \(x\in C\). Then \(x^*\in C\) solves the Stampacchia VI exactly when
\[0\in F(x^*)+N_C(x^*).\]
Because \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, this is also equivalent, for every \(\lambda>0\), to
\[x^*=P_C\bigl(x^*-\lambda F(x^*)\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a closed convex set, a VI is equivalently a normal-cone inclusion or a fixed point of a projected operator step.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection representation, exactness, and smoothness of the regularized gap function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fundamental properties of the regularized gap function and its associated maximizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed and convex, let \(F:\Omega\supseteq K\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuous on the open set \(\Omega\), let \(c>0\), and let \(G=G^T\succ0\). Then, for every \(x\in\Omega\), \[y_c(x)=\Pi_{K,G}\!\left(x-c^{-1}G^{-1}F(x)\right).\] Moreover, \(\theta_c\) is continuous on \(\Omega\), is nonnegative on \(K\), and \[x\in K:\quad \theta_c(x)=0\iff x\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F).\] If additionally \(F\in C^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^n)\), then \(\theta_c\in C^1(\Omega)\) and \[\nabla\theta_c(x)=F(x)+\bigl(JF(x)-cG\bigr)^T\bigl(x-y_c(x)\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regularized-gap maximizer is a metric projection. The gap is continuous, nonnegative on the feasible set, and vanishes there exactly at VI solutions. A continuously differentiable operator produces a continuously differentiable gap with the stated gradient.
assumptions_latex: K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is closed and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y_c(x)=\Pi_{K,G}(x-c^{-1}G^{-1}F(x));\quad \theta_c\in C(\Omega),\ \theta_c|_K\ge0;\quad [x\in K,\theta_c(x)=0]\iff x\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F);\quad F\in C^1\Rightarrow \theta_c\in C^1\text{ and }\nabla\theta_c(x)=F(x)+(JF(x)-cG)^T(x-y_c(x))

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Lipschitz continuity of the linearized VI auxiliary mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise local Lipschitz regularity of the auxiliary mapping and continuity of the associated merit function under Slater CQ.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\Omega\supset K\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuous on the open set \(\Omega\), and let \(K\) be defined by (10.2.10), where every \(g_i\) is convex and continuously differentiable on \(\Omega\). Fix \(c>0\) and a symmetric positive definite matrix \(G\). If Slater's constraint qualification holds for \(K\), then for every \(x\in\Omega\) there exist a neighborhood \(\mathcal N\subset\Omega\) of \(x\) and a constant \(\kappa>0\) such that \[\|y_c^{\operatorname{lin}}(x')-y_c^{\operatorname{lin}}(x)\|\leq\kappa\|x-x'\|\qquad\forall x'\in\mathcal N.\] Consequently, \(y_c^{\operatorname{lin}}\) and \(\theta_c^{\operatorname{lin}}\) are continuous on \(\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under Slater's constraint qualification, the linearized auxiliary mapping satisfies the stated local Lipschitz bound at every point of the ambient open set. It and the associated linearized merit function are continuous.

g_i\text{ is convex and }C^1\text{ on }\Omega\text{ for every }i

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero-value certificate for the linearized VI merit function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficiency, and Abadie-qualified necessity, of zero linearized merit value for a VI solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be defined by (10.2.10), where every \(g_i\) is convex and continuously differentiable on an open set \(\Omega\supset K\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stationary-point characterization for the VI merit problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence at a stationary point of the associated merit minimization problem; notation is retained from the extracted theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let K\subseteq\mathbb R^n be closed and convex, let F:\Omega\supseteq K\to\mathbb R^n be continuously differentiable on the open set \Omega, let c>0, and let G=G^T\succ0. If x is a stationary point of the associated merit problem (10.2.6), then the following are equivalent: (i) x\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F); (ii) T_c(x;K,F)\subseteq F(x)^\perp; (iii) for every d, \bigl[d\in T_c(x;K,F),\ JF(x)^Td\in-T_c(x;K,F)^*\bigr]\Rightarrow d^TF(x)=0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a stationary point of the associated VI merit problem, solving the VI is equivalent both to orthogonality of the relevant cone to the residual and to a stated cone-duality implication involving the Jacobian.
assumptions_latex: K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is closed and convex}
x\text{ is stationary for the associated problem }(10.2.6)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\iff T_c(x;K,F)\subseteq F(x)^\perp\iff \left(\forall d,\ [d\in T_c,\ JF(x)^Td\in-T_c^*]\Rightarrow d^TF(x)=0\right)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regularized gap function for a variational inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratically regularized VI gap function in a symmetric positive-definite metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the VI \((K,F)\) be given, with \(F\) defined on an open set \(\Omega\supseteq K\). For \(c>0\) and \(G=G^T\succ0\), its regularized gap function is \[\theta_c(x):=\sup_{y\in K}\left\{F(x)^T(x-y)-\frac{c}{2}(x-y)^TG(x-y)\right\},\qquad x\in\Omega.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regularized gap function is the supremum of the ordinary VI gap expression after subtracting a positive-definite quadratic regularization term.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coercivity of a regularized VI merit function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient asymptotic-positivity and parameter condition for coercivity of the regularized VI merit function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed and convex, let \(F:\Omega\supset K\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuous on the open set \(\Omega\), and suppose that some \(x^0\in K\) satisfies \[\eta:=\liminf_{\substack{x\in K\\ \|x\|\to\infty}}\frac{(F(x)-F(x^0))^T(x-x^0)}{\|x-x^0\|^2}>0.\] If \(G\) is symmetric positive definite and \(c>0\) satisfies \(c\|G\|<2\eta\), then \(\theta_c\) is coercive on \(K\): \[\lim_{\substack{x\in K\\ \|x\|\to\infty}}\theta_c(x)=+\infty.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the stated asymptotic positivity condition holds relative to a feasible reference point and c times the norm of G is less than twice the resulting constant, then the regularized VI merit function is coercive on K.
assumptions_latex: K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is closed and convex}
F:\Omega\supset K\to\mathbb R^n\text{ is continuous, with }\Omega\text{ open}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lim_{\substack{x\in K\\ \|x\|\to\infty}}\theta_c(x)=+\infty

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Copositivity conditions for exact and isolated VI solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consequences of Jacobian copositivity at a stationary point of the associated merit problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let K\subseteq\mathbb R^n be closed and convex, let F:\Omega\supseteq K\to\mathbb R^n be continuously differentiable on the open set \Omega, let c>0, let G=G^T\succ0, and suppose x is stationary for the associated merit problem (10.2.6). (a) If JF(x) is copositive on T_c(x;K,F), then x\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F) if and only if \mathcal K(T_c(x;K,F),JF(x))\subseteq F(x)^\perp. (b) If additionally (T_c(x;K,F),JF(x)) is an R_0 pair, then x\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F). (c) If JF(x) is strictly copositive on \mathcal T(x;K)\cap(-F(x))^*, then x is an isolated solution of \operatorname{VI}(K,F).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a stationary point of the merit problem, Jacobian copositivity yields a kernel-cone characterization of VI solutions; adding the R-zero property guarantees a solution, while strict copositivity on the specified tangent-dual intersection guarantees an isolated solution.
assumptions_latex: K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is closed and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}&JF(x)\text{ copositive on }T_c\Rightarrow\left[x\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\iff\mathcal K(T_c,JF(x))\subseteq F(x)^\perp\right];\\&JF(x)\text{ copositive on }T_c\ \land\ (T_c,JF(x))\text{ an }R_0\text{ pair}\Rightarrow x\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F);\\&JF(x)\text{ strictly copositive on }\mathcal T(x;K)\cap(-F(x))^*\Rightarrow x\text{ is an isolated VI solution.}\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.title: Box-Constrained VIs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite box with coordinatewise characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\in\mathbb N\), let \(C=\prod_{i=1}^n[\ell_i,u_i]\subset\mathbb R^n\), where \(-\infty<\ell_i<u_i<\infty\), and let \(F:C\to\mathbb R^n\). A point \(x^*\in C\) solves the Stampacchia variational inequality if and only if, for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\),
\[\begin{cases}F_i(x^*)\ge0,&x_i^*=\ell_i,\\F_i(x^*)=0,&\ell_i<x_i^*<u_i,\\F_i(x^*)\le0,&x_i^*=u_i.\end{cases}\]
These conditions are equivalent to \(0\in F(x^*)+N_C(x^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a finite box, each operator component is nonnegative at its lower bound, zero in the coordinate interior, and nonpositive at its upper bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\) solves the VI exactly when every coordinate satisfies the displayed bound-dependent sign condition.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The box has the polyhedral representation
\[C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:x_i\le u_i,
\ -x_i\le-\ell_i\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,n\}.\]
For \(x\in C\), its normal cone is
\[N_C(x)=\operatorname{cone}\bigl(\{e_i:x_i=u_i\}\cup\{-e_i:x_i=\ell_i\}\bigr).\]
Consequently, box-constrained VIs are polyhedral VIs whose active constraint normals are signed coordinate vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite box is a bounded polyhedron, and its normal cone is generated by signed coordinate vectors at active bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Cartesian-Product VIs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite Cartesian products of real Hilbert spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m\in\mathbb N\), let \(H_i\) be a real Hilbert space, and let \(C_i\subseteq H_i\) be nonempty for each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Equip \(H=H_1\times\cdots\times H_m\) with its canonical product inner product, set \(C=C_1\times\cdots\times C_m\), and let \(F=(F_1,\ldots,F_m):C\to H\). For \(x^*=(x_1^*,\ldots,x_m^*)\in C\),
\[\sum_{i=1}^m\langle F_i(x^*),y_i-x_i^*\rangle_{H_i}\ge0\qquad\text{for every }y=(y_1,\ldots,y_m)\in C\]
holds if and only if, for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\),
\[\langle F_i(x^*),z_i-x_i^*\rangle_{H_i}\ge0\qquad\text{for every }z_i\in C_i.\]
Each \(F_i(x^*)\) may depend on the full vector \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variational inequality on a finite Cartesian product of Hilbert spaces is equivalent to one inequality per block, while each block operator may depend on all blocks.
assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb N\), each \(H_i\) is a real Hilbert space, and each \(C_i\subseteq H_i\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The product-space VI holds exactly when every displayed component VI holds.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Surjectivity of a Monotone Coercive Operator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence of a solution to $Au=f$ for every dual-space right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $V$ be a reflexive Banach space and let $A:V\to V^*$ be weakly continuous on every finite-dimensional subspace and monotone. Assume that there exists $v_0\in V$ such that
\[
\frac{\langle Av,v-v_0\rangle}{\|v\|}\to+\infty\quad\text{as }\|v\|\to\infty.
\]
Then, for every $f\in V^*$, there exists $u\in V$ such that $Au=f$; equivalently, $A(V)=V^*$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone operator on a reflexive Banach space that has the stated finite-dimensional continuity and coercivity is surjective onto the dual space.
assumptions_latex: V\text{ is a reflexive Banach space}
A:V\to V^*\text{ is weakly continuous on every finite-dimensional subspace}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall f\in V^*\ \exists u\in V:\ Au=f

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The operator \(F\) is monotone on \(C\) when
\[\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle\ge0\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C.\]
This definition permits equality for distinct points; strict monotonicity instead requires a strict inequality whenever \(x\ne y\). No continuity, convexity of \(C\), or maximality is included in monotonicity itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operator is monotone when differences of its values have nonnegative inner product with the corresponding differences of points.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be a pointed, closed, convex cone and let F:K\to\mathbb{R}^n be continuous. Then
\[
\bigl[F\text{ is strictly monotone on }K\text{ and }\operatorname{FEA}(K,F)\neq\varnothing\bigr]
\Longleftrightarrow

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Solvability and error bounds for strictly and power-monotone VIs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates the strict-monotonicity uniqueness result, the power-monotonicity existence result, and the stronger domain assumptions required for the error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let K\subseteq\mathbb R^n be closed and convex, and let F:K\to\mathbb R^n be continuous. If F is strictly monotone on K, then \operatorname{VI}(K,F) has at most one solution. If F is \xi-monotone on K for some \xi>1, then \operatorname{VI}(K,F) has a unique solution x^*. If, further, F is defined, Lipschitz continuous, and \xi-monotone on a set \Omega\supseteq K, then there exists c'>0 such that \lVert x-x^*\rVert\le c'\lVert \mathbf F_K^{\mathrm{nat}}(x)\rVert^{1/(\xi-1)} for every x\in\Omega.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous strictly monotone VI operator gives at most one solution. Power monotonicity with exponent greater than one gives existence and uniqueness. If that power monotonicity and Lipschitz continuity hold on a containing set, distance to the unique solution is bounded by a constant times the natural-map residual raised to the reciprocal of xi minus one.
assumptions_latex: K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is closed and convex}
\text{For the error bound: }F\text{ is defined, Lipschitz continuous, and }\xi\text{-monotone on }\Omega\supseteq K
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ strictly monotone}\Rightarrow|\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)|\le1;\quad F\text{ \xi-monotone}\Rightarrow\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)=\{x^*\};\quad \lVert x-x^*\rVert\le c'\lVert\mathbf F_K^{\mathrm{nat}}(x)\rVert^{1/(\xi-1)}\ \forall x\in\Omega.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Separation of VI Solutions on Nested Convex Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A comparison theorem for classical variational inequalities posed on two nested feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K_2\subset K_1\subset\mathbb{R}^N\) be closed and convex, and let \(F:K_1\to(\mathbb{R}^N)'\) be continuous and strictly monotone. Suppose \(x_j\in K_j\) and \[\langle F(x_j),y-x_j\rangle\ge0\qquad\text{for every }y\in K_j,\quad j=1,2.\] If \(F(x_2)=0\), then \(x_1=x_2\). If \(F(x_2)\ne0\) and \(x_1\ne x_2\), then the hyperplane \[\langle F(x_2),y-x_2\rangle=0\] separates \(x_1\) from \(K_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For strictly monotone variational inequalities on nested closed convex sets, a zero operator value at the smaller-set solution forces the two solutions to coincide. If the operator value and the difference between the solutions are both nonzero, its associated hyperplane separates the larger-set solution from the smaller feasible set.

F:K_1\to(\mathbb{R}^N)'\text{ is continuous and strictly monotone}
x_j\in K_j,\ \langle F(x_j),y-x_j\rangle\ge0\ \forall y\in K_j,\quad j=1,2

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict and strong monotonicity on a set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines two monotonicity-strength regimes for a mapping on \(\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^m\). It is strictly monotone on \(\Omega\) if \[\langle F(v)-F(w),v-w\rangle>0\quad\text{for all }v,w\in\Omega\text{ with }v\ne w.\] It is strongly monotone on \(\Omega\) if there exists \(\alpha>0\) such that \[\langle F(v)-F(w),v-w\rangle\geq\alpha\lVert v-w\rVert^2\quad\text{for all }v,w\in\Omega.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict monotonicity requires a positive monotonicity pairing for every two distinct points of Ω. Strong monotonicity requires that pairing to dominate α times the squared distance for some α>0 and every pair of points in Ω.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is strictly monotone on }\Omega\iff\forall v,w\in\Omega,\ v\ne w:\ \langle F(v)-F(w),v-w\rangle>0;\quad F\text{ is strongly monotone on }\Omega\iff\exists\alpha>0\ \forall v,w\in\Omega:\ \langle F(v)-F(w),v-w\rangle\geq\alpha\lVert v-w\rVert^2\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Solution-set consequences of monotonicity for variational inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed convex feasible set and continuous finite-dimensional VI mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be closed and convex and let \(G:K\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuous. For the variational inequality solution set \(\operatorname{SOL}(G,K)\): (i) if \(G\) is monotone, then \(\operatorname{SOL}(G,K)\), when nonempty, is closed and convex; (ii) if \(G\) is strictly monotone, then \(|\operatorname{SOL}(G,K)|\le1\); (iii) if \(G\) is strongly monotone, then \(|\operatorname{SOL}(G,K)|=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous VI on a closed convex set, monotonicity makes every nonempty solution set closed and convex, strict monotonicity gives at most one solution, and strong monotonicity gives exactly one solution.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathcal H\) be nonempty, let \(T:D\to\mathcal H\), let \(\beta>0\), and let \(\gamma\in(0,2\beta)\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Co-coercivity and monotone-plus behavior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines co-coercivity on a subset of Euclidean space, states its monotone-plus consequence, and records the stated affine converse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A mapping \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is co-coercive on \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) if there exists \(c>0\) such that
\[
(F(x)-F(y))^\top(x-y)\ge c\lVert F(x)-F(y)\rVert_2^2\qquad\forall x,y\in S.
\]
Every co-coercive mapping is monotone-plus on \(S\):
\[
(F(x)-F(y))^\top(x-y)\ge0,
\]
and equality implies \(F(x)=F(y)\). Conversely, every affine mapping that is both monotone and symmetric is co-coercive on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mapping is co-coercive on a set when a positive constant times the squared distance between its values is bounded above by the corresponding monotonicity inner product. Co-coercivity implies monotonicity and the plus property. Conversely, an affine mapping that is monotone and symmetric is co-coercive on Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (F(x)-F(y))^\top(x-y)\ge c\lVert F(x)-F(y)\rVert_2^2;\quad F\text{ is monotone-plus on }S;\quad F\text{ affine, monotone, and symmetric}\Rightarrow F\text{ co-coercive on }\mathbb{R}^n.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Blockwise Convexity and Partial Subdifferentials of an Exact Potential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer of blockwise convexity and partial subdifferentials between an exact potential and player objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C=\prod_{i=1}^N C^i be convex, and let P be an exact potential for \{\zeta_i\}_{i=1}^N on C. Then P is blockwise convex on C if and only if, for every i and every x^{-i}\in C^{-i}, \zeta_i(\bullet,x^{-i}) is convex on C^i. Moreover, if P is blockwise convex on C and \operatorname{dom}P=\operatorname{dom}\zeta_i=C, then \partial_{x^i}P(x)=\partial_{x^i}\zeta_i(x) for every x\in C and every i.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an exact potential on a convex product set, the potential is blockwise convex exactly when each player's objective is convex in that player's own block. If the potential and player objective have common domain C, their corresponding partial subdifferentials coincide.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact and Generalized Potential Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Potential representations for player functions on a Cartesian strategy set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C=\prod_{i=1}^N C^i. A continuous function P:C\to\mathbb R is an exact potential for \{\zeta_i\}_{i=1}^N if, for all x,y,z\in C and every i, \zeta_i(y^i,x^{-i})-\zeta_i(z^i,x^{-i})=P(y^i,x^{-i})-P(z^i,x^{-i}). It is a generalized potential if it is continuous and, for every i, there is a forcing function \theta_i:\mathbb R_+\to\mathbb R_+ such that, for every sequence \{t_k\}\subseteq\mathbb R_+, \theta_i(t_k)\to0\Rightarrow t_k\to0, and \zeta_i(y^i,x^{-i})>\zeta_i(z^i,x^{-i}) implies P(y^i,x^{-i})-P(z^i,x^{-i})\geq\theta_i\!\left(\zeta_i(y^i,x^{-i})-\zeta_i(z^i,x^{-i})\right).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact potential reproduces each player's objective change under a unilateral change. A generalized potential turns every strict unilateral objective increase into a potential increase bounded below by a forcing function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The unilateral-difference identity defines an exact potential, and the forcing inequality defines a generalized potential.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rotation field as a canonical smooth nonpotential operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(F(x_1,x_2)=(-x_2,x_1)\), the Jacobian is
\[DF(x)=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\]
which is not symmetric. If \(F=\nabla\phi\) for some \(\phi\in C^2(\mathbb R^2)\), then \(DF=\nabla^2\phi\) would be symmetric. Therefore this smooth VI operator admits no twice continuously differentiable scalar potential.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine VI whose feasible set is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A conic affine variational inequality seeks \(x^\star\in K\) satisfying
\[
\langle Mx^\star+q,y-x^\star\rangle\ge 0\qquad\text{for every }y\in K.
\]
For the dual cone \(K^*=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle z,y\rangle\ge 0\text{ for every }y\in K\}\), this condition is equivalent to the conic complementarity system
\[
x^\star\in K,
\qquad Mx^\star+q\in K^*,
\qquad \langle x^\star,Mx^\star+q\rangle=0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic AVI is an affine VI on a closed convex cone, equivalently an affine conic complementarity system.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The affine field \(F(x)=Mx+q\) is monotone on \(C\) when
\[
\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle\ge0
\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C.
\]
Equivalently, it is monotone on \(C\) if and only if
\[
\langle Mz,z\rangle\ge0
\qquad\text{for every }z\in C-C.
\]
If monotonicity is required on all of \(\mathbb{R}^n\), this holds if and only if the symmetric part \(\tfrac12(M+M^\mathsf{T})\) is positive semidefinite, equivalently \(M+M^\mathsf{T}\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine field is monotone on the feasible set when its quadratic form is nonnegative on every feasible difference. Global monotonicity is equivalent to positive semidefiniteness of the symmetric part of its linear term, and the constant term has no effect.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotone AVIs

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent characterizations of nondegeneracy for monotone polyhedral AVIs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three-way equivalence among nondegeneracy, an invariant-based solution-set representation, and a linear gap-function error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a polyhedron, let \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be positive semidefinite, and assume \(\operatorname{SOL}(K,q,M)\neq\varnothing\). Let \(d\) and \(\sigma\) be the two invariants associated with the solutions of the AVI \((K,q,M)\). The following are equivalent: (a) the AVI \((K,q,M)\) has a nondegenerate solution; (b) \[\operatorname{SOL}(K,q,M)=\left\{x\in K:\omega(x)-(q+d)^Tx+\sigma\geq0\right\};\] (c) there exists \(L>0\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}\bigl(x,\operatorname{SOL}(K,q,M)\bigr)\leq L\theta_{\mathrm{gap}}(x),\qquad \forall x\in K.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a solvable monotone affine variational inequality over a polyhedron, existence of a nondegenerate solution, the stated invariant-based representation of the solution set, and a global linear gap-function error bound are equivalent.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Common invariants of monotone AVI solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantities constant across all solutions of a nonempty positive-semidefinite affine variational inequality, with a KKT identity in the polyhedral case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be closed and convex, let q\in\mathbb{R}^n, let M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} be positive semidefinite, and suppose \(\operatorname{SOL}(K,q,M)\neq\varnothing\). There exist d\in\mathbb{R}^n and \(\sigma\geq0\) such that every x\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,q,M) satisfies
\[
(M+M^T)x=d,\qquad x^TMx=\sigma.
\]
If additionally \(K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\leq b\}\) is polyhedral and \((x,\lambda)\) is any KKT pair of the AVI, then
\[
\sigma+q^Tx+b^T\lambda=0.
\]

assumptions_latex: \text{For the final identity: }K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\leq b\}\text{ and }(x,\lambda)\text{ is a KKT pair}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minty Weak-Limit Liminf Inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak-limit inequality for a monotone operator continuous on finite-dimensional subspaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $V$ be a reflexive Banach space and let $A:V\to V^*$ be monotone and weakly continuous on every finite-dimensional subspace of $V$. If $u_m\rightharpoonup u$ in $V$ and
\[
\limsup_m\langle Au_m,u_m-u\rangle\le0,
\]
then, for every $v\in V$,
\[
\liminf_m\langle Au_m,u_m-v\rangle\ge\langle Au,u-v\rangle.
\]

Under the transformed-point convention, an implicit variational inequality seeks \(x^\star\in X\) such that \(g(x^\star)\in C\) and
\[
\langle F(x^\star),y-g(x^\star)\rangle_H\ge0
\qquad\text{for every }y\in C.

\[
0\in F(x^\star)+N_C(g(x^\star)).
\]
The ordinary VI is recovered when \(X=H\) and \(g\) is the identity mapping.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Natural Map of a Quasi-Variational Inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the projection residual for a QVI with state-dependent closed convex feasible sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quasi-variational inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State-dependent feasible-set extension of a variational inequality, including the zero-field fixed-point specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) be a point-to-set map, possibly with empty values, and let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\). The quasi-variational inequality defined by \((K,F)\) is to find \(x\) such that \[x\in K(x),\qquad (y-x)^TF(x)\geq0\quad\forall y\in K(x).\] If \(F\equiv0\), it reduces to finding a fixed point \(x\in K(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quasi-variational inequality seeks a point feasible for its own state-dependent feasible set that satisfies the variational inequality over that set. With the zero field, it becomes a fixed-point problem for the set-valued map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in K(x)\ \text{and}\ (y-x)^TF(x)\geq0\ \forall y\in K(x);\qquad F\equiv0\Rightarrow x\in K(x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reference-Point Boundary Criterion for QVI Existence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Provides a QVI existence certificate based on a common feasible reference point and a boundary sign condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let K:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n be closed-valued, convex-valued, and nonempty-valued, and let F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n be continuous. Suppose there are a bounded open set \Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n and x^{\mathrm{ref}}\in\Omega such that: (i) \lim_{z\to\bar x}K(z)=K(\bar x) for every \bar x\in\operatorname{cl}\Omega; (ii) x^{\mathrm{ref}}\in K(x) for every x\in\operatorname{cl}\Omega; and (iii) \{x\in K(x):(x-x^{\mathrm{ref}})^TF(x)<0\}\cap\operatorname{bd}\Omega=\varnothing. Then the QVI (K,F) has a solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A QVI has a solution when its feasible sets vary continuously, share a reference point throughout the closed region, and no feasible boundary point has a strictly negative radial pairing with F.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\ne\varnothing

Let \(x\) be a control, let \((y,\mu,\lambda)\) solve the equilibrium problem, and let \((p,q,r)\) solve the adjoint problem. For a suitable \(M_i\),
\[
\begin{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The bifunction equilibrium problem associated with \(f\) and \(C\) is
\[
\text{find }x^\star\in C\text{ such that }f(x^\star,y)\ge0
\qquad\text{for every }y\in C.
\]
Thus its solution set is
\[
\operatorname{EP}(f,C)=\{x\in C:f(x,y)\ge0\text{ for every }y\in C\}.
\]
The normalization \(f(x,x)=0\) makes the comparison with the current point neutral and is part of the local convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An equilibrium point makes a scalar bifunction nonnegative against every feasible comparison point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selects pseudomonotonicity as the generalized monotonicity notion; terminology varies across sources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the pseudomonotone-bifunction convention, a generalized monotone equilibrium problem is the problem of finding \(x^\star\in C\) such that \(f(x^\star,y)\ge0\) for every \(y\in C\), where
\[
f(x,y)\ge0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(y,x)\le0
\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C.
\]
Ordinary monotonicity,
\[
f(x,y)+f(y,x)\le0
dot\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C,
\]
implies this pseudomonotonicity condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the selected convention, generalized monotonicity means pseudomonotonicity of the equilibrium bifunction; ordinary bifunction monotonicity is stronger.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke-NE representation as a generalized quasi-variational inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the playerwise and product-space GQVI characterization of Clarke-NE and defines general GQVI/GVI terminology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \Phi(x)=\prod_{i=1}^N\partial_{x^i}^{\mathrm C}\zeta_i(x) and \Xi_C(x)=\prod_{i=1}^N\Xi_C^i(x^{-i}). If every \Xi_C^i(\bar x^{-i}) is convex, then \bar x is a Clarke-NE if and only if, for every i, some a^i\in\partial_{x^i}^{\mathrm C}\zeta_i(\bar x) satisfies (a^i)^\top(x^i-\bar x^i)\ge0 for all x^i\in\Xi_C^i(\bar x^{-i}); equivalently, \bar x\in\Xi_C(\bar x) and some a\in\Phi(\bar x) satisfies a^\top(x-\bar x)\ge0 for all x\in\Xi_C(\bar x). More generally, for set-valued maps \Phi and \Psi, a GQVI seeks (\bar x,\bar y)\in\Psi(\bar x)\times\Phi(\bar x) such that \bar y^\top(x-\bar x)\ge0 for every x\in\Psi(\bar x). If \Psi is constant, the problem is a generalized variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With convex player feasible slices, a Clarke-NE is equivalent to a product-space generalized quasi-variational inequality whose operator is the product of the partial Clarke subdifferentials and whose feasible set depends on the candidate strategy. In general, a GQVI uses a set-valued operator and a state-dependent feasible map; it becomes a generalized VI when the feasible map is constant.
assumptions_latex: \Xi_C^i(\bar x^{-i})\text{ is convex for every }i\text{ in the Clarke-NE equivalence}
\Phi,\Psi\text{ are set-valued maps in the general GQVI definition}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar x\text{ is Clarke-NE}\iff\exists a\in\Phi(\bar x):\ \bar x\in\Xi_C(\bar x),\quad a^\top(x-\bar x)\ge0\ \forall x\in\Xi_C(\bar x);\qquad \Psi\text{ constant}\Longrightarrow\text{GQVI is a GVI}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact correspondence for the bifunction induced by a single-valued Hilbert-space operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the bifunction induced by \(F\) as
\[
f_F(x,y)=\langle F(x),y-x\rangle_H
\qquad\text{for }x,y\in C.
\]
Then \(f_F(x,x)=0\), and for every \(x^\star\in C\),
\[
\langle F(x^\star),y-x^\star\rangle_H\ge0\text{ for every }y\in C
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
f_F(x^\star,y)\ge0\text{ for every }y\in C.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{VI}(F,C)=\operatorname{EP}(f_F,C).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every single-valued VI is exactly an equilibrium problem for the bifunction formed by pairing the operator with feasible displacements.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variational inequality and elementary representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the defining inequality, global-normal inclusion, closedness boundary, and equation special cases stated in the extract; convexity of K is not assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For K\subseteq\mathbb R^n and F:K\to\mathbb R^n, \operatorname{VI}(K,F) asks for x\in K such that (y-x)^TF(x)\ge 0 for every y\in K; its solution set is \operatorname{SOL}(K,F). With \mathcal N(x;K):=\{d\in\mathbb R^n:d^T(y-x)\le0\ \forall y\in K\}, one has x\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F) iff 0\in F(x)+\mathcal N(x;K). If K is closed and F is continuous on an open neighborhood of K, then \operatorname{SOL}(K,F) is closed, though possibly empty. Moreover, \operatorname{SOL}(\mathbb R^n,F)=F^{-1}(0), and any x\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\cap\operatorname{int}K satisfies F(x)=0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-dimensional variational inequality seeks a point x in K whose operator value has nonnegative inner product with every feasible displacement. It is equivalently a global-normal-cone inclusion. For closed K and continuous F its solution set is closed but may be empty. On the whole space it is exactly the equation F(x)=0, and every interior VI solution is a zero of F. Convexity of K is not a blanket assumption.
assumptions_latex: \text{For solution-set closedness: }K\text{ is closed and }F\text{ is continuous on an open neighborhood of }K
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\iff (y-x)^TF(x)\ge0\ \forall y\in K\iff 0\in F(x)+\mathcal N(x;K);\quad K\text{ closed},\ F\text{ continuous}\Rightarrow\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\text{ closed};\quad \operatorname{SOL}(\mathbb R^n,F)=F^{-1}(0);\quad x\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\cap\operatorname{int}K\Rightarrow F(x)=0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: VI characterization, existence, and uniqueness of the constrained waterfilling equilibrium
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded four-part result using the model-specific feasible set, VI mapping, waterfilling maps, prices, and normalized interference factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the Nash-equilibrium problem \(\mathcal G_{\mathrm{VI}}\) with the model-defined set \(\mathcal K\) and mapping \(\mathbf F\). Its equilibria are exactly the vectors \(\mathbf p^\star\in\mathcal K\) satisfying \[(\mathbf p-\mathbf p^\star)^T\mathbf F(\mathbf p^\star)\geq0,\qquad\forall\mathbf p\in\mathcal K.\] This VI has a solution for every given set of channels, power budgets, and interference constraints. Given optimal prices \(\widehat\lambda\), the equilibrium allocation satisfies \[\mathbf p_q^\star(\widehat\lambda)=\operatorname{wf}_q(\mathbf p_{-q}^\star(\widehat\lambda);\widehat\lambda),\qquad\forall q\in\Omega.\] The allocation is unique if both \[\sum_{r\ne q}\max_k\left\{\frac{|H_{rq}(k)|^2}{|H_{qq}(k)|^2}\operatorname{innr}_{rq}(k)\right\}<1,\qquad\forall q\in\Omega,\] and \[\sum_{q\ne r}\max_k\left\{\frac{|H_{rq}(k)|^2}{|H_{qq}(k)|^2}\operatorname{innr}_{rq}(k)\right\}<1,\qquad\forall r\in\Omega.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The game's Nash equilibria coincide with the solutions of its variational inequality, and a solution always exists for the stated model data. At optimal prices, equilibrium powers satisfy coupled waterfilling fixed-point equations. The equilibrium allocation is unique when both stated low-received- and low-generated-interference conditions hold.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal G_{\mathrm{VI}},\ \mathcal K,\ \mathbf F,\ \operatorname{wf}_q,\text{ and }\operatorname{innr}_{rq}(k)\text{ are defined by the stated power-allocation model.}
\widehat\lambda\text{ is an optimal price vector for the fixed-point characterization.}
\text{The uniqueness conclusion assumes both strict inequalities in condition (C11).}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{NE}(\mathcal G_{\mathrm{VI}})=\operatorname{SOL}(\mathcal K,\mathbf F)\neq\varnothing;\quad \mathbf p_q^\star(\widehat\lambda)=\operatorname{wf}_q(\mathbf p_{-q}^\star(\widehat\lambda);\widehat\lambda)\ \forall q,\quad\text{and (C11) implies uniqueness of }\mathbf p^\star.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formulation interface only; stochastic approximation, sampling error, and convergence theory are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The expected-value stochastic VI seeks \(x^\star\in C\) such that
\[
\langle F(x^\star),y-x^\star\rangle\ge0
\qquad\text{for every }y\in C,
\quad
F(x)=\mathbb{E}[G(x,\xi)].
\]
Given samples \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_N\), its sample-average formulation replaces \(F\) by
\[
F_N(x)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N G(x,\xi_i)
\]
and solves the deterministic VI \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F_N)\). No assertion about consistency or sampling complexity is included.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stochastic VI applies the deterministic VI condition to an expected random field; sample-average models replace that expectation by an empirical mean.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a real Banach space, let \(C\subset X\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(F:C\to X^*\). The Banach-space variational inequality \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\) asks for \(\bar x\in C\) such that

\]

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed symmetric positive-definite metric in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the \(H\)-metric projection by \(P_C^H(u)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in C}\tfrac12\|y-u\|_H^2\). For every \(x\in C\) and \(\alpha>0\),
\[
x\in\operatorname{SOL}(C,F)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x=P_C^H\bigl(x-\alpha H^{-1}F(x)\bigr).
\]
The weighted projection condition is \(\langle H(x-u),y-x\rangle\ge0\) for every \(y\in C\). Substitution of \(u=x-\alpha H^{-1}F(x)\) reduces it to \(\langle F(x),y-x\rangle\ge0\) for every \(y\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The VI is equivalently a fixed-point equation for projection in any fixed positive-definite metric, with the operator step scaled by the inverse metric.
knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Metric Projection Representation

Define \(T:C\to C\) by \(T(x)=P_C(x-\alpha F(x))\) and set \(q=\sqrt{1-2\alpha\mu+\alpha^2L^2}\). Then \(0\le q<1\) and
\[
\|T(x)-T(y)\|\le q\|x-y\|\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C.
\]
The map \(T\) has a unique fixed point \(x^*\in C\), which is the unique solution of \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\). Moreover, for every \(x^0\in C\), the iteration \(x^{k+1}=T(x^k)\) satisfies
\[
\|x^k-x^*\|\le q^k\|x^0-x^*\|.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the strongly monotone and Lipschitz Euclidean regime, a suitable projected forward step is contractive, has the unique VI solution as its fixed point, and converges globally at a linear rate bounded by its contraction factor.
knowledge_statements.title: Contractive Fixed-Point Regime

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Averaged-operator regime without a strict contraction assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(F\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive, meaning
\[
\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle\ge\beta\|F(x)-F(y)\|^2
\]
for all \(x,y\in C\). For \(0<\alpha<2\beta\), the forward map \(I-\alpha F\) is averaged, and its composition with the firmly nonexpansive projection \(P_C\) is averaged. Hence \(T=P_C\circ(I-\alpha F)\) is nonexpansive but need not have Lipschitz modulus strictly below one. Nevertheless,
\[
\operatorname{Fix}T=\operatorname{SOL}(C,F).
\]
Thus fixed-point algorithms based on averagedness apply even when Banach contraction theory does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cocoercivity makes the projected forward map averaged and nonexpansive; its fixed points remain exactly the VI solutions even without strict contraction.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(N_C(x)=\{v\in H:\langle v,y-x\rangle\le0\text{ for every }y\in C\}\) for \(x\in C\), and \(N_C(x)=\varnothing\) otherwise. Then
\[
x\in\operatorname{SOL}(C,F)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
-F(x)\in N_C(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
0\in F(x)+N_C(x).
\]
Thus the feasible-set constraint and all VI test inequalities are encoded by the normal-cone operator. The equivalence is algebraic and does not require monotonicity of \(F\); monotonicity becomes relevant to the properties and solution methods of the resulting inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The VI is exactly the zero-inclusion problem obtained by adding the feasible set's normal cone to the original operator.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\gamma>0\), define the resolvent \(J_{\gamma A}=(I+\gamma A)^{-1}\). Then
\[
0\in A(x)+B(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x=J_{\gamma A}\bigl(x-\gamma B(x)\bigr).
\]
A constrained VI is recovered by taking \(A=N_C\) and \(B=F\), in which case \(J_{\gamma N_C}=P_C\). More generally, choosing \(A=\partial g+N_C\) separates nonsmooth and constraint structure from the explicit field \(B\). The equivalence itself requires only the resolvent definition; additional cocoercivity or Lipschitz assumptions govern convergence of forward-backward iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Splitting the VI operator into implicit and explicit parts turns its zero inclusion into a resolvent fixed-point equation suitable for operator splitting.
knowledge_statements.title: Structured Operator-Sum Reformulation

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\alpha>0\), define the natural map on \(\mathbb R^n\) by
\[
R_\alpha(x)=x-P_C\bigl(x-\alpha F(x)\bigr).
\]
Then
\[
R_\alpha(x)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x=P_C\bigl(x-\alpha F(x)\bigr)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x\in\operatorname{SOL}(C,F).
\]
In particular, any zero is automatically feasible because it equals a point in the range of \(P_C\). Thus the constrained variational inequality is represented by the unconstrained nonsmooth equation \(R_\alpha(x)=0\), and \(\|R_\alpha(x)\|\) is a residual vanishing exactly at solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting the projected forward step from the current point gives a natural residual whose zeros coincide exactly with VI solutions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unscaled Euclidean normal map for a polyhedral feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the normal map
\[
F_C(z)=F(P_Cz)+z-P_Cz,
\qquad z\in\mathbb R^n.
\]
If \(F_C(z)=0\) and \(x=P_Cz\), then \(z-x=-F(x)\in N_C(x)\), so \(x\in\operatorname{SOL}(C,F)\). Conversely, if \(x\) solves the VI, then \(z=x-F(x)\) satisfies \(P_Cz=x\) and \(F_C(z)=0\). For polyhedral \(C\), the projection \(P_C\) is piecewise affine on a finite polyhedral subdivision. Consequently, when \(F\) is affine, the normal map \(F_C\) is piecewise affine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polyhedral normal map converts the VI into an equation; affine fields yield a piecewise-affine equation because projection onto a polyhedron is piecewise affine.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Normal Maps

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a parameter \(\rho>0\), define
\[
F_{C,\rho}(z)=F(P_Cz)+\rho^{-1}(z-P_Cz).
\]
If \(F_{C,\rho}(z)=0\) and \(x=P_Cz\), then \(z-x=-\rho F(x)\in N_C(x)\), because the normal cone is positively homogeneous; hence \(x\) solves \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\). Conversely, if \(x\) solves the VI, then \(z=x-\rho F(x)\) satisfies \(P_Cz=x\) and \(F_{C,\rho}(z)=0\). Thus every positive scaling preserves the solution correspondence while changing the equation's scaling and potentially its numerical conditioning.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(p\in P\) and \(z\in\mathbb R^n\), the parametric normal map associated with \(F\) and \(C\) is
\[
M(p,z):=F\bigl(p,\Pi_{C(p)}z\bigr)+z-\Pi_{C(p)}z.
\]
Writing \(x:=\Pi_{C(p)}z\), the projection characterization gives \(z-x\in N_{C(p)}(x)\). Consequently,
\[
M(p,z)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
-F(p,x)\in N_{C(p)}(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\langle F(p,x),y-x\rangle\geq0\quad\text{for every }y\in C(p).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameterized VI is equivalent to finding a zero of the normal map formed from its field and the projector onto its parameterized feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Parametric Normal Maps

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The variational inequality
\[
\langle \nabla f(x^*),x-x^*\rangle\geq0\quad\text{for every }x\in C
\]
is equivalent to \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\). Under the stated constraint qualification, this is further equivalent to the existence of multipliers \(\lambda_i\geq0\) and \(\mu_j\in\mathbb R\) such that
\[
\nabla f(x^*)+\sum_i\lambda_i\nabla g_i(x^*)+\sum_j\mu_j\nabla h_j(x^*)=0,
\quad g_i(x^*)\leq0,
\quad h_j(x^*)=0,
\quad \lambda_i g_i(x^*)=0.
\]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
C:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_i(x)\leq0\ (i=1,\ldots,q),\ h_j(x)=0\ (j=1,\ldots,r)\}.
\]
A point \(x^*\in C\) solves \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\) if and only if there exist \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^q\) and \(\mu\in\mathbb R^r\) such that
\[
F(x^*)+\sum_{i=1}^q\lambda_i\nabla g_i(x^*)+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\nabla h_j(x^*)=0,
\qquad
\lambda_i g_i(x^*)=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,q).
\]
Primal feasibility is expressed by \(x^*\in C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Obstacle variational inequality as constrained energy minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of the elliptic obstacle variational inequality and a strictly convex quadratic minimization problem, together with uniqueness and the stated regularity conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q\in[2,\infty)\), let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2\) be nonempty, bounded, open, and have sufficiently smooth boundary, let \(g\in W^{2,q}(\Omega)\) satisfy \(g\le 0\) on \(\partial\Omega\), and let \(f\in L^q(\Omega)\). Let \(a:H_0^1(\Omega)\times H_0^1(\Omega)\to\mathbb R\) be a bounded symmetric bilinear form satisfying \(a(z,z)\ge \nu\lVert z\rVert_{H_0^1}^2\) for every \(z\in H_0^1(\Omega)\), where \(\nu>0\). Define \(\mathcal F=\{z\in H_0^1(\Omega):z\ge g\text{ on }\Omega\}\) and \(J(z)=\tfrac12a(z,z)-(f,z)_{L^2}\). Then \(y\in\mathcal F\) satisfies \(a(y,v-y)-(f,v-y)_{L^2}\ge0\) for every \(v\in\mathcal F\) if and only if \(y\) minimizes \(J\) over \(\mathcal F\). Since \(\mathcal F\) is closed and convex and \(J\) is strictly convex and coercive, the problem has a unique solution \(\bar y\). Under the elliptic regularity result invoked for these data and coefficients, \(\bar y\in H_0^1(\Omega)\cap W^{2,q}(\Omega)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The elliptic obstacle variational inequality is equivalent to minimizing its quadratic energy over the closed convex obstacle set. Ellipticity makes the energy strictly convex and coercive, yielding a unique solution; the invoked elliptic regularity result gives W^{2,q} regularity.
assumptions_latex: \varnothing\ne\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2\text{ is bounded and open with sufficiently smooth boundary}
a:H_0^1(\Omega)\times H_0^1(\Omega)\to\mathbb R\text{ is bounded, symmetric, and }a(z,z)\ge\nu\lVert z\rVert_{H_0^1}^2\ \forall z\in H_0^1(\Omega)\text{ for some }\nu>0
\mathcal F=\{z\in H_0^1(\Omega):z\ge g\text{ on }\Omega\}\text{ is closed and convex}
\text{The elliptic regularity result cited in the source applies to the stated domain, coefficients, and data}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y\text{ solves the obstacle VI}\iff y\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in\mathcal F}J(z),\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in\mathcal F}J(z)=\{\bar y\},\qquad \bar y\in H_0^1(\Omega)\cap W^{2,q}(\Omega).

assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) are nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\) is continuously differentiable, convex in \(x\), and concave in \(y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A pair is a saddle point of \(L\) exactly when it solves the VI on \(X\times Y\) with field \((\nabla_xL,-\nabla_yL)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional convex-concave saddle problems.

source_refs.locator: I.5 Some Problems Which Lead to Variational Inequalities p. 15

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A pair \((x^*,y^*)\in X\times Y\) is a saddle point when
\[
L(x^*,y)\leq L(x^*,y^*)\leq L(x,y^*)
\quad\text{for every }(x,y)\in X\times Y.
\]
Under convexity-concavity, this is equivalent to
\[
\left\langle\nabla_xL(x^*,y^*),x-x^*\right\rangle
-\left\langle\nabla_yL(x^*,y^*),y-y^*\right\rangle\geq0
\quad\text{for every }(x,y)\in X\times Y,
\]
which is \(\operatorname{VI}(X\times Y,F)\) for \(F(x,y):=(\nabla_xL(x,y),-\nabla_yL(x,y))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth convex-concave saddle point is precisely a VI solution for the primal gradient and negative dual gradient on the product set.

notation.meaning: Nonconvex objective used in the boundary example

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of converse first-order reductions without convexity-concavity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the unconstrained problem with
\[
f(x):=(x^2-1)^2,
\qquad \nabla f(x)=4x(x^2-1).
\]
The point \(x^*=0\) satisfies the associated variational inequality on \(\mathbb R\), because \(\nabla f(0)=0\). Nevertheless, \(f(0)=1\) while \(f(1)=f(-1)=0\), and \(x^*=0\) is a strict local maximum. Hence a first-order VI, KKT, or degenerate saddle representation is not equivalent to global optimization after convexity is removed. Analogously, without convexity in the primal variable and concavity in the dual variable, saddle-gradient VI solutions need not satisfy the global saddle inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without convexity-concavity, first-order VI or saddle systems may admit stationary points that are neither minimizers nor saddle points.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimization-to-Saddle Reduction Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample correctly demonstrates failure of the optimization-to-VI converse without convexity, but the record supplies no inspectable source for the broader optimization-to-saddle boundary claim.

knowledge_statements.title: Nash Equilibria as VIs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional differentiable convex games with uncoupled feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X:=\prod_{i=1}^N X_i\) and define
\[
F(x):=\bigl(\nabla_{x_1}J_1(x),\ldots,\nabla_{x_N}J_N(x)\bigr).
\]
A profile \(x^*\in X\) is a Nash equilibrium,
\[
J_i(x_i^*,x_{-i}^*)\leq J_i(x_i,x_{-i}^*)
\quad\text{for every }x_i\in X_i\text{ and }i=1,\ldots,N,
\]
if and only if
\[
\langle F(x^*),x-x^*\rangle\geq0
