knowledge_statements.statement_title: Radial coercivity implies surjectivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A global range theorem for continuous self-maps of finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \Phi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n be continuous. If \lim_{\|x\|\to\infty}\frac{x^T\Phi(x)}{\|x\|}=+\infty, then \Phi(\mathbb R^n)=\mathbb R^n.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous self-map of Euclidean space is surjective if its radial pairing with x, divided by the norm of x, tends to positive infinity at infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Phi(\mathbb R^n)=\mathbb R^n.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exceptional Set \(\mathcal L(M)\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-dimensional exceptional strata of the complementary-cone set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$. For $n>2$, let $\mathscr S(M)$ contain every subspace of the form $\{C_M(\alpha)_{\bullet\beta}x:x\in\mathbb R^{n-2}\}$ with $|\beta|=n-2$, together with every intersection of two geometrically distinct subspaces of the form $\{C_M(\alpha)_{\bullet\beta}x:x\in\mathbb R^{n-1}\}$ with $|\beta|=n-1$. Define $\mathcal L(M)=\mathcal K(M)\cap\bigcup_{S\in\mathscr S(M)}S$. For $n=1$, set $\mathcal L(M)=\varnothing$, and for $n=2$, set $\mathcal L(M)=\{0\}$. When $n>2$, $\mathcal L(M)$ is contained in a finite union of subspaces of dimension at most $n-2$ and contains the nonnegative parts of the coordinate axes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For dimensions above two, L(M) is the portion of K(M) lying in subspaces generated by codimension-two complementary-cone faces or by intersections of distinct facet hulls. It is empty for n=1, equals {0} for n=2, and for n>2 lies in finitely many subspaces of dimension at most n−2 while containing the nonnegative coordinate rays.
assumptions_latex: |\beta|=n-1\text{ for each subspace in the second family}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal L(M)=\begin{cases}\varnothing,&n=1,\\\{0\},&n=2,\\\mathcal K(M)\cap\displaystyle\bigcup_{S\in\mathscr S(M)}S,&n>2,\end{cases}\qquad \mathcal L(M)\subseteq\bigcup_{j=1}^{N}S_j,\ \dim S_j\le n-2\ (n>2).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(t\in[0,1]\), let \(H_t(x)=H(x,t)\). If \(H_t(x)\neq0\) for every \((x,t)\in\partial\Omega\times[0,1]\), then every degree \(\deg(H_t,\Omega,0)\) is defined and is independent of \(t\). Hence a computable nonzero degree at \(t=0\) transfers to \(t=1\), forcing a zero of \(H_1\) in \(\Omega\). When each \(H_t\) is a VI residual, that zero is a solution of the terminal variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous deformation that never creates a boundary zero preserves degree, so a nonzero degree for a simple VI transfers to the target VI.

children.top_down_role: Regimes where boundary behavior fails to preserve an admissible homotopy.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Brouwer-degree homotopy invariance at the value \(0\) requires \(0\notin H(\partial\Omega\times[0,1])\). If \(H(x_b,t_b)=0\) for some \((x_b,t_b)\in\partial\Omega\times[0,1]\), then \(H\) is not an admissible degree homotopy on the full parameter interval, and degrees on opposite sides of \(t_b\) cannot be identified solely by the standard homotopy-invariance principle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard degree-continuation argument becomes inadmissible when the homotopy has a zero on the domain boundary, so degrees across that parameter cannot be equated automatically.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Geometry and Degree Change Across a Facet Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local behavior at a nondegenerate path intersection with the complementary-cone critical set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let M\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}, \alpha\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}, i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}, and let q^t:[0,1]\to\mathbb R^n have a nondegenerate intersection q^s\in\operatorname{pos}C_M(\alpha)_{\cdot\bar i} with \mathcal K(M), where s\in(0,1). Let H, \delta, and the two open hemiballs B^+,B^- be the associated local objects, and let (\beta_k,j_k) describe the facet family around q^s. Each full endpoint cone contains exactly one hemiball and is disjoint from the other; every degenerate cone meets B(q^s,\delta) exactly in B(q^s,\delta)\cap H. For a proper family, the two full endpoint cones contain opposite hemiballs; for a reflecting family, they contain the same hemiball. If the family is not absorbing, its total local-degree contribution is constant on B^+\cup B^-; if it is absorbing, that contribution is separately constant on each hemiball and differs by one between them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a nondegenerate crossing, full endpoint cones occupy whole sides of the separating hyperplane while degenerate cones lie locally in it. Proper and reflecting families have different side-incidence patterns. A nonabsorbing family has constant total local-degree contribution across both sides; for an absorbing family the two side values differ by one.
assumptions_latex: q^s\in\operatorname{pos}C_M(\alpha)_{\cdot\bar i}\cap\mathcal K(M)\text{ is a nondegenerate path intersection}
H,\delta,B^+,B^-\text{ are the associated local hyperplane, radius, and hemiballs}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Full and degenerate cones have the stated local incidence with }B^\pm\text{ and }H;\text{ proper and reflecting families have the stated side patterns; nonabsorbing families have constant contribution on }B^+\cup B^-;\text{ and absorbing-family contributions differ by }1\text{ between the hemiballs.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization under total nondegeneracy and pointedness of the complementary-column cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be totally nondegenerate and suppose \(\operatorname{pos}(I,-M)\) is pointed. Then \[M\in\mathbf Q_0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \bigcup\{[A]:[A]\text{ is a complementary simplex relative to }M\}=[I,-M].\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Distinctly labelled column sets and complementary simplices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions relative to a fixed matrix \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}\) be a submatrix of \((I,-M)\). The simplex \([A]\) is distinctly labelled if, for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(A\) does not contain both \(I_{\cdot i}\) and \(-M_{\cdot i}\). If additionally \(k=n\), then a distinctly labelled \([A]\) is a complementary simplex relative to \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simplex generated by columns selected from I and −M is distinctly labelled when no index contributes both its identity column and its corresponding negative M-column. When exactly n columns are selected, such a simplex is a complementary simplex relative to M.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}\text{ is a submatrix of }(I,-M)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: [A]\text{ is distinctly labelled}\iff\forall i\in\{1,\ldots,n\},\ \{I_{\cdot i},-M_{\cdot i}\}\nsubseteq\operatorname{cols}(A);\quad k=n\Rightarrow [A]\text{ is complementary relative to }M.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Adjacency Relation on Complementary Simplices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines when two simplices in the restricted complementary complex are related through identical restricted indices or a chain of admissible shared facets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), \(n\ge 3\), be totally nondegenerate, let \(\operatorname{pos}(I,-M)\) be pointed, and suppose all facets of \([I,-M]\) are distinctly labeled. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degree Law for Principal Pivotal Transforms of R0 Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States class preservation and the signed degree transformation under a nonsingular principal pivot block.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence and Classification of a Facet Family Around a Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complementary-cone facets associated with an LCP matrix and a point outside the exceptional set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let M\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}, q\in\mathbb R^n, \alpha\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}, and i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}, with q\in\operatorname{pos}C_M(\alpha)_{\cdot\bar i}\setminus\mathcal L(M). Then for some m\ge0 there are indices j_0,\ldots,j_m and sets \beta_0,\ldots,\beta_{m+1} such that \beta_k\triangle\beta_{k+1}=\{j_k\}, consecutive j_k are distinct, every intermediate cone \operatorname{pos}C_M(\beta_k) is weakly degenerate, each traversed facet has dimension n-1 and contains q, and (\alpha,i)=(\beta_k,j_k) for some k. Exactly one endpoint regime occurs: equal-sign nonzero endpoint determinants, opposite-sign endpoint determinants, one full and one strongly degenerate endpoint cone, two strongly degenerate endpoint cones, or a closed weakly degenerate cycle with \beta_0=\beta_{m+1} and j_0\ne j_m. All \beta_k are distinct except for the stated cyclic repetition. In the first four regimes the sequences are unique; in the cyclic regime they are unique after fixing (\alpha,i)=(\beta_0,j_0).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every eligible complementary-cone facet containing q belongs to a finite adjacent facet chain through weakly degenerate cones. The chain has exactly one of five endpoint types, has no repeated index set except when cyclic, and is unique, with the cyclic case requiring a specified starting facet.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists m\ge0,\ (j_k)_{k=0}^m,\ (\beta_k)_{k=0}^{m+1}\text{ satisfying (a)--(e), exactly one of endpoint cases (1)--(5), the stated distinctness, and the stated uniqueness conditions.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Restricted Property of a Pseudomanifold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines restrictions of a pseudomanifold by fixing a vertex subset and the condition that every such restriction remains a pseudomanifold of the expected dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be an \(n\)-dimensional pseudomanifold on a vertex set \(V\). For \(S\subseteq V\), define \[P(S)=\{S'\subseteq V\setminus S:S\cup S'\in P\}.\] The pseudomanifold \(P\) has the restricted property if, for every \(S\subseteq V\), \(P(S)\) is a possibly empty \((n-|S|)\)-dimensional pseudomanifold; each \(P(S)\) is then called a restricted pseudomanifold of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given an n-dimensional pseudomanifold P on V, its restriction at S consists of the subsets of V outside S whose union with S is a face of P. The pseudomanifold has the restricted property when every such restriction is possibly empty but otherwise has dimension n minus the size of S and is itself a pseudomanifold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P(S)=\{S'\subseteq V\setminus S:S\cup S'\in P\},\quad P\text{ has the restricted property}\iff \forall S\subseteq V,\ P(S)\text{ is a possibly empty }(n-|S|)\text{-dimensional pseudomanifold}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward preservation of complementary-cone types, exceptional-set membership, and facet classes under a principal pivotal transform.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between endpoint degree parity, endpoint solution-count parity, and parity of degeneracy events along an LCP path.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reference-Point Level-Set and Boundary Criteria for VI Solvability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preserves the separate existential quantifiers in the implication chain and the stronger compactness conclusion under bounded nonpositive level sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let K\subseteq\mathbb R^n be closed and convex and let F:K\to\mathbb R^n be continuous. For x^{\mathrm{ref}}\in K, define L_{<}(x^{\mathrm{ref}}):=\{x\in K:F(x)^T(x-x^{\mathrm{ref}})<0\} and L_{\leq}(x^{\mathrm{ref}}):=\{x\in K:F(x)^T(x-x^{\mathrm{ref}})\leq0\}. If L_{<}(x^{\mathrm{ref}}) is bounded for some x^{\mathrm{ref}}\in K, then there exist a bounded open set \Omega and y^{\mathrm{ref}}\in K\cap\Omega such that F(x)^T(x-y^{\mathrm{ref}})\geq0 for all x\in K\cap\operatorname{bd}\Omega. This boundary condition implies \operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\neq\varnothing. Moreover, if L_{\leq}(x^{\mathrm{ref}}) is bounded for some x^{\mathrm{ref}}\in K, then \operatorname{SOL}(K,F) is nonempty and compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous VI on a closed convex set, boundedness of a strict negative reference-point level set yields an outward boundary condition on a bounded region, and that boundary condition guarantees a solution. Boundedness of the corresponding nonpositive level set guarantees that the solution set is nonempty and compact.
assumptions_latex: K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is closed and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[\exists x^{\mathrm{ref}}\in K:\ L_{<}(x^{\mathrm{ref}})\text{ is bounded}\bigr]\Rightarrow\bigl[\exists\Omega\text{ bounded open},\ \exists y^{\mathrm{ref}}\in K\cap\Omega:\ F(x)^T(x-y^{\mathrm{ref}})\geq0\ \forall x\in K\cap\operatorname{bd}\Omega\bigr]\Rightarrow\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\neq\varnothing;\quad \bigl[\exists x^{\mathrm{ref}}\in K:\ L_{\leq}(x^{\mathrm{ref}})\text{ is bounded}\bigr]\Rightarrow\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\text{ is nonempty and compact}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence, Uniqueness, and Lipschitz Stability for a Coercive Variational Inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coercive bilinear variational inequalities on closed convex subsets of a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $H$ be a Hilbert space, $K\subset H$ be closed and convex, and $a:H\times H\to\mathbb{R}$ be a coercive bilinear form with coercivity constant $\alpha>0$. For every $f\in H'$, there exists a unique $u\in K$ such that $a(u,v-u)\geq\langle f,v-u\rangle$ for all $v\in K$. If $u_i$ corresponds to $f_i\in H'$ for $i=1,2$, then $\|u_1-u_2\|\leq \alpha^{-1}\|f_1-f_2\|_{H'}$. If $K$ is a linear subspace of $H$, the solution map $f\mapsto u$ is linear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coercive bilinear variational inequality on a closed convex subset of a Hilbert space has a unique solution for every continuous linear functional. The solution depends Lipschitz-continuously on the functional with constant 1/alpha, and the solution map is linear when the constraint set is a subspace.
assumptions_latex: K\subset H\text{ is closed and convex}
a\text{ is bilinear and coercive with }a(v,v)\geq\alpha\|v\|^2\text{ for some }\alpha>0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists!u\in K\ \forall v\in K:\ a(u,v-u)\geq\langle f,v-u\rangle,\qquad \|u_1-u_2\|\leq\alpha^{-1}\|f_1-f_2\|_{H'};\quad K\text{ linear}\Rightarrow(f\mapsto u)\text{ linear}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The fifth condition retains the extract's dependency on the five map conditions designated in its referenced preceding theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be polyhedral, \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), and let \(f\) be either \(\mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{nor}}_K\) or \(\mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{nat}}_K\). The following are equivalent: (a) \(f\) is bijective; (b) for every \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(\operatorname{AVI}(K,q,M)\) has a unique solution; (c) \(f\) is coherently oriented; (d) for every \(q^\infty\in\mathcal R(K,M)\) and every sequence \(q^k\to q^\infty\), one has \(q^k\in\mathcal R(K,M)\) for all sufficiently large \(k\); (e) any one of the five equivalent conditions (a)--(e) specified for \(f\) in Theorem 4.2.11 holds. Whenever these conditions hold, the unique AVI solution is a piecewise-affine, hence B-differentiable, function of \(q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a polyhedral set K, the normal or natural map is bijective exactly when every right-hand side produces a unique AVI solution, exactly when the map is coherently oriented, exactly when the AVI range has the stated eventual-sequence stability, and exactly when any of the five referenced equivalent map conditions holds. Under these conditions, the unique solution depends piecewise affinely, and therefore B-differentiably, on q.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Conditions (a)--(e) are equivalent, and they imply that }q\mapsto x(q)\text{ is piecewise affine and B-differentiable}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representative matrix-class theorem: the global P-matrix property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matrix \(M\) is a P-matrix when every principal minor of \(M\) is positive. If \(M\) has this property, then for every \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\) there exists a unique pair \((x,w)\) satisfying \[x\,\geq0,\qquad w=Mx+q\,\geq0,\qquad x^{\mathsf T}w=0.\] Equivalently, the variational inequality on \(\mathbb{R}^n_+\) with affine map \(x\mapsto Mx+q\) has exactly one solution for every right-hand side \(q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A P-matrix guarantees that every associated linear complementarity problem, equivalently every orthant affine VI, has a unique solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Class Existence

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence and boundedness for a nonlinear complementarity problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonlinear complementarity problems with a positive-semidefinite linear term and a continuous nonlinear perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let h:\mathbb{R}_+^n\to\mathbb{R}^n be continuous, let M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} be positive semidefinite, and let q\in\mathbb{R}^n. The problem 0\le x\perp q+Mx+h(x)\ge0 has a nonempty bounded solution set if either (a) x^Th(x)\ge0 for every x\in\mathbb{R}_+^n, M is positive semidefinite plus, and there exists z\in\mathbb{R}^n such that q+Mz>0; or (b) \lim_{\substack{x\ge0\\\|x\|\to\infty}}\frac{x^Th(x)}{\|x\|}=+\infty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonlinear complementarity problem has a nonempty bounded solution set under either the stated positive-semidefinite-plus condition together with nonnegativity of the nonlinear pairing and strict feasibility, or the stated coercivity condition.
assumptions_latex: \left[(\forall x\in\mathbb{R}_+^n,\ x^Th(x)\ge0)\land(M\text{ is positive semidefinite plus})\land(\exists z\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ q+Mz>0)\right]\lor\left[\lim_{\substack{x\ge0\\\|x\|\to\infty}}\frac{x^Th(x)}{\|x\|}=+\infty\right]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x\in\mathbb{R}_+^n:0\le x\perp q+Mx+h(x)\ge0\}\text{ is nonempty and bounded}

knowledge_statements.title: Browder–Minty Surjectivity Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coercive Browder–Minty route for constrained variational inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a real reflexive Banach space, let \(K\subseteq X\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(A:X\to X^*\) be monotone, hemicontinuous, and bounded on bounded sets. Suppose that for some \(u_0\in K\), \[\frac{\langle Au,u-u_0\rangle}{\lVert u\rVert}\longrightarrow +\infty\quad\text{as }u\in K,\ \lVert u\rVert\to\infty.\] Then, for every \(f\in X^*\), there exists \(u\in K\) such that \[\langle Au-f,v-u\rangle\geq0\qquad\text{for every }v\in K.\] Equivalently, \(f\in Au+N_K(u)\). If \(A\) is strictly monotone on \(K\), this solution is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coercive, monotone, hemicontinuous operator on a reflexive Banach space yields a solution of every corresponding constrained variational inequality; strict monotonicity additionally gives uniqueness.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real reflexive Banach space and \(K\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(A:X\to X^*\) is monotone, hemicontinuous, and bounded on bounded sets.
For some \(u_0\in K\), \(\langle Au,u-u_0\rangle/\lVert u\rVert\to+\infty\) as \(u\in K\) and \(\lVert u\rVert\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(f\in X^*\), there exists \(u\in K\) such that \(\langle Au-f,v-u\rangle\geq0\) for every \(v\in K\).

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Monotonicity Uniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness only; existence must be supplied separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a nonempty convex subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\), and let \(F:K\to H\) be strictly monotone, meaning that \[\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle>0\qquad\text{whenever }x,y\in K\text{ and }x\neq y.\] Then the variational inequality for \(F\) on \(K\) has at most one solution: \[\lvert\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\rvert\leq1.\] Strict monotonicity alone does not ensure existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict monotonicity gives at most one variational-inequality solution but does not by itself ensure that a solution exists.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(K\subseteq H\) is nonempty and convex.
\(F:K\to H\) is strictly monotone: \(\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle>0\) whenever \(x,y\in K\) and \(x\neq y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lvert\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\rvert\leq1\).

assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space.

For each \(p\in H\), the perturbed VI uses the map \(F+p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The solution map \(p\mapsto x(p)\) is \(1/\mu\)-Lipschitz, and \(\kappa=L/\mu\) is the natural operator condition ratio.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x(p)\) denote the unique solution of the VI with map \(x\mapsto F(x)+p\). For all \(p,r\in H\), \[\lVert x(p)-x(r)\rVert\leq\frac{1}{\mu}\lVert p-r\rVert.\] Thus \(1/\mu\) controls absolute sensitivity to additive perturbations. When the scale of the forward operator is measured by its Lipschitz modulus \(L\), the dimensionless ratio \[\kappa:=\frac{L}{\mu}\] serves as the natural strong-monotonicity conditioning parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong monotonicity bounds additive-perturbation sensitivity by the reciprocal modulus; relative conditioning is measured by the Lipschitz-to-monotonicity ratio.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Monotonicity Conditioning

knowledge_statements.statement_title: P-property of a block multifunction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the strict blockwise P-property used in variational-inequality and equilibrium uniqueness theory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widehat K=\prod_{i=1}^N K^i\), where \(K^i\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_i}\). A multifunction \(\Phi:\widehat K\to\mathbb R^n\) has the P-property on \(\widehat K\) if, for every pair \(\widehat x=(\widehat x^i)_{i=1}^N\ne\widetilde x=(\widetilde x^i)_{i=1}^N\) in \(\widehat K\) and every \(\widehat y=(\widehat y^i)_{i=1}^N\in\Phi(\widehat x)\), \(\widetilde y=(\widetilde y^i)_{i=1}^N\in\Phi(\widetilde x)\), one has \[\max_{1\le i\le N}(\widehat x^i-\widetilde x^i)^T(\widehat y^i-\widetilde y^i)>0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block multifunction has the P-property if every two distinct domain points and every corresponding pair of multifunction values have a block with strictly positive displacement–value-difference inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max_{1\le i\le N}(\widehat x^i-\widetilde x^i)^T(\widehat y^i-\widetilde y^i)>0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: P0-property of a block multifunction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the nonstrict P0 analogue of the P-property and records the single-block boundary case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widehat K=\prod_{i=1}^N K^i\). A block multifunction \(\Phi:\widehat K\to\mathbb R^n\) has the \(P_0\)-property on \(\widehat K\) if, for every \(\widehat x=(\widehat x^i)_{i=1}^N\ne\widetilde x=(\widetilde x^i)_{i=1}^N\) in \(\widehat K\) and every \(\widehat y\in\Phi(\widehat x)\), \(\widetilde y\in\Phi(\widetilde x)\), there exists an index \(i\) such that \(\widehat x^i\ne\widetilde x^i\) and \[(\widehat x^i-\widetilde x^i)^T(\widehat y^i-\widetilde y^i)\ge0.\] For \(N=1\), this is precisely monotonicity of \(\Phi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block multifunction has the P0-property when every two distinct domain points and every pair of corresponding values admit a changed block whose displacement–value-difference inner product is nonnegative. With one block, this reduces to ordinary monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists i:\ \widehat x^i\ne\widetilde x^i\ \text{ and }\ (\widehat x^i-\widetilde x^i)^T(\widehat y^i-\widetilde y^i)\ge0;\qquad N=1\Rightarrow \Phi\text{ is monotone}

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is a P-function on \(K\) exactly when the displayed strict maximum condition holds for every distinct pair.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional coordinatewise definition on an arbitrary domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is a P-function on \(K\) if and only if, for every distinct \(x,y\in K\), \[\max_{1\le i\le n}(x_i-y_i)\bigl(F_i(x)-F_i(y)\bigr)>0.\] Equivalently, for every \(x\ne y\), at least one coordinate simultaneously gives a strictly positive displacement and operator-difference product.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mapping is a P-function when every distinct pair has at least one coordinate whose displacement and operator change have a strictly positive product.
knowledge_statements.title: P-Function Conditions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed condition is the standard finite-dimensional definition of a P-function and the condition role fits the leaf, but no inspectable citation or authoritative locator is supplied.

children.title: Uniform P-Function Conditions
children.top_down_role: Quantitatively strengthened P-function conditions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is uniformly P on \(K\) exactly when the displayed inequality holds for some \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic-growth version of the coordinatewise P condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is a uniform P-function on \(K\) if and only if there exists \(\alpha>0\) such that, for all \(x,y\in K\), \[\max_{1\le i\le n}(x_i-y_i)\bigl(F_i(x)-F_i(y)\bigr)\ge \alpha\|x-y\|^2.\] Any admissible \(\alpha\) is a uniform P-function modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform P behavior requires the largest coordinate product to dominate the squared distance by one positive constant for every pair.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform P-Function Conditions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quadratic uniform P-function condition is precise and the condition role fits the leaf, but the record has no source supporting the selected normalization and definition.

children.title: Uniformity Strengthening Boundary
children.top_down_role: Structural distinction between ordinary and uniform P-function regimes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is a P-function on \(K\) but is not a uniform P-function there.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete boundary showing that strict P behavior need not be uniform.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For distinct \(s,t\in K\), strict increase of \(F\) gives \((s-t)(s^3-t^3)>0\), so \(F\) is a P-function. Uniformity would require some \(\alpha>0\) satisfying \(t^4\ge\alpha t^2\) for every \(t\in K\), by comparing \(t\) with \(0\). This is impossible as nonzero \(t\to0\). Hence the implication uniform P \(\Rightarrow\) P is strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The scalar map t cubed is strictly P on a bounded interval but has no positive uniform P modulus near zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniformity Strengthening Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar example correctly separates P-function behavior from uniform P-function behavior and failure_boundary fits the terminal container. However, it has no citation and its statement includes a derivation rather than only the knowledge statement.

assumptions_latex: \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is a P-matrix, meaning every principal minor of \(M\) is positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The linear complementarity problem \(\operatorname{LCP}(M,q)\) has exactly one solution for every \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical global unique-solvability characterization for linear complementarity problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the complementarity system \[z\ge0,\qquad w=Mz+q\ge0,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle=0.\] If \(M\) is a P-matrix, then for every \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\) this system has a unique solution \(z\). Conversely, if the system has a unique solution for every \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\), then \(M\) is a P-matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix is a P-matrix exactly when its linear complementarity problem has one and only one solution for every right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.title: P-Matrix Global Uniqueness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The P-matrix characterization of unique solvability of LCP(M,q) for every right-hand side is a theorem matching this topic, but no authoritative theorem or page locator is cited.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: P-Matrix Characterization by Global LCP Uniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform uniqueness of the LCP over all right-hand-side vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), \(M\) is a \(\mathbf P\)-matrix if and only if \(\operatorname{LCP}(q,M)\) has a unique solution for every \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real square matrix is a P-matrix exactly when its linear complementarity problem has a unique solution for every right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\in\mathbf P\iff \forall q\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ \operatorname{LCP}(q,M)\text{ has a unique solution}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block P-function uniqueness on Cartesian-product feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that for every distinct \(x,y\in K\), \[\max_{1\le i\le N}\langle x_i-y_i,F_i(x)-F_i(y)\rangle>0.\] Then there is at most one \(x\in K\) satisfying \[\langle F(x),y-x\rangle\ge0\qquad\text{for every }y\in K.\] The Cartesian-product structure permits each block to be varied separately and is essential to this blockwise uniqueness criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a Cartesian-product feasible set, a block P-function admits at most one variational-inequality solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Cartesian-Product VI Uniqueness

children.title: P-Zero Relaxation
children.top_down_role: The weakened P-property regime based on P-zero behavior.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The P-zero condition is the nonstrict relaxation of the P-function condition.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise nonstrict relaxation of the P-function predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is a P-zero function on \(K\) if, for every distinct \(x,y\in K\), \[\max_{1\le i\le n}(x_i-y_i)\bigl(F_i(x)-F_i(y)\bigr)\ge0.\] Replacing this nonstrict inequality by strict positivity yields the P-function condition; consequently every P-function is P-zero, but the reverse implication need not hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A P-zero function replaces the strict positive coordinate product required of a P-function by a nonnegative one.
knowledge_statements.title: P-Zero Relaxation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nonstrict coordinatewise condition correctly defines the finite-dimensional P-zero relaxation, and definition is appropriate for the leaf. No source or locator is provided.

children.title: Nonuniqueness Boundary
children.top_down_role: Regimes where global uniqueness can no longer be maintained.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains at least two points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is P-zero but not P, and every point of \(K\) solves \(\operatorname{VI}(K,F)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp loss of uniqueness after strict P positivity is removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any distinct \(x,y\in K\), every coordinate product \((x_i-y_i)(F_i(x)-F_i(y))\) equals \(0\). Thus \(F\) satisfies the P-zero condition but not the P-function condition. Moreover, every \(x\in K\) satisfies \[\langle F(x),y-x\rangle=0\qquad\text{for every }y\in K,\] so P-zero structure alone does not ensure uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The zero mapping is P-zero, yet every feasible point solves the variational inequality, showing exactly where P-based uniqueness can fail.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonuniqueness Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The zero-map example correctly marks the loss-of-uniqueness boundary and failure_boundary is the right role. The record lacks a citation, and the statement contains explanatory derivation that should not appear in a proof-free knowledge statement.

children.title: Multiplicity under P-Zero Structure
children.top_down_role: Solution multiplicity patterns compatible with P-zero structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The solution set is \(\{0\}\times[0,1]\), although \(F\) is P-zero.

notation.meaning: solution set of the variational inequality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonconstant P-zero mapping with a continuum of VI solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x,y\in K\), the coordinate products are \((x_1-y_1)^2\) and \(0\), so \(F\) is P-zero. The variational inequality is \[x_1(y_1-x_1)\ge0\qquad\text{for every }y_1\in[0,1].\] This holds exactly when \(x_1=0\), while \(x_2\) is unrestricted. Hence \[\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)=\{0\}\times[0,1].\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconstant P-zero mapping on the unit square can have an entire line segment of variational-inequality solutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicity under P-Zero Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mapping is P-zero and its VI solution set is correctly stated as {0} times [0,1]; counterexample fits the multiplicity leaf. The record nevertheless has no source and includes the calculation establishing the result.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform Growth Implies Coercivity on Critical-Cone Spans
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary Lagrangian Hessian bounds, with a stronger domain under strong extended polyhedricity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let x_0 be a locally optimal solution and \lambda_0 its unique associated Lagrange multiplier. If uniform second-order growth with respect to the canonical parameterization holds at x_0, then there exists \alpha>0 such that D^2_{xx}L(x_0,\lambda_0)(h,h)\ge \alpha\|h\|^2 for every h\in\operatorname{Sp}[C_R(x_0)]. If, additionally, strong extended polyhedricity holds, then such an \alpha>0 exists with the inequality valid for every h\in\operatorname{Sp}[C(x_0)].
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Canonical uniform second-order growth and multiplier uniqueness force uniform positive definiteness of the Lagrangian Hessian on the span of the reduced critical cone. Strong extended polyhedricity extends the bound to the span of the full critical cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Critical-Cone Sufficient Condition for Local VI and KKT Uniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local uniqueness of a smoothly constrained VI solution and conditional characterization of locally unique KKT triples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\operatorname{VI}(K,F)\), with \(K\) represented by the stated constraint system. Let \(x\) be a solution. Assume \(F\) is continuously differentiable near \(x\), all \(h_j\) and \(g_i\) are twice continuously differentiable near \(x\), and \(x\) satisfies SBCQ. If, for every \((\mu,\lambda)\in\mathcal M(x)\), the system \(\mathcal C(x;K,F)\ni v\perp J_x\mathbf L(x,\mu,\lambda)v\in\mathcal C(x;K,F)^*\) has only the solution \(v=0\), then \(x\) is locally unique. Under these assumptions, \((x,\mu,\lambda)\) is a locally unique solution of the KKT system if and only if \(\mathcal M(x)=\{(\mu,\lambda)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under SBCQ, smoothness, and zero-only solvability of every multiplier-specific homogeneous critical-cone complementarity system, the VI solution is locally unique. A KKT triple is locally unique exactly when its multiplier pair is the unique multiplier pair at that solution.
assumptions_latex: \forall(\mu,\lambda)\in\mathcal M(x),\ \{v:\mathcal C(x;K,F)\ni v\perp J_x\mathbf L(x,\mu,\lambda)v\in\mathcal C(x;K,F)^*\}=\{0\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is locally unique},\qquad (x,\mu,\lambda)\text{ is a locally unique KKT triple}\iff\mathcal M(x)=\{(\mu,\lambda)\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Stability of a Minimum Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An unperturbed sequential stability notion for a local minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A local minimum point x^* of f is locally stable if there exists \delta>0 such that, for every sequence (x^k), the conditions \|x^k-x^*\|\le\delta for all k and f(x^k)\to f(x^*) imply x^k\to x^*.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local minimum is locally stable when every sequence staying in some fixed neighborhood and whose objective values approach the minimum value must converge to that minimum point.
assumptions_latex: x^*\text{ is a local minimum point of }f
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\delta>0\;\forall(x^k),\quad \bigl[(\forall k,\ \|x^k-x^*\|\le\delta)\land f(x^k)\to f(x^*)\bigr]\Rightarrow x^k\to x^*

knowledge_statements.title: KKT-Triple Local Uniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth constrained VI; strong metric regularity gives local uniqueness of the entire primal-dual triple.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), \(h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p\), and \(z=(x,\lambda,\mu)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R_+^m\times\mathbb R^p\). Define \[\mathcal K(z):=\begin{pmatrix}F(x)+\nabla g(x)^\mathsf T\lambda+\nabla h(x)^\mathsf T\mu\\ h(x)\\-g(x)\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\N_{\mathbb R_+^m}(\lambda)\end{pmatrix}.\] If \(0\in\mathcal K(\bar z)\) and \(\mathcal K\) is strongly metrically regular at \((\bar z,0)\), then there are neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar z\) and \(V\) of \(0\) such that \(p\mapsto\mathcal K^{-1}(p)\cap U\) is single-valued and Lipschitz on \(V\). In particular, \(\mathcal K^{-1}(0)\cap U=\{\bar z\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong metric regularity of the KKT generalized equation makes the nearby primal-dual solution single-valued and Lipschitz, so the reference KKT triple is locally unique.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\), \(g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), and \(h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p\) are continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
The feasible set is locally \(K=\{x:g(x)\leq0,\ h(x)=0\}\), and \(\bar z=(\bar x,\bar\lambda,\bar\mu)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R_+^m\times\mathbb R^p\) is a KKT triple.
The KKT generalized equation is strongly metrically regular at \((\bar z,0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There are neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar z\) and \(V\) of \(0\) such that every \(p\in V\) has exactly one solution \(z(p)\in U\), and \(p\mapsto z(p)\) is Lipschitz; hence \(\bar z\) is locally unique for \(p=0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Uniqueness Transfer from KKT Triples to VI Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-way transfer from local uniqueness of a KKT representation to local uniqueness of the underlying VI solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\operatorname{VI}(K,F)\), where \(K\) is represented by the stated constraint system. Let \(x\) solve the VI, assume \(F\) is continuous near \(x\), and assume every \(h_j\) and \(g_i\) is continuously differentiable near \(x\). If \((x,\mu,\lambda)\) is a locally unique KKT triple, then \(x\) is a locally unique solution of the VI.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the stated constrained VI, local uniqueness of a KKT triple implies local uniqueness of its primal VI solution.
assumptions_latex: (x,\mu,\lambda)\text{ is a locally unique KKT triple}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is a locally unique solution of }\operatorname{VI}(K,F).

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Map Local Invertibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local-homeomorphism formulation for a finite-dimensional VI over a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(z\in\mathbb R^n\), define \[F_K^{\mathrm{nor}}(z):=F(\Pi_K z)+z-\Pi_K z.\] Suppose \(F_K^{\mathrm{nor}}(\bar z)=0\) and there are neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar z\) and \(V\) of \(0\) such that \(F_K^{\mathrm{nor}}:U\to V\) is a homeomorphism. Then \(\bar z\) is the unique zero in \(U\), and \(\bar x=\Pi_K(\bar z)\) is locally unique among solutions of \(0\in F(x)+N_K(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the normal map is a local homeomorphism at a zero, that zero and its corresponding nearby variational-inequality solution are locally unique.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
The normal map is a homeomorphism between a neighborhood of its zero \(\bar z\) and a neighborhood of \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The point \(\bar x=\Pi_K(\bar z)\) is the unique solution of \(0\in F(x)+N_K(x)\) in some neighborhood of \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean projector onto the feasible set.
Normal map associated with the VI.
Reference zero and projected VI solution.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional characterization of isolated complementarity solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient B-derivative condition, with an affine converse, for isolation of a componentwise complementarity solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F,G:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be B-differentiable on the open set \(\mathcal D\), and let \(x\) solve the complementarity problem. Suppose the only \(v\) satisfying \(F_i'(x;v)=0\) for every \(i\) with \(F_i(x)=0<G_i(x)\), \(\min\{F_i'(x;v),G_i'(x;v)\}=0\) for every \(i\) with \(F_i(x)=G_i(x)=0\), and \(G_i'(x;v)=0\) for every \(i\) with \(F_i(x)>0=G_i(x)\), is \(v=0\). Then \(x\) is an isolated complementarity solution. Conversely, if \(F\) and \(G\) are affine and \(x\) is an isolated solution, then this directional system has the unique solution \(v=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the active-pattern directional system of a complementarity problem has only the zero solution, then the reference solution is isolated. For affine complementarity maps, isolation also implies this directional condition.
assumptions_latex: F,G:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\text{ are B-differentiable and }\mathcal D\text{ is open}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is isolated; if }F,G\text{ are affine, isolation is equivalent to uniqueness of }v=0\text{ in the directional system}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Row and column representative matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A rowwise or columnwise selection construction for two matrices of the same dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A,B\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\). A matrix \(C\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) is a row representative matrix of \((A,B)\) if \(C_{i\cdot}\in\{A_{i\cdot},B_{i\cdot}\}\) for every row index \(i\). It is a column representative matrix of \((A,B)\) if \(C_{\cdot j}\in\{A_{\cdot j},B_{\cdot j}\}\) for every column index \(j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A row representative matrix independently takes each row from the corresponding row of either of two matrices. A column representative matrix is formed analogously by choosing corresponding columns.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C_{i\cdot}\in\{A_{i\cdot},B_{i\cdot}\}\ \forall i\quad\text{or, respectively,}\quad C_{\cdot j}\in\{A_{\cdot j},B_{\cdot j}\}\ \forall j

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Critical-cone characterization of VI nondegeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes a nondegenerate VI solution through its critical cone and identifies that cone with the tangent cone's lineality space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed and convex, let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\), and let \(x\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\). Then \(x\) is nondegenerate if and only if \(\mathcal C(x;K,F)\) is a linear subspace. When these equivalent conditions hold, \(\mathcal C(x;K,F)=\operatorname{lin}\mathcal T(x;K)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a VI over a closed convex set, a solution is nondegenerate exactly when its critical cone is a linear subspace. In that case, the critical cone equals the lineality space of the tangent cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ is nondegenerate}\iff\mathcal C(x;K,F)\text{ is a linear subspace}\), and under these conditions \(\mathcal C(x;K,F)=\operatorname{lin}\mathcal T(x;K)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Solution structure of positive-semidefinite linear complementarity problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear complementarity solution-set geometry for a possibly nonsymmetric positive-semidefinite matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) satisfy \(x^{\mathsf T}Mx\ge 0\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), let \(q\in\mathbb R^n\), and write \(\operatorname{SOL}(q,M)=\{z\ge0:q+Mz\ge0,\ z^{\mathsf T}(q+Mz)=0\}\). Then: (a) any \(z^1,z^2\in\operatorname{SOL}(q,M)\) satisfy \((z^1)^{\mathsf T}(q+Mz^2)=(z^2)^{\mathsf T}(q+Mz^1)=0\); (b) if \(z^*\in\operatorname{SOL}(q,M)\) is nondegenerate and \(M_{\alpha\alpha}\) is nonsingular for \(\alpha=\{i:z_i^*>0\}\), then \(z^*\) is the unique solution; (c) if the problem is solvable, then for any \(\bar z\in\operatorname{SOL}(q,M)\), \[\operatorname{SOL}(q,M)=\{z\in\mathbb R_+^n:q+Mz\ge0,\ q^{\mathsf T}(z-\bar z)=0,\ (M+M^{\mathsf T})(z-\bar z)=0\},\] hence the solution set is polyhedral; and (d) if \(M=M^{\mathsf T}\), then \(Mz^1=Mz^2\) for all solutions \(z^1,z^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a positive-semidefinite linear complementarity problem, every pair of solutions is cross-complementary. A nondegenerate solution whose positive-index principal submatrix is nonsingular is unique. Whenever solutions exist, their set has the displayed polyhedral representation relative to any fixed solution. If the matrix is also symmetric, all solutions have the same image under the matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Properties (a)--(d) above hold for }\operatorname{SOL}(q,M).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded-set comparison of complementarity residuals under nondegeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For a parametric AVI KKT system, nondegeneracy of every solution yields a uniform residual comparison on each bounded portion of the relaxed feasible region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(W\) and \(\Omega\) be the relaxed feasible region and full solution set of the parametric-AVI KKT system. Suppose every \((x,y,\lambda)\in\Omega\) is nondegenerate in the componentwise sense \[\lambda-(Dx+Ey+b)>0.\] Then, for every \(\rho>0\), there exists \(\tau>0\) such that every \((x,y,\lambda)\in W\cap\mathbb{B}(0,\rho)\) satisfies \[\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\min\{\lambda_i,-(Dx+Ey+b)_i\}\leq-\tau\lambda^T(Dx+Ey+b).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every solution satisfies the stated nondegeneracy condition, then on every bounded part of the relaxed KKT region the summed minimum complementarity residual is bounded by a constant multiple of the complementarity-product residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\min\{\lambda_i,-(Dx+Ey+b)_i\}\leq-\tau\lambda^T(Dx+Ey+b)

knowledge_statements.title: Connectedness of Solution Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Connectivity consequence of convexity for a nonempty continuous monotone VI solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(F:K\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuous and monotone. If \(\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\neq\varnothing\), then \(\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\) is path connected. More precisely, for all \(x^0,x^1\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\) and every \(t\in[0,1]\), \[(1-t)x^0+tx^1\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty solution set of a continuous monotone VI on a closed convex feasible set is path connected; the segment joining any two solutions remains in the solution set.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
The VI has at least one solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The solution set \(\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\) is path connected, and hence connected.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mapping $f:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ is weakly univalent on $\mathcal D$ if it is continuous and there exists a sequence of continuous injective mappings $f^\nu:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $f^\nu\to f$ uniformly on every bounded subset of $\mathcal D$.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedrality of AVI Solution Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General affine VI over a polyhedron, with the monotone case distinguished.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty polyhedral convex set and let \(F(x)=Mx+q\). For every face \(G\) of \(K\), set \[S_G:=\{x\in G:-Mx-q\in N_K(G)\}.\] Then each \(S_G\) is a polyhedral convex set and \[\operatorname{SOL}(K,Mx+q)=\bigcup_{G\in\mathcal F(K)}S_G,\] where \(\mathcal F(K)\) is the finite face family of \(K\). If \(M\) is positive semidefinite, then the solution set is a convex polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine VI over a polyhedron has a solution set representable as a finite union of polyhedral face pieces; when the affine field is monotone, the complete solution set is a convex polyhedron.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty polyhedral convex set.
The VI field is affine: \(F(x)=Mx+q\), where \(M\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) and \(q\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The AVI solution set is a finite union of polyhedral convex sets; if \(M\) is positive semidefinite, it is a convex polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Convexity and Polyhedrality Conditions for AVI Solution Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent geometric and algebraic conditions for the solution set of an affine variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\operatorname{SOL}(K,q,M)\). The following statements are equivalent: \(S\) is convex; for every \(x^1,x^2\in S\), \((x^1)^T(q+Mx^1)=(x^2)^T(q+Mx^1)\); for every \(x^1,x^2\in S\), \((x^1-x^2)^TM(x^1-x^2)=0\); and \(S\) is polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an affine variational inequality, convexity of the solution set, the stated pairwise equality, vanishing of the quadratic form on every difference of solutions, and polyhedrality of the solution set are equivalent.
assumptions_latex: \(S=\operatorname{SOL}(K,q,M)\) is the solution set of the affine variational inequality \(\operatorname{AVI}(K,q,M)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine variational inequalities and their equivalent representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine variational inequalities on polyhedral sets, including orthant and explicit inequality representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For $M\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$, $q\in\mathbb R^m$, and a polyhedral set $X\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $\operatorname{AVI}(q,M,X)$ asks for $x^*\in X$ such that $(x-x^*)^T(q+Mx^*)\ge 0$ for every $x\in X$. Its solution set satisfies $x\in\operatorname{SOL}(q,M,X)\iff x=\Pi_X(x-Mx-q)$. If $X=\mathbb R_+^m$, this AVI is equivalent to $\operatorname{LCP}(q,M)$. If $X=\{x:Ax\ge b\}$, then $x\in\operatorname{SOL}(q,M,X)$ iff there exists $\lambda\ge0$ such that $q+Mx-A^T\lambda=0$, $Ax-b\ge0$, and $\lambda^T(Ax-b)=0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine variational inequality seeks a point in a polyhedral set whose affine residual has a nonnegative inner product with every feasible displacement. Solutions are exactly fixed points of the projected affine-residual map. On the nonnegative orthant the problem is a linear complementarity problem, while an inequality description of the polyhedron yields an equivalent mixed linear complementarity system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in\operatorname{SOL}(q,M,X)\iff x=\Pi_X(x-Mx-q),\quad\text{with the stated LCP and mixed-complementarity specializations.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong regularity of a variational inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition at a solution using the perturbed affine linearization of the VI.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\bar w$ solve $\operatorname{VI}(F,S)$. The variational inequality is strongly regular at $\bar w$ if there exist open neighborhoods $U_p\subset\mathbb R^n$ of $0$ and $U_w\subset\mathbb R^n$ of $\bar w$, and a Lipschitz map $w:U_p\to U_w$, such that for every $p\in U_p$, $w(p)$ is the unique solution in $U_w$ of $\operatorname{VI}(F(\bar w)+F'(\bar w)(\cdot-\bar w)-p,S)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variational inequality is strongly regular at a solution when every sufficiently small perturbation of its affine linearization has a unique nearby solution, and that solution depends Lipschitz continuously on the perturbation.

U_w\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ is an open neighborhood of }\bar w

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The compactness conclusion uses an interior dual-recession-cone condition at a reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let K\subseteq\mathbb R^n be closed and convex, let F:K\to\mathbb R^n be continuous, and suppose F is pseudomonotone on K. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regular and strongly regular isolated zeros
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local solvability and localization for right-hand-side perturbations, strengthened by single-valued Lipschitz dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R^n\), where \(\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is open, and let \(x\in\mathcal D\) be an isolated zero of \(H\). The zero \(x\) is regular if, for every open neighborhood \(\mathcal N\) of \(x\) satisfying \(\operatorname{cl}\mathcal N\subset\mathcal D\) and \(H^{-1}(0)\cap\operatorname{cl}\mathcal N=\{x\}\), there exist an open neighborhood \(\mathcal U\) of \(0\) and \(c>0\) such that \(\varnothing\ne H^{-1}(u)\cap\mathcal N\subseteq\mathbb B(x,c\|u\|)\) for every \(u\in\mathcal U\). It is strongly regular if, in addition, \(H^{-1}(u)\cap\mathcal N=\{x_{\mathcal N}(u)\}\) for every \(u\in\mathcal U\) and \(\|x_{\mathcal N}(u)-x_{\mathcal N}(u')\|\le c\|u-u'\|\) for every \(u,u'\in\mathcal U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regularity requires every sufficiently small right-hand side to have a local solution whose displacement from the isolated zero is proportional to the perturbation. Strong regularity additionally requires that local solution to be unique and Lipschitz-continuous in the right-hand side.
assumptions_latex: \(H:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R^n\) is a given map
\(x\in\mathcal D\) is an isolated zero of \(H\)
\(\mathcal N\ni x\) is open, \(\operatorname{cl}\mathcal N\subset\mathcal D\), and \(H^{-1}(0)\cap\operatorname{cl}\mathcal N=\{x\}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{regular}:\ \exists\mathcal U\ni0,\exists c>0\ \forall u\in\mathcal U,\ \varnothing\ne H^{-1}(u)\cap\mathcal N\subseteq\mathbb B(x,c\|u\|);\quad \text{strongly regular}:\ \forall u\in\mathcal U,\ H^{-1}(u)\cap\mathcal N=\{x_{\mathcal N}(u)\},\ \forall u,u'\in\mathcal U,\ \|x_{\mathcal N}(u)-x_{\mathcal N}(u')\|\le c\|u-u'\|.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent error bounds for a B-differentiable equation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between nonsingularity of the Bouligand derivative, its global homogeneous error bound, and a local residual error bound at a zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuous, where \(\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is open. Suppose \(H(x)=0\) and \(H\) is B-differentiable at \(x\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Chain rule for Bouligand derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition and preservation of strong Bouligand differentiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(\mathcal D'\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be open. Let \(\Phi:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R^m\) be B-differentiable at \(x\in\mathcal D\), let \(\Psi:\mathcal D'\to\mathbb R^p\) be B-differentiable at \(\Phi(x)\in\mathcal D'\), and suppose \(\Phi(\mathcal D)\subseteq\mathcal D'\). Then \(\Gamma=\Psi\circ\Phi\) is B-differentiable at \(x\), and for every \(d\in\mathbb R^n\), \[\Gamma'(x;d)=\Psi'\bigl(\Phi(x);\Phi'(x;d)\bigr).\] If additionally \(\Psi\) is strongly F-differentiable at \(\Phi(x)\) and \(\Phi\) has a strong B-derivative at \(x\), then \(\Gamma\) has a strong B-derivative at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bouligand differentiability is preserved under composition, with the directional chain rule. Strong B-differentiability of the composition follows when the outer map is strongly F-differentiable and the inner map has a strong B-derivative.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(\mathcal D'\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) are open.
For the strong conclusion, \(\Psi\) is strongly F-differentiable at \(\Phi(x)\) and \(\Phi\) has a strong B-derivative at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\Psi\circ\Phi)'(x;d)=\Psi'(\Phi(x);\Phi'(x;d))\ \forall d\in\mathbb R^n\), and under the additional strong hypotheses \(\Psi\circ\Phi\) has a strong B-derivative at \(x\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bouligand and strong Bouligand differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for finite-dimensional mappings on open domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), where \(\mathcal D\) is open, and let \(x\in\mathcal D\). The map \(\Phi\) is B-differentiable at \(x\) if it is Lipschitz continuous on a neighborhood of \(x\) and directionally differentiable at \(x\); its directional derivative \(\Phi'(x;d)\) is then called its B-derivative along \(d\). Define \(e(y)=\Phi(y)-\Phi(x)-\Phi'(x;y-x)\). The B-derivative is strong, and \(\Phi\) is strongly B-differentiable at \(x\), if \(\lim_{y^1\ne y^2,\,(y^1,y^2)\to(x,x)}\frac{e(y^1)-e(y^2)}{\|y^1-y^2\|}=0\). The map is B-differentiable near \(x\) if it is B-differentiable at every point of some neighborhood of \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bouligand differentiability at a point means local Lipschitz continuity together with directional differentiability. It is strong when the first-order remainder has vanishing local difference quotient, and it holds near a point when it holds throughout some neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi\text{ is B-differentiable at }x\iff \Phi\text{ is locally Lipschitz near }x\text{ and directionally differentiable at }x\), with strong B-differentiability characterized by the stated remainder limit.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuous, where \(\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is open, and let \(x\in\mathcal D\) be an isolated zero of \(H\). The zero \(x\) is semistable if, for every open neighborhood \(\mathcal N\) of \(x\) satisfying \(\operatorname{cl}\mathcal N\subset\mathcal D\) and \(H^{-1}(0)\cap\operatorname{cl}\mathcal N=\{x\}\), there exist \(\varepsilon,c>0\) such that for every \(G\in\operatorname{IB}(H;\varepsilon,\operatorname{cl}\mathcal N)\) and every \(x'\in G^{-1}(0)\cap\mathcal N\), \(\|x'-x\|\le c\|H(x')\|\). It is stable if, for every such \(\mathcal N\), there exist \(\varepsilon,c>0\) such that every such \(G\) has a zero in \(\mathcal N\) and the same inequality holds for every \(x'\in G^{-1}(0)\cap\mathcal N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Semistability imposes a uniform residual bound on any nearby perturbed zeros but does not itself require such zeros to exist. Stability requires both existence and that bound for every perturbation in the stated class.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathcal D\) is an isolated zero of \(H\)
\(\mathcal N\ni x\) is open, \(\operatorname{cl}\mathcal N\subset\mathcal D\), and \(H^{-1}(0)\cap\operatorname{cl}\mathcal N=\{x\}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{semistable}:\ \forall\mathcal N\ \exists\varepsilon,c>0\ \forall G\in\operatorname{IB}(H;\varepsilon,\operatorname{cl}\mathcal N)\ \forall x'\in G^{-1}(0)\cap\mathcal N,\ \|x'-x\|\le c\|H(x')\|;\quad \text{stable}:\ \text{the same bound and }G^{-1}(0)\cap\mathcal N\ne\varnothing\text{ for every }G.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transfer of zero stability to first-order approximations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preservation of stable and strongly stable zeros by first-order approximation models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) and \(h\) be locally Lipschitz continuous at \(x\), and suppose \(h\) is a first-order approximation of \(H\) at \(x\). Then: (i) if \(x\) is a stable zero of \(H\) and \(\operatorname{ind}(H,x)\ne0\), then \(x\) is a stable zero of \(h\); and (ii) if \(h\) is a strong first-order approximation of \(H\) at \(x\), then \(x\) is a strongly stable zero of \(H\) if and only if it is a strongly stable zero of \(h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Lipschitz first-order model inherits stability from a stable zero of nonzero index. For a strong first-order model, strong stability of the original equation and of the model are equivalent.

\(h\) is a first-order approximation of \(H\) at \(x\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stable-zero criteria via the B-derivative model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between stability of a B-differentiable equation and stability, uniqueness, and bounded-inverse properties of its directional model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be a zero of a continuous map \(H:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R^n\), where \(\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is open. Suppose \(H\) is B-differentiable at \(x\), define \(\Gamma(y)=H'(x;y-x)\), and assume \(\Gamma\) has the nonvanishing property at \(x\). Then the following are equivalent: (a) \(x\) is a stable zero of \(\Gamma\); (b) \(\Gamma\) is surjective and \(\Gamma^{-1}(\mathbb B(0,1))\) is bounded; (c) \(x\) is the unique zero of \(\Gamma\); (d) \(x\) is a stable zero of \(H\); and (e) there exist an open neighborhood \(\mathcal N\) of \(x\) satisfying (5.2.3) and \(\varepsilon,c>0\) such that, for every \(G\in\mathbb B(H;\varepsilon,\operatorname{cl}\mathcal N)\), the set \(G^{-1}(0)\cap\mathcal N\) is nonempty and (5.2.5) holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under B-differentiability and the nonvanishing property, stability of the original zero is equivalent to stability and uniqueness for the B-derivative model, its surjectivity with bounded unit-ball preimage, and the source's stated uniform perturbation condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ stable for }\Gamma\iff[\Gamma\text{ surjective and }\Gamma^{-1}(\mathbb B(0,1))\text{ bounded}]\iff x\text{ is the unique zero of }\Gamma\iff x\text{ stable for }H\iff\text{condition (e), including (5.2.3) and (5.2.5), holds}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider: (a) for every open \(\mathcal U\supseteq\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\), there exists \(\delta>0\) such that every continuous \(G\) satisfying condition (5.5.1) has \(\operatorname{SOL}(K,G)\cap\mathcal U\neq\varnothing\); and (b) for every such \(\mathcal U\), there exists \(\varepsilon>0\) such that every \(G\in\mathbb B(F;\varepsilon,K_{\mathcal U})\) has \(\operatorname{SOL}(K,G)\cap\mathcal U\neq\varnothing\). Then \((a)\Rightarrow(b)\). If \(\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\) is bounded, then also \((b)\Rightarrow(a)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The continuous-perturbation solvability condition implies solvability persistence for operators in the indicated local uniform ball. The converse holds when the original VI solution set is bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (a)\Rightarrow(b),\qquad \operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\text{ bounded}\Rightarrow\bigl((b)\Rightarrow(a)\bigr).

children.title: Semistability
children.top_down_role: Semistable behavior of VI solution mappings.

assumptions_latex: \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\) is a solution mapping between metric spaces and \(\bar x\in S(\bar p)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Semistability at \((\bar p,\bar x)\) means that every sequence \(p_k\to\bar p\) admits \(x_k\in S(p_k)\) with \(x_k\to\bar x\).
review_flags: Semistability has multiple conventions; an exact VI-specific source is needed to confirm this inner-persistence definition.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential inner-persistence convention for semistability of a parameterized solution mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The reference solution \(\bar x\in S(\bar p)\) is semistable if, for every sequence \(p_k\to\bar p\), there exist an index \(k_0\) and selections \(x_k\in S(p_k)\) for all \(k\ge k_0\) such that \(x_k\to\bar x\). Equivalently in metric spaces, \[\bar x\in\liminf_{p\to\bar p}S(p).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Semistability means every sufficiently small parameter sequence admits solutions converging to the designated reference solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Semistability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sequential condition is a valid inner-persistence property in metric spaces, but “semistability” has multiple inequivalent conventions. No VI-specific source identifies this as the intended definition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semistability and stability of a VI solution set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: VI-specific solution-set stability under locally uniform operator perturbations, including the singleton-solution failure boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\neq\varnothing\). For every open set \(\mathcal U\supseteq\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\), let \(K_{\mathcal U}=K\cap\operatorname{cl}\mathcal U\). The VI \((K,F)\) is semistable if there exist \(c,\varepsilon>0\) such that every \(G\in\mathbb B(F;\varepsilon,K_{\mathcal U})\) satisfies \[\operatorname{SOL}(K,G)\cap\mathcal U\subseteq\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)+c\omega\mathbb B(0,1),\qquad \omega=\sup_{x\in K_{\mathcal U}}\|G(x)-F(x)\|.\] It is stable if, in addition, \(\operatorname{SOL}(K,G)\cap\mathcal U\neq\varnothing\) for every such \(G\). The open set \(\mathcal U\) need not be bounded. If \(\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)=\{x^*\}\), solution-set semistability implies pointwise semistability of \(x^*\), whereas the converse can fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A VI is solution-set semistable when every open neighborhood of its nonempty solution set admits a perturbation threshold and a linear containment bound for perturbed solutions lying in that neighborhood. Stability additionally requires such a perturbed solution to exist. The neighborhood may be unbounded. For a singleton solution set, solution-set semistability implies pointwise semistability, but not conversely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists c,\varepsilon>0\ \forall G\in\mathbb B(F;\varepsilon,K_{\mathcal U}):\ \operatorname{SOL}(K,G)\cap\mathcal U\subseteq\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)+c\omega\mathbb B(0,1),\quad \omega=\sup_{x\in K_{\mathcal U}}\|G(x)-F(x)\|;\ \text{stability additionally requires }\operatorname{SOL}(K,G)\cap\mathcal U\neq\varnothing.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semistability and epsilon-solution boundedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two directional implications relating semistability, boundedness, epsilon-solution boundedness, pointwise semiregularity, and finiteness of the VI solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed and convex, let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuous, and assume \(\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\neq\varnothing\). (a) If \(\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\) is bounded and \((K,F)\) is semistable, then \((K,F)\) is \(\varepsilon\)-solution bounded for some \(\varepsilon>0\). (b) Conversely, if \((K,F)\) is \(\varepsilon\)-solution bounded for some \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\) is pointwise semiregular, then \(\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\) is finite and \((K,F)\) is semistable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A semistable VI with a bounded nonempty solution set is epsilon-solution bounded. Conversely, epsilon-solution boundedness together with pointwise semiregularity makes the solution set finite and yields semistability.
assumptions_latex: K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is closed and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\text{ bounded and }(K,F)\text{ semistable}\bigr]\Rightarrow\exists\varepsilon>0:\ (K,F)\text{ is }\varepsilon\text{-solution bounded};\quad \bigl[\exists\varepsilon>0:\ (K,F)\text{ is }\varepsilon\text{-solution bounded and }\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\text{ is pointwise semiregular}\bigr]\Rightarrow\bigl[\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\text{ is finite and }(K,F)\text{ is semistable}\bigr].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semistability equivalences via constant perturbations and the normal-map residual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent quantitative characterizations of semistability for a continuous VI on a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed and convex and let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuous. The following are equivalent: (a) \((K,F)\) is semistable; (b) there exist \(c,\varepsilon>0\) such that for every \(q\in\mathbb R^n\), \[\|q\|<\varepsilon\Rightarrow\operatorname{SOL}(K,F+q)\subseteq\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)+\mathbb B(0,c\|q\|);\] (c) there exist \(c,\varepsilon>0\) such that for every \(z\in\mathbb R^n\), \[\|\mathbf F_K^{\mathrm{nor}}(z)\|<\varepsilon\Rightarrow\operatorname{dist}\!\left(\Pi_K(z),\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\right)\le c\|\mathbf F_K^{\mathrm{nor}}(z)\|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous VI on a closed convex set, semistability is equivalent to linear control of all solutions under sufficiently small constant operator perturbations and to a local error bound expressed through the normal-map residual.
assumptions_latex: K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is closed and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (a)\Longleftrightarrow(b)\Longleftrightarrow(c).

children.title: Perturbed Solvability
children.top_down_role: Persistence of VI solvability under problem perturbations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The VI is locally solvable under perturbation at \(\bar p\) when some neighborhood \(V\) of \(\bar p\) satisfies \(S(p)\ne\varnothing\) for every \(p\in V\).
review_flags: A source explicitly defining local perturbed solvability in this VI context is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local nonemptiness of every sufficiently small parameter perturbation of a finite-dimensional VI.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each parameter \(p\), define \[S(p):=\{x\in C(p):\langle F(x,p),y-x\rangle\ge0\ \text{for every }y\in C(p)\}.\] The reference VI is persistently solvable under small perturbations if there exists a neighborhood \(V\) of \(\bar p\) such that \(S(p)\ne\varnothing\) for every \(p\in V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Perturbed solvability means that every sufficiently small parameter perturbation retains at least one variational-inequality solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Perturbed Solvability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local nonemptiness definition is precise and fits the terminal container, but it has no cited source or explicit standard-field rationale.

children.title: Semistability-Based Solvability Persistence
children.top_down_role: Structural links between semistability and continued solvability.

assumptions_latex: \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\) is a solution mapping between metric spaces, \(\bar x\in S(\bar p)\), and \(\bar x\) is semistable in the sequential inner-persistence sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a neighborhood \(V\) of \(\bar p\) such that \(S(p)\ne\varnothing\) for every \(p\in V\).
review_flags: Depends on the selected semistability convention; an exact VI-specific source is needed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solvability consequence of sequential inner persistence in metric parameter spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose semistability holds at \((\bar p,\bar x)\). Then perturbed solvability must persist locally: there is a neighborhood \(V\) of \(\bar p\) for which \[S(p)\ne\varnothing\quad\text{for every }p\in V.\] Otherwise one could choose \(p_k\to\bar p\) with \(S(p_k)=\varnothing\), contradicting the semistability requirement that solutions \(x_k\in S(p_k)\) converge to \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential semistability forces all sufficiently small parameter perturbations to remain solvable.
knowledge_statements.title: Semistability-Based Solvability Persistence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The implication follows from the stated sequential inner-persistence convention in metric parameter spaces, but that convention for semistability remains unsupported. The final contradiction sentence is also proof text and should be removed once the result is sourced.

children.title: Degenerate Solution Regimes
children.top_down_role: VI solution regimes exhibiting degeneracy.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is polyhedral, \(\bar x\) solves \(0\in F(x,\bar p)+N_C(x)\), and \(F\) is differentiable at \((\bar x,\bar p)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reference solution is linearly degenerate when the homogeneous critical-cone generalized equation has a nonzero solution.

notation.meaning: Critical cone at the reference solution
State Jacobian at the reference point

review_flags: Degeneracy admits several inequivalent VI definitions; the intended normal-map or critical-cone convention needs a source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Critical-cone linearization criterion for a degenerate polyhedral VI solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K:=T_C(\bar x)\cap F(\bar x,\bar p)^\perp\) and \(A:=\nabla_xF(\bar x,\bar p)\). The reference solution lies in a linearly degenerate regime when the homogeneous linearized generalized equation \[0\in Az+N_K(z)\] admits some \(z\ne0\). Equivalently, the critical linearization fails to isolate the zero response; in normal-map coordinates this corresponds to failure of invertibility of at least one relevant linear selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral VI solution is linearly degenerate when its homogeneous critical-cone linearization has a nonzero solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Solution Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The homogeneous critical-cone condition is a plausible linear-degeneracy criterion, but VI degeneracy has several inequivalent definitions, and the asserted normal-map equivalence requires an exact supporting result.

children.title: Solution-Mapping Discontinuity
children.top_down_role: Discontinuous response of solution mappings to perturbations.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Mapping Discontinuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete finite-dimensional failure of lower semicontinuity caused by solution-set expansion at the reference parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(p\in\mathbb R\), define \(S(p)=\{x\in K:\langle F(x,p),y-x\rangle\geq0\text{ for every }y\in K\}\). Then \[S(p)=\begin{cases}\{-1\},&p>0,\\[-1,1],&p=0,\\\{1\},&p<0.\end{cases}\] The mapping \(S\) is outer semicontinuous but not lower semicontinuous, and hence not Painlevé--Kuratowski continuous, at \(p=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For this linear VI on an interval, every feasible point is a solution at zero, whereas only an endpoint is a solution at each nonzero nearby parameter; the solution map is outer semicontinuous but not lower semicontinuous at zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is not lower semicontinuous at \(p=0\), although it is outer semicontinuous there.

children.title: Degeneracy-Induced Discontinuity
children.top_down_role: Mechanisms linking solution degeneracy to mapping discontinuity.

knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy-Induced Discontinuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar generalized-equation example in which singular linearization coincides with loss of nearby solvability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The variational inequality is equivalent to \(x^2+p=0\), and its solution mapping is \[S(p)=\begin{cases}\{-\sqrt{-p},\sqrt{-p}\},&p<0,\\\{0\},&p=0,\\\varnothing,&p>0.\end{cases}\] At \((x,p)=(0,0)\), \(D_xF(0,0)=0\). The solution mapping has no nonempty-valued localization on a full neighborhood of \(p=0\); local solvability, a calm single-valued localization, and the Aubin property therefore fail at \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the equation x squared plus p equals zero, the singular solution at zero disappears under every positive perturbation, so local solvability and the stated stable-localization properties fail.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The degenerate solution at \(p=0\) is destroyed by every sufficiently small positive perturbation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar boundary example separating continuity from Lipschitz stability at a singular solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The variational inequality is the equation \(x^3-p=0\), with unique solution mapping \(S(p)=\{p^{1/3}\}\) for every \(p\in\mathbb R\). At \((x,p)=(0,0)\), \(D_xF(0,0)=0\). The mapping \(S\) is continuous at \(p=0\) but is not locally Lipschitz there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cube-root solution map remains continuous at its singular reference solution, although it is not locally Lipschitz there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Degeneracy does not force discontinuity: \(S\) is continuous at \(0\) but is not locally Lipschitz there.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Establishes generic nonemptiness and finiteness within any open set of solvable right-hand-side parameters.
