knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hyperplane Projection Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected backtracking algorithm for variational inequalities using a hyperplane correction followed by projection onto the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x^0\in K\), \(\tau>0\), and \(\sigma\in(0,1)\), set \(k=0\). If \(x^k\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\), stop. Otherwise compute \(y^k=\Pi_K(x^k-\tau F(x^k))\) and choose the smallest \(i_k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) such that, with \(z^k=2^{-i_k}y^k+(1-2^{-i_k})x^k\), \[F(z^k)^T(x^k-y^k)\ge \frac{\sigma}{\tau}\|x^k-y^k\|^2.\] Then set \[w^k=\Pi_{H^k}(x^k)=x^k-\frac{F(z^k)^T(x^k-z^k)}{\|F(z^k)\|^2}F(z^k),\qquad x^{k+1}=\Pi_K(w^k),\] increment \(k\), and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a point in K, compute a projected forward step and backtrack along the segment joining it to the current iterate until the stated inequality holds. Project the current iterate onto the resulting hyperplane, project that point onto K, and repeat until a VI solution is reached.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y^k=\Pi_K(x^k-\tau F(x^k)),\quad z^k=2^{-i_k}y^k+(1-2^{-i_k})x^k,\quad w^k=\Pi_{H^k}(x^k),\quad x^{k+1}=\Pi_K(w^k)

assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a nonempty closed convex solution set in a real Hilbert space.
At iteration \(k\), an oracle returns \(a_k\neq0\) and \(b_k\) such that \(S\subset H_k=\{z:\langle a_k,z\rangle\leq b_k\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each correction is Fejér nonincreasing with respect to the certified solution-containing halfspace.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract halfspace-projection template once a valid VI separation oracle is available.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose \(x_0\in H\). Given the certified halfspace \(H_k\), update
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k-\lambda_k
\frac{[\langle a_k,x_k\rangle-b_k]_+}{\|a_k\|^2}a_k.
\]
Stop when \([\langle a_k,x_k\rangle-b_k]_+/\|a_k\|\leq\varepsilon\), or return the last iterate. For every \(x^\star\in S\subset H_k\), relaxed projection with \(0<\lambda_k<2\) satisfies
\[
\|x_{k+1}-x^\star\|^2
\leq\|x_k-x^\star\|^2-
\lambda_k(2-\lambda_k)d(x_k,H_k)^2.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separation oracle supplies a solution-containing halfspace; relaxed projection onto it decreases distance to every solution by a computable amount.
knowledge_statements.title: Separating-Hyperplane Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The relaxed halfspace projection formula and Fejér decrease are mathematically standard, but the record supplies no source connecting this abstract oracle template to the separating-hyperplane VI-method leaf.

assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a nonempty closed convex solution set and \(Q_0\) is a closed convex set containing \(S\).
Each generated closed halfspace \(H_k\) contains \(S\), and \(Q_{k+1}=Q_k\cap H_k\) remains nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(Q_k\) is an outer approximation of \(S\), and the approximations are nested.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested cutting-halfspace approximation of the VI solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Select an anchor \(x_0\in H\). After obtaining a valid halfspace \(H_k\), set
\[
Q_{k+1}=Q_k\cap H_k,
\qquad x_{k+1}=P_{Q_{k+1}}(x_0).
\]
Terminate when a prescribed VI residual at \(x_{k+1}\) is at most \(\varepsilon\), or return the last projection. Inductively,
\[
S\subset Q_{k+1}\subset Q_k
\]
for every \(k\). Thus no valid cut removes a solution, while the fixed-anchor projections provide canonical representatives of successively tighter outer approximations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intersect accumulated valid halfspaces to obtain nested supersets of the solution set, then project a fixed anchor onto each refined approximation.
knowledge_statements.title: Outer-Approximation Projection Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nested-set invariant is correct under the stated containment assumptions and the algorithm kind fits, but no source is supplied and the ambient Hilbert space used by the projection is not explicitly introduced.

assumptions_latex: The VI solution set is nonempty and \(0<\alpha<1/L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two-projection extragradient iteration converges to a VI solution under the stated finite-dimensional regime.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Korpelevich theorem with constant stepsize below the inverse Lipschitz modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Starting from any \(x_0\in C\), define
\[
y_k=P_C(x_k-\alpha F(x_k)),
\qquad
x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha F(y_k)).
\]
Then \((x_k)\) is bounded, \(\|x_k-y_k\|\to0\), and every cluster point solves
\[
\langle F(x^\star),z-x^\star\rangle\geq0
\quad\text{for all }z\in C.
\]
Because the space is finite-dimensional and the standard extragradient estimate is quasi-Fejér with respect to the nonempty solution set when \(\alpha L<1\), the full sequence \((x_k)\) converges to a solution \(x^\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a monotone Lipschitz operator, Korpelevich extragradient with a constant stepsize below one over the Lipschitz constant converges to a solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Lipschitz Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a substantive finite-dimensional convergence theorem, and its hypotheses and conclusion are plausible, but no authoritative source with a theorem, section, or page locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict boundary between strong, ordinary, and pseudomonotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The implications are \(\mu\text{-strongly monotone}\Rightarrow\text{monotone}\Rightarrow\text{pseudomonotone}\). Both reverse implications fail. On \(C=[-1,1]\), the zero map is monotone but is not \(\mu\)-strongly monotone for any \(\mu>0\). Also, \(F(x)=x(2+\sin(10x))\) is pseudomonotone because it has the sign of \(x\), but it is not monotone since its derivative \(2+\sin(10x)+10x\cos(10x)\) is negative at some points. Thus uniqueness and linear-rate conclusions cannot be transferred below the strong regime merely from pseudomonotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong monotonicity, monotonicity, and pseudomonotonicity form strict regimes; weaker regimes do not inherit uniqueness or linear convergence automatically.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity-Regime Transition Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, and the separating examples appear plausible, but the strict implications and examples lack citations and are partly presented as proofs.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Generate \(y_k=P_C(x_k-\gamma F(x_k))\) and \(x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\gamma F(y_k))\), and set \(\bar y_N=N^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}y_k\). For every \(z\in C\), monotonicity and the extragradient estimate give \(\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\gamma\langle F(z),y_k-z\rangle\le \tfrac12\|x_0-z\|^2\). Consequently, \(G_D(\bar y_N)=\sup_{z\in C}\langle F(z),\bar y_N-z\rangle\le D^2/(2\gamma N)\). The displayed supremum is therefore a verifiable termination certificate whenever it can be evaluated or bounded.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(x_0\in C\) and \(\gamma_0>0\), then compute the ordinary prediction and correction. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additively inexact Hilbert-space extragradient with summable errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_0\in C\), compute
\[
y_k=P_C\bigl(x_k-\gamma(F(x_k)+e_k)\bigr),\qquad x_{k+1}=P_C\bigl(x_k-\gamma(F(y_k)+d_k)\bigr).
\]
Terminate when \(\|x_k-y_k\|\leq\tau\), returning \(x_k\); otherwise continue. If the method is run indefinitely and the solution set \(S=\{x\in C:0\in F(x)+N_C(x)\}\) is nonempty, summability of the two error sequences preserves the standard quasi-Fejér convergence mechanism, and every weak cluster point belongs to \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extragradient remains convergent when both projection stages use summably inaccurate operator values; a small predictor displacement supplies a practical stopping rule.

assumptions_latex: The real cube-root convention is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The solution \(0\) is locally repelling for the fixed-step extragradient map.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete loss of local stability without Lipschitz regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The operator \(F(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}\) is continuous and monotone but is not locally Lipschitz at its unique zero. The unconstrained extragradient update is
\[
G_\gamma(x)=x-\gamma\sqrt[3]{x-\gamma\sqrt[3]{x}}.
\]
For sufficiently small \(x>0\), the predictor \(x-\gamma\sqrt[3]{x}\) is negative, and
\[
G_\gamma(x)=x+\gamma\sqrt[3]{\gamma x^{1/3}-x},\qquad \frac{G_\gamma(x)}{x}\longrightarrow+\infty
\]
as \(x\downarrow0\). Thus no neighborhood of the solution admits a contraction estimate for this fixed-step extragradient map; the usual Lipschitz-based stepsize argument breaks down.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone but non-Lipschitz cube-root operator makes the fixed-step extragradient solution locally repelling, so the usual Lipschitz stepsize analysis cannot apply.
knowledge_statements.title: Extragradient Regularity Breakdown

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and cube-root calculation fit the regularity-breakdown container, but the record supplies no inspectable source for the counterexample or for interpreting the displayed expansion as local repulsion. The calculation is plausible but requires independent citation or verification.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space.
\(F:C\to H\) is available through point evaluations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is an iterate satisfying the prescribed projected-residual tolerance, or the final iterate when the iteration budget is exhausted.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose \(x_{-1}=x_0\in C\). For \(k=0,1,\ldots\), form
\[
z_k=x_k+\theta_k(x_k-x_{k-1}),\qquad x_{k+1}=P_C\bigl(x_k-\gamma_kF(z_k)\bigr).
\]
The point \(z_k\) predicts a future location using the last displacement, while the projection keeps the new iterate feasible. Stop and return \(x_k\) when
\[
\bigl\|x_k-P_C(x_k-\gamma_kF(x_k))\bigr\|\leq\tau;
\]
if a finite iteration budget is imposed, return its last iterate. Particular extrapolation methods are obtained by prescribing \(\theta_k\), stepsize controls, and any safeguards ensuring that \(z_k\) lies in the domain of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The family evaluates the operator at a history-extrapolated point, then performs one projected forward step, with parameters and safeguards defining particular methods.

children.title: Extragradient–Extrapolation Relations
children.top_down_role: Structural relationships between extragradient corrections and extrapolation mechanisms.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space and \(C\subseteq H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(D\subseteq H\) contains \(C\), and \(F:D\to H\) is single-valued.
\(x_{k-1},x_k\in C\), \(\gamma_k>0\), \(\theta_k\geq0\), and the extrapolated point \(z_k=x_k+\theta_k(x_k-x_{k-1})\) belongs to \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two constructions generally define different updates; \(F(z_k)=F(y_k)\) is sufficient for equality of the displayed updates, but equality can also occur after projection even when the evaluation points or operator values differ.

notation.meaning: metric projection onto the feasible set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural comparison of projected extragradient and history-based extrapolation; no universal equivalence is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the projected extragradient step by
\[
y_k=P_C\bigl(x_k-\gamma_kF(x_k)\bigr),\qquad x_{k+1}^{\mathrm{EG}}=P_C\bigl(x_k-\gamma_kF(y_k)\bigr),
\]
and the projected history-extrapolation step by
\[
z_k=x_k+\theta_k(x_k-x_{k-1}),\qquad x_{k+1}^{\mathrm{EX}}=P_C\bigl(x_k-\gamma_kF(z_k)\bigr).
\]
The extragradient evaluation point is produced by a current projected forward prediction, whereas the extrapolation point is produced from stored iterates. Thus the methods generally differ. The identity \(F(z_k)=F(y_k)\) is sufficient for \(x_{k+1}^{\mathrm{EX}}=x_{k+1}^{\mathrm{EG}}\), but it is not necessary because the projection can map distinct forward points to the same feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extragradient obtains its off-iterate evaluation point from a fresh projected prediction, whereas history extrapolation obtains it from stored iterates. Their updates generally differ; matching operator values is sufficient but not necessary for the projected updates to coincide.
knowledge_statements.title: Extragradient–Extrapolation Relations

children.title: Exact Proximal Point Methods
children.top_down_role: Proximal-point methods based on exact proximal subproblems.

assumptions_latex: \(T=F+N_C\) is maximal monotone on a Hilbert space and \(\operatorname{zer}T\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each step is the exact resolvent evaluation \(x_{k+1}=J_{\lambda_kT}x_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact resolvent form of the proximal point method for a VI.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Starting from \(x_0\in H\), compute \(x_{k+1}\) as the exact solution of
\[
0\in F(x_{k+1})+N_C(x_{k+1})+\lambda_k^{-1}(x_{k+1}-x_k).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
x_{k+1}=J_{\lambda_kT}x_k.
\]
No residual or subproblem error is admitted in this accuracy regime. Stop and return \(x_{k+1}\) when \(\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|\leq\tau\); otherwise continue, or return the last iterate at the iteration limit. Every fixed point of \(J_{\lambda_kT}\) is a zero of \(T\), hence a solution of the original variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each iteration solves the regularized variational inequality exactly, equivalently applying the resolvent of the VI operator, and stops when successive iterates nearly coincide.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Proximal Point Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact-resolvent algorithm fits the leaf and its central inclusion is standard, but no proximal-point source is supplied. The assumptions do not independently introduce H, F, C, or the tolerance tau, and a positive displacement tolerance is only a stopping heuristic rather than an exact zero certificate.

children.title: Inexact Proximal Point Methods

assumptions_latex: \(T=F+N_C\) is maximal monotone and has a zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under the stated summability regime, the inexact proximal sequence converges weakly to a point of \(\operatorname{zer}T\).
review_flags: alternative relative-error models are excluded from this record
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute-error inexact proximal point method with summable residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_0\in H\), choose \(x_{k+1}\), \(v_{k+1}\in T(x_{k+1})\), and a residual \(r_{k+1}\) satisfying
\[
r_{k+1}=x_{k+1}-x_k+\lambda_kv_{k+1},
\qquad \|r_{k+1}\|\leq\eta_k.
\]
Thus each proximal inclusion is solved only to prescribed absolute accuracy. Stop and return \(x_{k+1}\) when both \(\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|\leq\tau\) and \(\eta_k\leq\tau\); otherwise continue. When run indefinitely with summable tolerances, this is a summably perturbed resolvent iteration and converges weakly to a zero of \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal inclusion may be solved with a summable absolute residual; convergence is retained when proximal parameters stay positive and the solution set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Proximal Point Methods

The record currently supplies none, and its stopping condition is not separately justified as an approximate-zero certificate.

children.title: Proximal Accuracy Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes connecting subproblem accuracy to method behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(x_k\) is the current point, \(x_{k+1}\) is an approximate proximal point, and \(v_{k+1}\in T(x_{k+1})\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact, absolute-error, and relative-error proximal regimes correspond respectively to \(r_{k+1}=0\), \(\|r_{k+1}\|\leq\eta_k\), and \(\|r_{k+1}\|\leq\sigma\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|\).
review_flags: relative-error conventions differ among proximal frameworks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three common residual criteria for proximal subproblem accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the proximal inclusion residual by
\[
r_{k+1}=x_{k+1}-x_k+\lambda_kv_{k+1},
\qquad v_{k+1}\in T(x_{k+1}).
\]
The exact regime requires \(r_{k+1}=0\). An absolute-error regime requires \(\|r_{k+1}\|\leq\eta_k\), commonly with \(\sum_k\eta_k<\infty\). A relative-error regime requires
\[
\|r_{k+1}\|\leq\sigma\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|,
\qquad 0\leq\sigma<1.
\]
These predicates regulate different quantities and are not interchangeable without additional bounds relating the step length, residual, and prescribed tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proximal subproblems can be exact, controlled by an absolute residual, or controlled relative to the current step; convergence assumptions depend on the chosen criterion.
knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Accuracy Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition is the correct role for an accuracy-regime container, but the relative residual rule is framework-dependent and has no cited source. assumptions_latex: \(T=F+N_C\) is maximal monotone with a nonempty zero set.
Each \(M_k\) is bounded, self-adjoint, and satisfies \(mI\preceq M_k\preceq MI\) for fixed \(0<m\leq M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update is the resolvent of \(T\) in the metric induced by \(M_k\).
review_flags: metric-variation conditions needed for convergence are not standardized here
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact variable-metric resolvent iteration for a monotone VI.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Starting from \(x_0\in H\), compute \(x_{k+1}\) from
\[
0\in T(x_{k+1})+\lambda_k^{-1}M_k(x_{k+1}-x_k),
\]
or equivalently
\[
x_{k+1}=\bigl(I+\lambda_kM_k^{-1}T\bigr)^{-1}x_k.
\]
Stop and return \(x_{k+1}\) when \(\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|_{M_k}\leq\tau\); otherwise continue. Uniform spectral bounds prevent degeneration of the metric. Weak convergence additionally requires an appropriate control on metric variation, such as \(M_{k+1}\preceq(1+\xi_k)M_k\) with \(\sum_k\xi_k<\infty\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_0\in H\), choose \(y_k\in H\), \(v_k\in H\), and \(\varepsilon_k\geq0\) such that
\[
v_k\in T^{[\varepsilon_k]}(y_k),
\qquad
\|\lambda_kv_k+y_k-x_k\|^2+2\lambda_k\varepsilon_k
\leq\sigma^2\|y_k-x_k\|^2.
\]
Then perform the extragradient update
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k-\lambda_kv_k.
\]
Stop and return \(y_k\) when \(\|v_k\|\leq\rho\) and \(\varepsilon_k\leq\epsilon\); otherwise continue. The displayed inequality is a directly checkable relative-error certificate for the approximate proximal computation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Tikhonov selection by a strongly convex merit function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(\varepsilon>0\), let \(x_\varepsilon\) solve
\[
0\in T(x_\varepsilon)+\varepsilon\nabla\phi(x_\varepsilon).
\]
Strong convexity makes the regularized operator strongly monotone, so the assumed regularized solution is unique. The unregularized solution set \(S\) is closed and convex, and coercive strong convexity gives a unique point
\[
x^\dagger=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S}\phi(x).
\]
As \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), the regularized solutions converge to \(x^\dagger\). Thus the vanishing Tikhonov term selects a distinguished solution rather than merely an arbitrary zero of \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vanishing strongly convex Tikhonov regularization selects the unique unregularized solution minimizing the chosen merit function.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed and convex, let \(F:K\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuous and monotone on \(K\), and let \(G:K\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuous and strongly monotone on \(K\). For the \(G\)-trajectory, the following are equivalent: its limit as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) exists; it is bounded near zero; and \(\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\ne\varnothing\). Whenever these conditions hold, the limit is the unique solution of \(\operatorname{VI}(\operatorname{SOL}(K,F),G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous monotone VI regularized by a continuous strongly monotone operator, convergence, boundedness near zero, and solvability are equivalent; the limit uniquely solves the secondary VI over the original solution set.
assumptions_latex: K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is closed and convex}
F:K\to\mathbb R^n\text{ is continuous and monotone on }K
G:K\to\mathbb R^n\text{ is continuous and strongly monotone on }K
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[\exists\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}x_G(\varepsilon)\right]\Longleftrightarrow\left[\limsup_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\|x_G(\varepsilon)\|<\infty\right]\Longleftrightarrow\left[\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\ne\varnothing\right],\quad \lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}x_G(\varepsilon)\text{ is the unique solution of }\operatorname{VI}(\operatorname{SOL}(K,F),G).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Least-norm selection by vanishing Tikhonov regularization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes solvability, boundedness near zero, and the selected limit for a continuous monotone VI.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed and convex, let \(F:K\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuous and monotone on \(K\), and let \(x(\varepsilon)\) be the Tikhonov trajectory. Then the following are equivalent: \(\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}x(\varepsilon)\) exists; \(\limsup_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\|x(\varepsilon)\|<\infty\); and \(\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\ne\varnothing\). Whenever these conditions hold, the limit is the least-norm solution of \(\operatorname{VI}(K,F)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous monotone VI on a closed convex set, existence of the vanishing-regularization limit, boundedness of the trajectory near zero, and solvability are equivalent; the limit is the least-norm solution.
assumptions_latex: K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is closed and convex}
F:K\to\mathbb R^n\text{ is continuous and monotone on }K
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[\exists\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}x(\varepsilon)\right]\Longleftrightarrow\left[\limsup_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\|x(\varepsilon)\|<\infty\right]\Longleftrightarrow\left[\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\ne\varnothing\right],\quad \lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}x(\varepsilon)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)}\|x\|.

assumptions_latex: \(T:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\) is maximal monotone with a nonempty zero set.
\(\phi\) is continuously differentiable, coercive, and strongly convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accumulation point obtained with sufficiently accurate regularized solves is the \(\phi\)-minimizing point of \(\operatorname{zer}T\).
review_flags: required coupling between solve errors and regularization requires certification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuation through approximately solved Tikhonov-regularized inclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose decreasing parameters \(\varepsilon_k>0\). At stage \(k\), warm-start from the preceding point and compute \(x_k\) with some \(v_k\in T(x_k)\) such that
\[
\|v_k+\varepsilon_k\nabla\phi(x_k)\|\leq\eta_k.
\]
Stop when the regularized residual is at most \(\tau\) and \(\varepsilon_k\leq\tau\); otherwise reduce \(\varepsilon_k\) and continue. Return the last \(x_k\). For solution-selection convergence, the inner accuracy must vanish faster than the regularization scale, for example \(\eta_k/\varepsilon_k\to0\); under the stated finite-dimensional assumptions, accumulation points then equal
\[
x^\dagger=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\operatorname{zer}T}\phi(x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method approximately solves increasingly weak Tikhonov regularizations, with inner errors vanishing faster than regularization, to approach the selected original solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Vanishing-Regularization Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is appropriate for the vanishing-regularization method leaf, but the required coupling between eta_k and epsilon_k and the resulting selection conclusion need a specific source. The conclusion's phrase 'sufficiently accurate' is not a quantified hypothesis; the ratio condition appears only later as an example.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convergence of a Subanalytic Tikhonov Trajectory
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundedness and convergence of the vanishing-regularization trajectory for a subanalytic P0 variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) have the structure specified in (12.2.1), with every \(K_\nu\) closed, convex, and subanalytic, and let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuous, \(\mathrm P_0\), and subanalytic. If \(x(\varepsilon)\) is the Tikhonov trajectory of \(\operatorname{VI}(K,F)\), then
\[
\limsup_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\|x(\varepsilon)\|<\infty
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}x(\varepsilon)\text{ exists}.
\]
Moreover, if \(\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\) is nonempty and bounded, then \(x(\varepsilon)\) converges as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) to a member of \(\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the stated structured feasible set and a continuous subanalytic P0 mapping, the Tikhonov trajectory is bounded as the regularization parameter approaches zero if and only if the trajectory converges. If the original VI has a nonempty bounded solution set, its limit is a solution of that VI.
assumptions_latex: K_\nu\text{ is closed, convex, and subanalytic for every }\nu
F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is continuous, }\mathrm P_0\text{, and subanalytic}
x(\varepsilon)\text{ is the Tikhonov trajectory of }\operatorname{VI}(K,F)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \limsup_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\|x(\varepsilon)\|<\infty\iff\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}x(\varepsilon)\text{ exists};\qquad \varnothing\ne\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\text{ bounded}\Rightarrow x(\varepsilon)\to x^*\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F).

assumptions_latex: \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone and \(B:H\to H\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iteration \(x_{k+1}=J_{\gamma A}(x_k-\gamma Bx_k)\) converges weakly to a point of \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space forward-backward convergence under cocoercivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Cocoercivity means
\[
\langle Bx-By,x-y\rangle\geq\beta\|Bx-By\|^2
\]
for all \(x,y\in H\). For \(0<\gamma<2\beta\), define
\[
x_{k+1}=T_\gamma x_k=J_{\gamma A}(x_k-\gamma Bx_k).
\]
The forward map \(I-\gamma B\) is averaged, the resolvent \(J_{\gamma A}\) is firmly nonexpansive, and their composition is averaged. Its fixed-point set equals \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\). Consequently, from any \(x_0\in H\), the iterates converge weakly to a zero of \(A+B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cocoercive forward operator permits forward-backward stepsizes below twice its cocoercivity constant, yielding weak convergence to a zero of the summed operators.
knowledge_statements.title: Cocoercive Forward–Backward Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind and stepsize range fit the cocoercive forward-backward regime, but no authoritative forward-backward section or theorem is cited. The statement also contains proof-outline material about averagedness and fixed-point sets, which should not remain in a proof-free knowledge statement.

children.title: Relaxed Forward–Backward Variants
children.top_down_role: Forward–backward variants organized by relaxation mechanisms.

assumptions_latex: \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone and \(B:H\to H\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_k\) is returned when a prescribed residual tolerance holds; otherwise any weak cluster limit under standard relaxation bounds solves \(0\in Ax+Bx\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space relaxed forward–backward iteration with a fixed metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_0\in H\), compute \(p_k=J_{\gamma A}(x_k-\gamma Bx_k)\) and update
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k+\lambda_k(p_k-x_k).
\]
Stop when \(\|x_k-p_k\|\leq\varepsilon\), and otherwise continue. Since \(T_\gamma\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged with \(\alpha=2\beta/(4\beta-\gamma)\), the displayed upper bound on \(\lambda_k\) is the admissible overrelaxation threshold; convergence additionally requires the relaxation sequence to remain suitably separated from its endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Apply a relaxed step toward the forward–backward resolvent point, allowing controlled overrelaxation; stop when the fixed-point residual is small.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxed Forward–Backward Variants

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the relaxed forward-backward leaf, but no citation is supplied. The assertion about weak cluster limits also depends on a precisely stated relaxation condition and nonemptiness of the zero set; the phrase "standard relaxation bounds" is not sufficient to determine the claimed convergence result.

children.title: Variable-Metric Forward–Backward Variants
children.top_down_role: Forward–backward variants using iteration-dependent metrics.

assumptions_latex: \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone and \(B:H\to H\) is single-valued.
\(U_k\) is self-adjoint and \(mI\preceq U_k\preceq MI\) for constants \(0<m\leq M<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is an approximate zero of \(A+B\), measured by the variable-metric fixed-point residual.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variable-metric forward–backward update; convergence conditions are separated into the interaction-regime record.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_0\in H\), positive steps \(\gamma_k\), relaxation parameters \(\lambda_k>0\), and metrics \(U_k\), compute
\[
p_k=J_{\gamma_kU_kA}(x_k-\gamma_kU_kBx_k),\qquad x_{k+1}=x_k+\lambda_k(p_k-x_k).
\]
Stop when \(\|x_k-p_k\|_{U_k^{-1}}\leq\varepsilon\). The metric bounds ensure that every metric norm is equivalent to the original Hilbert norm; admissible steps and relaxations must match the cocoercivity of \(U_kB\) in the \(U_k^{-1}\)-metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each iteration, precondition the forward step and resolvent by a uniformly positive metric, then relax toward the resulting point.
knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Metric Forward–Backward Variants

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The update has the correct variable-metric forward-backward form and algorithm is the correct content kind, but no citation is supplied. Moreover, the assumptions require only that B be single-valued, whereas the statement invokes cocoercivity of the preconditioned forward operator; admissible step, relaxation, and metric-variation hypotheses therefore cannot be verified.

children.title: Relaxation–Metric Interaction Regimes
children.top_down_role: Compatibility regimes for simultaneous relaxation and metric variation.

assumptions_latex: \(T_k:H\to H\) is \(\alpha_k\)-averaged in the norm induced by \(U_k^{-1}\), where \(0<\alpha_k<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under the stated coupling, \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\lambda_k(T_kx_k-x_k)\) is variable-metric quasi-Fejér with respect to \(S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract averaged-operator regime governing simultaneous relaxation and metric variation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose a constant \(\delta>0\) such that
\[
\delta\leq\lambda_k\leq\alpha_k^{-1}-\delta
\]
for every \(k\), and require the displayed summable metric variation. Then, for every \(s\in S\), the relaxed iteration satisfies a perturbed descent inequality of the form
\[
\|x_{k+1}-s\|_{U_{k+1}^{-1}}^2\leq(1+q_k)\|x_k-s\|_{U_k^{-1}}^2-c_k\|T_kx_k-x_k\|_{U_k^{-1}}^2,
\]
where \(\sum_kq_k<\infty\) and \(c_k>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxation must stay below each map’s averagedness threshold, while metric growth must be summable; together these conditions yield variable-metric quasi-Fejér descent.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation–Metric Interaction Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition is the appropriate content kind for this interaction-regime leaf, but the precise variable-metric quasi-Fejer inequality is not reliable without a source. In particular, an order condition on U_k does not automatically give the displayed comparison for the inverse-metric norms in the stated direction, and q_k and c_k are not defined quantitatively.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(z_k\) converges to \(z_\star\in\operatorname{Fix}T_{\mathrm{DR}}\), then \(x_\star=J_{\gamma B}z_\star\) satisfies \(0\in Ax_\star+Bx_\star\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-operator Hilbert-space Douglas–Rachford iteration with relaxed fixed-point updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(z_0\in H\). For \(k=0,1,\ldots\), compute
\[
x_k=J_{\gamma B}z_k,\qquad y_k=J_{\gamma A}(2x_k-z_k),\qquad z_{k+1}=z_k+\lambda_k(y_k-x_k).
\]
Stop when \(\|y_k-x_k\|\leq\varepsilon\), and output \(x_k\). Equivalently, \(z_{k+1}=z_k+\lambda_k(T_{\mathrm{DR}}z_k-z_k)\). Standard convergence requires relaxation parameters bounded away from \(0\) and \(2\), or an appropriate divergent-relaxation condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternate the two resolvents through reflection and update an auxiliary point; the shadow resolvent sequence approximates a zero of the operator sum.
knowledge_statements.title: Douglas–Rachford Splitting

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed Douglas-Rachford iteration and shadow-solution implication are standard and algorithm is the correct content kind, but no source is cited. The convergence discussion also refers only informally to an "appropriate divergent-relaxation condition," so its exact hypothesis cannot be reviewed.

assumptions_latex: \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) and \(B:G\rightrightarrows G\) are maximally monotone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A zero \((x,u)\) of \(\mathcal M+\mathcal K\) is exactly a primal–dual solution of the coupled inclusions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product-space interface converting a primal–dual system into a two-operator monotone inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The coupled primal–dual system
\[
0\in Ax+L^*u,
\qquad
0\in B^{-1}u-Lx
\]
is equivalent to
\[
0\in\mathcal M(x,u)+\mathcal K(x,u)
\]
on \(H\times G\). Here \(\mathcal M\) is maximally monotone and block-separable, while \(\mathcal K\) is bounded, linear, and skew-adjoint. Consequently, resolvent splitting on the product space evaluates \(J_A\) and \(J_{B^{-1}}\) separately and handles the coupling through multiplications by \(L\) and \(L^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coupled primal–dual system becomes a sum of a block-separable monotone operator and a skew linear operator on a product space.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Splitting Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The product-space representation matches the primal-dual interface leaf and representation is the correct content kind. However, no source is supplied, and the final implementation claim about resolvent splitting requires a specified splitting scheme and scaling or preconditioning conventions.

children.title: Regularized-Gap Algorithms
children.top_down_role: Gap-merit algorithms based on regularized gap constructions.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) is continuously differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the algorithm terminates at \(x_k\), then \(g_\alpha(x_k)\leq\varepsilon\); moreover, for every \(x\in K\), \(g_\alpha(x)=0\) if and only if \(x\) solves \(\operatorname{VI}(K,F)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected-gradient descent applied to the Euclidean regularized-gap merit function; the conclusion records only the certified termination property, not unconditional convergence to a minimizer.

source_refs.locator: 10.2.1 The regularized gap function p. 913
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
g_\alpha(x)=\max_{y\in K}\left\{\langle F(x),x-y\rangle-\frac{\alpha}{2}\|x-y\|^2\right\},
\qquad y_\alpha(x)=P_K\bigl(x-\alpha^{-1}F(x)\bigr).
\]
Starting from \(x_0\in K\), compute \(y_k=y_\alpha(x_k)\) and
\[
\nabla g_\alpha(x_k)=F(x_k)+F'(x_k)^\top(x_k-y_k)-\alpha(x_k-y_k).
\]
For a trial step \(t>0\), set \(z_k(t)=P_K(x_k-t\nabla g_\alpha(x_k))\). Use backtracking to choose \(t_k>0\) satisfying
\[
g_\alpha(z_k(t_k))\leq g_\alpha(x_k)+\sigma\langle\nabla g_\alpha(x_k),z_k(t_k)-x_k\rangle,
\]
then set \(x_{k+1}=z_k(t_k)\). Stop when \(g_\alpha(x_k)\leq\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Apply projected-gradient descent to the regularized gap using a projected Armijo test; termination certifies the requested gap tolerance, and zero gap exactly identifies a VI solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Regularized-Gap Algorithms

children.top_down_role: Gap-merit algorithms based on linearized gap constructions.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(g:K\to\mathbb R_+\) is a differentiable exact gap merit function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accepted iterates decrease \(g\), and termination at \(g(x_k)\leq\varepsilon\) yields an \(\varepsilon\)-gap solution.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic local-model algorithm for a differentiable exact gap function.

source_refs.locator: 10.2.2 The linearized gap function p. 921
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_k\in K\), choose a symmetric matrix \(H_k\succeq\mu I\) with \(\mu>0\), and form
\[
m_k(d)=g(x_k)+\langle\nabla g(x_k),d\rangle+\tfrac12\langle d,H_kd\rangle.
\]
Compute
\[
d_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{d:\,x_k+d\in K}m_k(d).
\]
Select \(t_k\in(0,1]\) by backtracking until \(g(x_k+t_kd_k)\leq g(x_k)+\sigma t_k\langle\nabla g(x_k),d_k\rangle\), where \(0<\sigma<1\), then set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+t_kd_k\). Stop when \(g(x_k)\leq\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize a linear-quadratic local model of an exact gap function, globalizing each feasible direction by an Armijo line search.
knowledge_statements.title: Linearized-Gap Algorithms

children.top_down_role: Structural comparison of the two gap constructions.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, \(F:K\to\mathbb R^n\), and \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(x\in K\), \(0\leq g_\alpha(x)\leq g_0(x)\), and both vanish exactly at solutions of \(\operatorname{VI}(K,F)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of unregularized and quadratically regularized primal gap constructions.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in K\), subtracting the nonnegative quadratic term gives
\[
0\leq g_\alpha(x)\leq g_0(x).
\]
Moreover, if \(0<\alpha_1<\alpha_2\), then
\[
g_{\alpha_2}(x)\leq g_{\alpha_1}(x),
\]
and \(g_\alpha(x)\uparrow g_0(x)\) as \(\alpha\downarrow0\), with extended-real values allowed. Unlike \(g_0\), the regularized gap has the unique maximizer \(P_K(x-\alpha^{-1}F(x))\), making its evaluation a strongly concave subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic regularization lowers the primal gap, gives a unique projection-based maximizer, preserves the zero set, and approaches the unregularized gap as regularization vanishes.
knowledge_statements.title: Gap-Construction Comparison

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
g_c(x)=\max_{y\in K}\left\{\langle F(x),x-y\rangle-\frac c2\|x-y\|^2\right\},
\qquad G_{a,b}(x)=g_a(x)-g_b(x).
\]
Initialize \(x_0\in K\). At iteration \(k\), compute both projection maximizers, evaluate \(G_{a,b}(x_k)\) and its gradient, choose a feasible descent direction \(d_k\), and select \(t_k>0\) by Armijo backtracking. Set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+t_kd_k\), and stop when \(G_{a,b}(x_k)\leq\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize the nonnegative difference of two regularized gaps using projection evaluations and line-search descent; its zeros are precisely VI solutions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global and local convergence of Algorithm 10.4.14
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence guarantees for the source-defined D-gap merit-function algorithm; condition (10.3.3) remains an unresolved source-defined hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be closed and convex, let F be continuously differentiable, let b>a>0, and let \{x^k\} be an infinite sequence generated by Algorithm 10.4.14. Every accumulation point of \{x^k\} is stationary for \theta_{ab}. If an accumulation point x^* satisfies (10.3.3), then x^* solves \operatorname{VI}(K,F). If \{x^k\} has an isolated limit point, the whole sequence converges to that point. If x^* is both a limit point and a stable solution of \operatorname{VI}(K,F), then x^k\to x^*. Furthermore, if p>2 and \gamma<\tfrac12 in Algorithm 10.4.14, then eventually d^k=x^{k+1/2}-x^k, unit steps are accepted, and convergence is Q-superlinear; if JF is also Lipschitz continuous near x^*, convergence is Q-quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every accumulation point generated by Algorithm 10.4.14 is stationary for the D-gap merit function. Under the source-defined condition (10.3.3), an accumulation point solves the VI. An isolated limit point attracts the whole sequence, while a stable solution that is a limit point yields whole-sequence convergence and, under the stated algorithm parameters, eventual unit steps and superlinear or locally quadratic convergence.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asymptotic upper bound for normalized D-gap merit values
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter-scaling property of the normalized D-gap merit function over a compact convex VI set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be compact and convex. For every x\in\mathbb{R}^n and every 0<\bar a<\bar b, \limsup_{\substack{a\downarrow0\\b\to\infty}}\frac{\theta_{ab}(x)}{b-a}\le\frac{\theta_{\bar a\bar b}(x)}{\bar b-\bar a}. Consequently, for every \eta>0, there exist a,b>0 such that a\le\tfrac12\bar a, b\ge2\bar b, and \frac{\theta_{ab}(x)}{b-a}\le\frac{\theta_{\bar a\bar b}(x)}{\bar b-\bar a}+\eta.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a compact convex feasible set, the limsup of the normalized D-gap merit value as the lower parameter decreases to zero and the upper parameter tends to infinity is no greater than its value at any fixed positive parameter pair. Consequently, the parameters can be reduced and enlarged by the stated factors while increasing the normalized value by at most any prescribed positive tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \limsup_{\substack{a\downarrow0\\b\to\infty}}\frac{\theta_{ab}(x)}{b-a}\le\frac{\theta_{\bar a\bar b}(x)}{\bar b-\bar a},\quad\text{and }\exists a,b>0:\ a\le\tfrac12\bar a,\ b\ge2\bar b,\ \frac{\theta_{ab}(x)}{b-a}\le\frac{\theta_{\bar a\bar b}(x)}{\bar b-\bar a}+\eta.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithm 10.4.11 retains Algorithm 10.4.8 except for an adaptive Step 5.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given c>0 and \varepsilon>0, follow Algorithm 10.4.8 except in Step 5. knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose \(x_0\in K\), \(0<\sigma<1\), and \(0<\rho<1\). At iteration \(k\), select \(d_k\) satisfying
\[
\langle\nabla\mathcal L(x_k),d_k\rangle<0

\mathcal L(x_k+\rho^{j_k}d_k)\leq\mathcal L(x_k)+\sigma\rho^{j_k}\langle\nabla\mathcal L(x_k),d_k\rangle.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(z_0\in\mathbb R^n\). At iteration \(k\), set \(x_k=P_Kz_k\), form
\[
\Phi'(z_k)=F'(x_k)P_K'(z_k)+I-P_K'(z_k),
\]
and solve
\[
\Phi'(z_k)d_k=-\Phi(z_k).
\]
Set \(z_{k+1}=z_k+d_k\), optionally replacing the unit step by a merit-function line search. Stop when \(\|\Phi(z_k)\|\leq\varepsilon\), and output \(x_k=P_Kz_k\). A zero of \(\Phi\) is equivalent to a solution of \(\operatorname{VI}(K,F)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Restricted Jacobian nonsingularity implies natural-map regularity and semistability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient regularity conditions for natural-map Newton approximations of a polyhedrally constrained VI.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Bx\le d\}, let x^* solve \operatorname{VI}(K,F), and suppose F is continuously differentiable near x^*. For each \mathcal J\in\mathcal B_*', let L_{\mathcal J}=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:B_{\mathcal J}v=0\}. If JF(x^*) is nonsingular on L_{\mathcal J} for every \mathcal J\in\mathcal B_*', then, for every a>0, every matrix in \mathcal A_a^{\mathrm{nat}}(x^*) is nonsingular. Moreover, x^* is a semistable solution of \operatorname{VI}(K,F), and v^THv>0 for every v\ne0 and every H\in\partial_v^2\theta_{ab}(x^*).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the Jacobian is nonsingular on every relevant active-set subspace, all source-defined natural-map Newton matrices are nonsingular for every positive scaling parameter. The VI solution is semistable, and every stated generalized second-order merit matrix is positive definite.
assumptions_latex: JF(x^*)\text{ is nonsingular on }L_{\mathcal J}\text{ for every }\mathcal J\in\mathcal B_*'
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\forall a>0)(\forall H\in\mathcal A_a^{\mathrm{nat}}(x^*))\ H\text{ is nonsingular};\qquad x^*\text{ is semistable};\qquad (\forall v\ne0)(\forall H\in\partial_v^2\theta_{ab}(x^*))\ v^THv>0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Rate Regimes for the Inexact Josephy–Newton Method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniformly small, vanishing, and residual-proportional forcing sequences yield progressively stronger local convergence rates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $F$ be continuously differentiable, and assume that $x^*$ is a stable solution of $\operatorname{VI}(K,F^*)$, where $F^*$ is defined by (7.3.7). There exists $\bar\eta>0$ such that, if $\eta_k\leq\bar\eta$ for every $k$, then for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $\delta>0$ such that every admissible initial point $x^0\in K\cap\mathbb B(x^*,\delta)$ makes Algorithm 7.3.7 generate a well-defined sequence in $\mathbb B(x^*,\delta)$, and every such sequence converges Q-linearly to $x^*$. If $\eta_k\to0$, convergence is Q-superlinear. If additionally $JF$ is Lipschitz continuous near $x^*$ and $\eta_k\leq\widetilde\eta\|\mathbf F_K^{\mathrm{nat}}(x^k)\|$ for some $\widetilde\eta>0$ and every $k$, convergence is Q-quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniformly small forcing terms give local Q-linear convergence of every generated inexact Josephy–Newton sequence; vanishing forcing terms give Q-superlinear convergence, and residual-proportional forcing together with a locally Lipschitz Jacobian gives Q-quadratic convergence.
assumptions_latex: x^*\text{ is a stable solution of }\operatorname{VI}(K,F^*)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^k\to x^*\text{ Q-linearly};\quad \eta_k\to0\Rightarrow x^k\to x^*\text{ Q-superlinearly};\quad JF\text{ Lipschitz near }x^*\text{ and }\eta_k\leq\widetilde\eta\|\mathbf F_K^{\mathrm{nat}}(x^k)\|\Rightarrow x^k\to x^*\text{ Q-quadratically.}

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Map Irregularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of Clarke-generalized-Jacobian regularity at a normal-map root in semismooth Newton analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the semismooth Newton regularity notion used here, a root \(z^*\) is Clarke-regular when every \(V\in\partial G(z^*)\) is nonsingular. Its corresponding irregularity boundary is \[G(z^*)=0\quad\text{and}\quad \exists V\in\partial G(z^*)\text{ such that }\det V=0.\] At this boundary, the uniform inverse condition used by the standard local semismooth Newton theorem is not satisfied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the Clarke-generalized-Jacobian sense used for this Newton analysis, a normal-map root is irregular when at least one generalized Jacobian at the root is singular.
assumptions_latex: \(G:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is locally Lipschitz near a root \(z^*\).
\(\partial G(z^*)\) denotes the Clarke generalized Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Clarke regularity fails exactly when \(\exists V\in\partial G(z^*)\) with \(\det V=0\).

notation.meaning: Clarke generalized Jacobian of the normal map at the root

children.title: Path-Search Methods
children.top_down_role: Globalization methods organized around searches over solution paths.

knowledge_statements.title: Path-Search Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Merit globalization by backtracking along a differentiable nonlinear Newton-related path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x^0\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(\beta,c\in(0,1)\), and \(\varepsilon>0\), construct at each nonterminal iteration a path \(p_k:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(p_k(0)=x^k\) and a strictly descending initial merit derivative. Choose the first \(t_k=\beta^{j_k}\), \(j_k\geq0\), for which \(p_k(t_k)\neq x^k\) and \[\Psi(p_k(t_k))\leq\Psi(x^k)-c\|p_k(t_k)-x^k\|^2.\] Set \(x^{k+1}=p_k(t_k)\), and stop when \(\|H(x^k)\|\leq\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Backtrack along a differentiable curved path whose initial motion decreases the residual merit, accepting only a nonzero trial point with the prescribed strict merit decrease.
assumptions_latex: For each nonterminal iterate, \(p_k:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is differentiable at \(0\), satisfies \(p_k(0)=x^k\), and the right derivative of \(t\mapsto\Psi(p_k(t))\) at \(0\) exists and is negative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted nonterminal update satisfies \(p_k(t_k)\neq x^k\) and \(\Psi(x^{k+1})<\Psi(x^k)\).

notation.meaning: Equation residual and squared-residual merit function

children.title: Search-Framework Comparison
children.top_down_role: Structural distinctions between path-based and step-based globalization.

knowledge_statements.title: Search-Framework Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric relation between line-search and path-search globalization frameworks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(k\), line search considers trial points \(x^k+td^k\) with \(t\in[0,1]\), whereas path search considers \(p_k(t)\) with \(t\in[0,1]\), where \(p_k(0)=x^k\) and \(p_k'(0)=d^k\). Choosing \(p_k(t)=x^k+td^k\) recovers line search as a special case of the path-search framework. For a genuinely curved \(p_k\), the trial set is generally different from, and need not contain, the straight line-search segment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Line search is the special path search obtained from a straight path; a curved path generally supplies a different trial set, not necessarily a superset of the Newton ray.
assumptions_latex: The path \(p_k:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is differentiable at \(0\), with \(p_k(0)=x^k\) and \(p_k'(0)=d^k\).
Both frameworks evaluate the same merit function \(\Psi(x)=\tfrac12\|H(x)\|^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Line search is obtained by the special choice \(p_k(t)=x^k+td^k\); a curved path generally yields a different trial set without implying set inclusion.

knowledge_statements.title: Trust-Region Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trust-region globalization for a locally Lipschitz residual equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x^0\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(\Delta_0>0\), \(\eta\in(0,1)\), and \(\varepsilon>0\), compute a trial step \(d^k\) with \(\|d^k\|\leq\Delta_k\) and positive predicted reduction \(m_k(0)-m_k(d^k)>0\). Define \[\rho_k=\frac{\Psi(x^k)-\Psi(x^k+d^k)}{m_k(0)-m_k(d^k)}.\] If \(\rho_k\geq\eta\), set \(x^{k+1}=x^k+d^k\); otherwise set \(x^{k+1}=x^k\). Adjust \(\Delta_k\) using fixed thresholds for poor or good model agreement, and stop when \(\|H(x^k)\|\leq\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a model-reducing step inside the trust region, accept it when actual reduction is a sufficient positive fraction of predicted reduction, and adapt the radius using model agreement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Whenever \(\rho_k\geq\eta>0\), the accepted step satisfies \(\Psi(x^k+d^k)<\Psi(x^k)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Potential-Reduction Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interior logarithmic-potential reduction template for nonlinear complementarity equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\rho>0\), define \[\Phi_\rho(x,y)=(n+\rho)\log(x^Ty)-\sum_{i=1}^n\log(x_iy_i)\] on strictly positive pairs. At an interior iterate \((x^k,y^k)\), compute a Newton-type direction from the linearization of \(F(x)-y=0\) together with a positively perturbed complementarity equation \(Xy=\tau_ke\), where \(\tau_k>0\). Select a step length that preserves \(x^{k+1}>0\) and \(y^{k+1}>0\), and accept it only when the prescribed potential-and-feasibility merit test decreases. Stop when both \(\|F(x^k)-y^k\|\) and \((x^k)^Ty^k\) do not exceed \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute a Newton step for feasibility and positively perturbed complementarity, shorten it to preserve strict positivity, and accept it only under the chosen potential-and-feasibility decrease test.
assumptions_latex: The nonlinear complementarity problem is \(x\geq0\), \(y=F(x)\geq0\), and \(x^Ty=0\).
Every trial step begins from a strictly interior pair \(x>0\), \(y>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted update preserves strict positivity and satisfies the prescribed potential-and-feasibility merit decrease; no convergence-to-zero conclusion is asserted without additional global assumptions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fischer–Burmeister noninterior path-following algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Newton correction with residual backtracking followed by backtracking reduction of the smoothing parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \((\mu_0,\eta)>0\), \((x^0,y^0,z^0)\) with \(\|\mathbf\Psi_{\mu_0}(x^0,y^0,z^0)\|^2\le\eta\mu_0\), and \(\gamma,\gamma',\rho,\rho'\in(0,1)\). At iteration \(k\), terminate if \(H(x^k,y^k,z^k)=0\) and \(\mathbf\Psi_{\mathrm{FB}}(x^k,y^k,z^k)=0\). Otherwise solve \(\mathbf H_{\mathrm{FB}_{\mu_k}}(w^k)+J\mathbf H_{\mathrm{FB}_{\mu_k}}(w^k)d^k=0\). If the residual is zero set \(\tau_k=0\); otherwise select the first \(\tau_k\in\{1,\rho,\rho^2,\ldots\}\) satisfying \(\|\mathbf H_{\mathrm{FB}_{\mu_k}}(w^k+\tau_kd^k)\|^2\le(1-\gamma\tau_k)\|\mathbf H_{\mathrm{FB}_{\mu_k}}(w^k)\|^2\), and set \(w^{k+1}=w^k+\tau_kd^k\). Select the first \(\delta_k\in\{1,\rho',({\rho'})^2,\ldots\}\) such that \(\|\mathbf H_{\mathrm{FB}_{(1-\gamma'\delta_k)\mu_k}}(w^{k+1})\|^2\le\|H(w^0)\|^2+(1-\gamma'\delta_k)\eta\mu_k\), and set \(\mu_{k+1}=(1-\gamma'\delta_k)\mu_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a point whose smoothed residual is controlled by the initial smoothing parameter, repeatedly compute a Newton correction, backtrack until the fixed-parameter smoothed residual decreases sufficiently, then backtrack the smoothing-parameter reduction until the prescribed neighborhood condition is retained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{(x^k,y^k,z^k),\mu_k\}\text{ is generated by the stated Newton and two-stage backtracking updates until the complementarity system is solved.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Accumulation-Point Solvability and Boundedness for Noninterior Path-Following
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithm-specific conditional guarantees for an infinite sequence generated by Algorithm 11.7.2 for the implicit mixed complementarity problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H:\mathbb{R}^{2n+m}\to\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\) be continuously differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}_+^{2n}\times\mathbb{R}^m\), and suppose that \(JH(x,y,z)\) has the mixed \(P_0\) property for every \((x,y,z)\in\mathcal N(\mu_0,\eta)\). Let \(\{(x^k,y^k,z^k)\}\) be an infinite sequence generated by Algorithm 11.7.2. (a) Let \((x^\infty,y^\infty,z^\infty)\) be the limit of a convergent subsequence indexed by \(\kappa\). If conditions (a) and (b) of Lemma 11.7.4 hold for every accumulation point \((D_x^\infty,D_y^\infty)\) of the bounded sequence \(\{(D_x^k,D_y^k):k\in\kappa\}\), then \((x^\infty,y^\infty,z^\infty)\) is a solution of the implicit MiCP (11.1.3). (b) If \(\mathcal N(\mu_0,\eta)\) is bounded, then \(\{(x^k,y^k,z^k)\}\) is bounded.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonsingularity of the limiting noninterior smoothing Jacobian
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A limiting regularity condition based on an active complementary principal block and its reduced Schur complement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H:\mathbb R^{2n+m}\to\mathbb R^{n+m}\) be continuously differentiable, let \((x^k,y^k,z^k)\to(x^\infty,y^\infty,z^\infty)\), and let \(\mu_k>0\). Define diagonal \(D_x^k,D_y^k\) by \(((D_x^k)_{ii},(D_y^k)_{ii})=(x_i^k,y_i^k)/\sqrt{(x_i^k)^2+(y_i^k)^2+2\mu_k}-(1,1)\), and suppose \((D_x^k,D_y^k)\to(D_x^\infty,D_y^\infty)\). Put \(\mathcal J_x=\{i:(D_x^\infty)_{ii}=0\}\), \(\mathcal J_y=\{i:(D_y^\infty)_{ii}=0\}\), and \(\mathcal J=\mathcal J_x\cup\mathcal J_y\). If the corresponding complementary principal submatrix \([J_xH^\infty\ J_yH^\infty]_{\mathcal J\mathcal J}\) is nonsingular and its reduced Schur complement in \(JH^\infty\) has the mixed \(P_0\) property, then \(\begin{bmatrix}D_x^\infty&D_y^\infty&0\\J_xH^\infty&J_yH^\infty&J_zH^\infty\end{bmatrix}\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convergent sequence of smoothed complementarity systems, the limiting augmented Jacobian is nonsingular when its zero-diagonal active block is a nonsingular complementary principal submatrix and the associated reduced Schur complement has the mixed-P0 property.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{bmatrix}D_x^\infty&D_y^\infty&0\\J_xH^\infty&J_yH^\infty&J_zH^\infty\end{bmatrix}\text{ is nonsingular.}

children.title: Exterior Barrier Reductions

assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuous, and solutions of the penalized equations remain bounded as \(\rho\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any accumulation point with vanishing violation solves the original VI when the limiting multiplier \(\nu=\lim\rho(Gx-h)_+\) exists and satisfies stationarity and complementarity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exterior penalty interpretation; the taxonomy’s barrier terminology requires confirmation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\rho>0\), permit inequality-infeasible trial points and solve the exterior reduction \[F(x)+A^\top\lambda+G^\top\nu_\rho(x)=0,
\qquad Ax=b,\qquad \nu_\rho(x)=\rho(Gx-h)_+.\] Increase \(\rho\) and terminate when both the equation residual and \(\|(Gx-h)_+\|\) meet prescribed tolerances. Unlike an interior barrier equation, this residual is defined on infeasible points and drives violations toward zero through an exterior penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exterior reduction allows infeasible iterates and penalizes positive constraint violations increasingly strongly until feasibility and stationarity are recovered.

Under boundedness and consistency of their induced multipliers, both limiting processes yield \[F(x)+A^\top\lambda+G^\top\nu=0,\qquad Ax=b,\qquad 0\leq\nu\perp h-Gx\geq0.\] They therefore differ in path geometry, not in the target complementarity system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interior reductions maintain strict feasibility, whereas exterior reductions may violate constraints; under consistency assumptions, both converge to the same KKT-complementarity system.
knowledge_statements.title: Barrier-Regime Comparison

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The comparison is coherent only after interpreting the exterior sibling as the proposed penalty method. children.title: Pointwise Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Guarantees attached to individually selected iterates.

assumptions_latex: An algorithm generates \(x_0,\ldots,x_N\in C\) for a VI on \(C\).
\(R:C\to[0,\infty]\) is a specified residual with \(R(x)=0\) exactly at solutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The run has an \(N\)-step pointwise guarantee at level \(\varepsilon_N\) when \(\min_{0\leq k\leq N}R(x_k)\leq\varepsilon_N\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best-individual-iterate output guarantee, distinct from averaging and terminal output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an iteration budget \(N\), select \[k_N\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{0\leq k\leq N}R(x_k)\] and output \(x_{k_N}\). A pointwise complexity statement is a bound \[R(x_{k_N})=\min_{0\leq k\leq N}R(x_k)\leq\varepsilon_N.\] Equivalently, achieving tolerance \(\varepsilon\) requires at most the least \(N\) for which \(\varepsilon_N\leq\varepsilon\), with one iteration counted according to the declared oracle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pointwise guarantee certifies that at least one individual iterate among the first N has small residual and outputs the best such iterate.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Guarantees

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed inequality defines a best-individual-iterate output condition but supplies no instantiated rate, algorithm, residual, or oracle cost, so it is not yet a complexity bound. No source confirms that this is the intended meaning of 'pointwise' in the exact container.

children.title: Last-Iterate Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Guarantees attached specifically to the terminal iterate.

assumptions_latex: An algorithm generates \(x_0,\ldots,x_N\in C\) for a VI on \(C\).
\(R:C\to[0,\infty]\) is a specified residual with \(R(x)=0\) exactly at solutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The run has an \(N\)-step last-iterate guarantee at level \(\varepsilon_N\) precisely when \(R(x_N)\leq\varepsilon_N\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminal-iterate output guarantee without best-iterate selection or averaging.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After exactly \(N\) declared oracle iterations, output the terminal point \(x_N\). A last-iterate complexity statement has the form \[R(x_N)\leq\varepsilon_N.\] Consequently, tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\) is reached within the least budget \(N\) satisfying \(\varepsilon_N\leq\varepsilon\). This requirement is stronger than the corresponding pointwise assertion \(\min_{0\leq k\leq N}R(x_k)\leq\varepsilon_N\), because it certifies the prescribed terminal output itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A last-iterate guarantee bounds the VI residual of the terminal iterate itself, without selecting an earlier or averaged output.
knowledge_statements.title: Last-Iterate Guarantees

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record accurately distinguishes a terminal residual condition from a best-iterate condition, but an arbitrary sequence epsilon_N without an algorithm, rate, residual, or oracle model is a definition or condition rather than a complexity bound. A specific source is also absent.

children.title: Pointwise-to-Terminal Transfer
children.top_down_role: Regimes where pointwise control informs terminal-iterate behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(r_k\ge 0\) is a pointwise residual or gap attached to iterate \(x_k\).
A nonincreasing bound \(B:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}_+\) satisfies \(r_k\le B(k)\) for every generated index \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_N\le B(N)\) for every terminal index \(N\).

notation.meaning: residual or gap at the kth iterate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer requires a bound valid at every index, not merely at one selected or averaged iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((x_k)_{k\ge 0}\) be iterates and let \(r_k\ge 0\) measure their VI error. If an analysis establishes the pointwise estimate \(r_k\le B(k)\) simultaneously for every \(k\), where \(B\) is nonincreasing, then choosing the algorithm's terminal output as \(x_N\) gives \(r_N\le B(N)\). An estimate only of the form \(\min_{0\le k\le N}r_k\le B(N)\) does not imply this terminal guarantee without an additional relation controlling \(r_N\) by earlier residuals.

assumptions_latex: The weighted cumulative estimate \(\sum_{k=0}^{N}w_kr_k\le E_N\) holds for some \(E_N\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(k_*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{0\le k\le N}r_k\) satisfies \(r_{k_*}\le E_N/\sum_{k=0}^{N}w_k\).

notation.meaning: nonnegative VI error measure at iterate k
an index attaining the smallest observed residual

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a weighted minimum is bounded by the corresponding weighted average
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is a best-iterate certificate, not by itself an iteration-complexity rate or a last-iterate guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N\in\mathbb{N}\). Given iterates \(x_0,\ldots,x_N\), errors \(r_k\ge 0\), and weights \(w_k>0\), suppose \(\sum_{k=0}^{N}w_kr_k\le E_N\). For any \(k_*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{0\le k\le N}r_k\), \[r_{k_*}=\min_{0\le k\le N}r_k\le \frac{\sum_{k=0}^{N}w_kr_k}{\sum_{k=0}^{N}w_k}\le \frac{E_N}{\sum_{k=0}^{N}w_k}.\] Therefore the first \(N+1\) iterates contain an output with error at most \(\varepsilon\) whenever \(E_N\le\varepsilon\sum_{k=0}^{N}w_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted cumulative error estimate certifies that a best iterate has error no larger than the corresponding weighted average.
knowledge_statements.title: Best-Iterate Guarantees

assumptions_latex: The dual gap \(g_D(x)=\sup_{y\in C}\langle F(y),x-y\rangle\) is finite at the relevant points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(\bar x_N=(\sum_{k=0}^{N}w_kx_k)/(\sum_{k=0}^{N}w_k)\), \(g_D(\bar x_N)\le(\sum_{k=0}^{N}w_kg_D(x_k))/(\sum_{k=0}^{N}w_k)\).

auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the weighted-average guarantee for the dual gap, which is convex in its iterate argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For generated points \(x_0,\ldots,x_N\in C\) and weights \(w_k>0\), define \(W_N=\sum_{k=0}^{N}w_k\) and \(\bar x_N=W_N^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{N}w_kx_k\). Because \(g_D(x)=\sup_{y\in C}\langle F(y),x-y\rangle\) is a supremum of affine functions of \(x\), it is convex. Consequently, \[g_D(\bar x_N)\le \frac{1}{W_N}\sum_{k=0}^{N}w_kg_D(x_k).\] Hence any cumulative estimate \(\sum_{k=0}^{N}w_kg_D(x_k)\le E_N\) yields the ergodic certificate \(g_D(\bar x_N)\le E_N/W_N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual gap at a weighted average of iterates is at most the weighted average of their dual gaps.
knowledge_statements.title: Ergodic Guarantees

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and has diameter at most \(D\).
Exact operator evaluations and Euclidean projections are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After \(N\) extragradient steps, an ergodic output satisfies \(g_D(\bar x_N)\le cLD^2/N\) using at most \(2N\) evaluations and \(2N\) projections, for an absolute constant \(c\).

dual gap of the ergodic output

review_flags: Exact algorithmic convention and constant require an authoritative complexity reference.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean deterministic first-order complexity for bounded, monotone, Lipschitz variational inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the VI on \(C\) with monotone, \(L\)-Lipschitz operator \(F\), and define \(g_D(x)=\sup_{y\in C}\langle F(y),x-y\rangle\). A Euclidean extragradient method with a constant step proportional to \(1/L\) forms two projected points and uses two operator evaluations per iteration. For its standard weighted-average output \(\bar x_N\), there is an absolute constant \(c>0\) such that \[g_D(\bar x_N)\le \frac{cLD^2}{N}.\] Therefore \(g_D(\bar x_N)\le\varepsilon\) requires \(O(LD^2/\varepsilon)\) operator evaluations and projections in this oracle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extragradient attains an ergodic dual-gap accuracy of order one over the iteration count for bounded monotone Lipschitz VIs.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotone VI Complexity

assumptions_latex: Euclidean projections and exact evaluations of \(F\) are available.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: contraction follows from strong monotonicity, Lipschitz continuity, and nonexpansiveness of projection

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A conservative projected-gradient complexity bound; accelerated or extragradient variants may improve condition-number dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^*\) be the unique VI solution and set \(\alpha=\mu/L^2\). The projected iteration \[x_{k+1}=P_C\bigl(x_k-\alpha F(x_k)\bigr)\] uses one operator evaluation and one projection per iteration and satisfies \[\|x_{k+1}-x^*\|\le q\|x_k-x^*\|,\qquad q=\sqrt{1-\mu^2/L^2}<1.\] Consequently, \(\|x_k-x^*\|\le q^k\|x_0-x^*\|\), and distance accuracy \(\varepsilon\) is attained after at most \[\left\lceil\frac{\log(\|x_0-x^*\|/\varepsilon)}{-\log q}\right\rceil\] operator evaluations and projections.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong monotonicity makes projected iteration contract linearly, yielding logarithmic dependence on the requested distance accuracy.
knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Monotone VI Complexity

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the projected natural residual by \[R_\gamma(x)=\frac{1}{\gamma}\bigl\|x-P_C(x-\gamma F(x))\bigr\|.\] For every \(\gamma>0\), \(R_\gamma(x)=0\) if and only if \(x\) solves \(\langle F(x),y-x\rangle\ge 0\) for all \(y\in C\). children.title: Operator-Evaluation Oracles
children.top_down_role: Computational interfaces for accessing operator values.

assumptions_latex: Queries are made only at points \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An exact evaluation oracle returns \(\mathcal{O}_F(x)=F(x)\), and evaluation complexity is the number of such calls.

notation.meaning: number of oracle calls made by an algorithm

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact deterministic black-box evaluations; stochastic and inexact evaluation models are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An exact operator-evaluation oracle for \(F:C\to\mathbb{R}^d\) is a mapping \(\mathcal{O}_F\) that, on every admissible query \(x\in C\), returns \[\mathcal{O}_F(x)=F(x).\] The algorithm may choose each query adaptively from previous oracle responses and internal computations. Its operator-evaluation complexity is \(N_F\), the total number of calls to \(\mathcal{O}_F\) before producing its declared output. Arithmetic, projection, and proximal-subproblem costs are not included in \(N_F\) unless the stated cost model explicitly assigns them evaluation-equivalent weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact evaluation oracle returns the operator value at a queried feasible point; complexity counts how many such queries are made.
knowledge_statements.title: Operator-Evaluation Oracles

children.title: Projection Oracles
children.top_down_role: Computational interfaces for projections onto feasible sets.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The projection oracle returns \(\mathcal{O}_{P_C}(z)=P_C(z)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in C}\tfrac12\|y-z\|^2\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact single-valued Euclidean projection onto a closed convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a query \(z\in\mathbb{R}^d\), an exact Euclidean projection oracle returns \[\mathcal{O}_{P_C}(z)=P_C(z)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in C}\frac12\|y-z\|^2.\] Closedness and convexity of \(C\) make this minimizer unique. The projection complexity \(N_P\) of an algorithm is the number of calls to \(\mathcal{O}_{P_C}\) before termination. This count treats each projection as one oracle operation, independently of the internal arithmetic needed to solve the projection subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projection oracle returns the unique closest feasible point to its query, and projection complexity counts these calls.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Oracles

assumptions_latex: An algorithm makes \(N_F\) exact operator evaluations and \(N_P\) exact projections.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Its weighted oracle cost is \(C_{EP}=c_FN_F+c_PN_P\), while the pair \((N_F,N_P)\) retains separate resource counts.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: additive two-resource oracle accounting model
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates oracle counts before optionally scalarizing them with implementation-dependent unit costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The evaluation-projection resource profile of an algorithm is the ordered pair \((N_F,N_P)\), where \(N_F\) counts operator evaluations and \(N_P\) counts projections. Given declared unit costs \(c_F,c_P\ge 0\), its scalarized cost is \[C_{EP}=c_FN_F+c_PN_P.\] A complexity claim must report either the pair \((N_F,N_P)\) or the weights used in \(C_{EP}\). Consequently, two methods with equal iteration counts need not have equal cost when they use different numbers of evaluations or projections per iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cost model records evaluation and projection counts separately, or combines them using explicitly declared per-call weights.
knowledge_statements.title: Evaluation–Projection Cost Models

children.title: Proximal Oracles
children.top_down_role: Computational interfaces providing proximal subproblem solutions.

assumptions_latex: \(h:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex, with \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}h\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The proximal oracle returns the unique minimizer of \(h(y)+\iota_C(y)+(2\lambda)^{-1}\|y-z\|^2\).

notation.meaning: proximal mapping of h restricted to C

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Euclidean proximal oracle for a convex function with an optional convex constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each query \((z,\lambda)\in\mathbb{R}^d\times(0,\infty)\), the exact proximal oracle returns \[\operatorname{prox}^{C}_{\lambda h}(z)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in C}\left\{h(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|y-z\|^2\right\}.\] Equivalently, it minimizes \(h+\iota_C+(2\lambda)^{-1}\|\cdot-z\|^2\) over \(\mathbb{R}^d\). The quadratic term makes the objective strongly convex on its effective domain, so the returned point is unique. Proximal-oracle complexity counts the number of such exact subproblem solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximal oracle exactly minimizes a convex function plus a quadratic regularizer, optionally subject to the feasible-set constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Oracles

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(h:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex with \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}h\ne\varnothing\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in C\), define the dual gap \(g_D(x)=\max_{y\in C}\langle F(y),x-y\rangle\). The maximum exists and \(g_D(x)\geq0\), since \(y=x\) is admissible. Thus, for every tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq0\), the condition \(g_D(x)\leq\varepsilon\) is a nonnegative gap certificate.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F:\mathbb R_+^N\to\mathbb R^N and x_0\in\mathbb R_+^N. Then F(x_0)\in\mathbb R_+^N and \langle F(x_0),x_0\rangle=0 if and only if \langle F(x_0),y-x_0\rangle\ge 0 for every y\in\mathbb R_+^N.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative point satisfies the orthant complementarity conditions exactly when it solves the corresponding variational inequality over the nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(F(x_0)\in\mathbb R_+^N\ \land\ \langle F(x_0),x_0\rangle=0\bigr)\iff\bigl(\langle F(x_0),y-x_0\rangle\ge0\quad\forall y\in\mathbb R_+^N\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Big-M linearization of lower-level complementarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear bilevel programs represented through lower-level primal-dual feasibility and complementary slackness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each complementary pair \(a_i\ge 0\), \(b_i\ge 0\), \(a_i b_i=0\), introduce \(z_i\in\{0,1\}\) and impose \(a_i\le Mz_i\), \(b_i\le M(1-z_i)\). Applied componentwise to the lower-level primal and dual slacks, these constraints convert the KKT single-level formulation of a linear bilevel program into a mixed \(0\)-\(1\) linear program, provided \(M>0\) is a valid bound preserving every bilevel optimum. An inadequately chosen trial-and-error value of \(M\) can exclude optimal points and yield a nonoptimal reported solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each nonnegative complementary pair can be encoded by one binary variable and two big-M inequalities. Componentwise application to the lower-level primal and dual slacks yields an equivalent mixed-binary linear formulation only when M is a valid bound that preserves all bilevel optima; heuristic trial-and-error tuning can otherwise lose optimal solutions.
assumptions_latex: \text{The lower-level problem is linear and its KKT conditions characterize lower-level optimality.}
a_i\ge 0,\quad b_i\ge 0,\quad a_i b_i=0\quad\text{for every encoded pair}.
M>0\quad\text{bounds the relevant primal and dual slack components over all bilevel-optimal points}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: a_i b_i=0\iff \exists z_i\in\{0,1\}:\ a_i\le Mz_i,\ b_i\le M(1-z_i),\quad\text{and the resulting formulation is an equivalent MILP under valid bounds.}
