knowledge_statements.statement_title: Schur-Complement Criterion for Local LCP Solvability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient and, under global uniqueness, necessary Q-matrix conditions for solvability under nearby right-hand-side perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), \(\bar q\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(\bar z\) be a locally unique solution of \(\operatorname{LCP}(\bar q,M)\). Define \(\alpha=\{i:\bar z_i>0=(\bar q+M\bar z)_i\}\) and \(\beta=\{i:\bar z_i=0=(\bar q+M\bar z)_i\}\), and suppose \(M_{\alpha\alpha}\) is nonsingular. Set \(H=M_{\beta\beta}-M_{\beta\alpha}M_{\alpha\alpha}^{-1}M_{\alpha\beta}\). If \(H\in\mathbf Q\), then there is a neighborhood \(V\) of \(\bar q\) such that \(S(q)\neq\varnothing\) for every \(q\in V\). Conversely, if \(\bar z\) is globally unique and \(\operatorname{LCP}(q,M)\) is solvable for every \(q\) sufficiently close to \(\bar q\), then \(H\in\mathbf Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a locally unique LCP solution whose positive-support principal block is nonsingular, a Q-matrix condition on the biactive Schur complement guarantees solvability for every nearby right-hand side. Conversely, global uniqueness together with solvability for all nearby right-hand sides forces that Schur complement to be a Q-matrix.
assumptions_latex: \bar z\text{ is a locally unique solution of }\operatorname{LCP}(\bar q,M)
\alpha=\{i:\bar z_i>0=(\bar q+M\bar z)_i\},\quad \beta=\{i:\bar z_i=0=(\bar q+M\bar z)_i\}
\text{For the converse, }\bar z\text{ is globally unique and }\operatorname{LCP}(q,M)\text{ is solvable for all }q\text{ sufficiently close to }\bar q
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H\in\mathbf Q\Rightarrow\exists V\ni\bar q\;\forall q\in V:\ S(q)\neq\varnothing;\qquad [\bar z\text{ globally unique and nearby universal solvability}]\Rightarrow H\in\mathbf Q

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multivariate Parametric Linear Complementarity Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameterized LCP family in which both the vector and matrix data may depend on a parameter vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb R^m\), \(q:\Lambda\to\mathbb R^n\), and \(M:\Lambda\to\mathbb R^{n\times n}\). A multivariate parametric linear complementarity problem is the family \(\{\operatorname{LCP}(q(\varepsilon),M(\varepsilon)):\varepsilon\in\Lambda\}\). The one-parameter affine-vector, constant-matrix case is obtained when \(m=1\), \(q(\varepsilon)=q+\varepsilon d\) for \(q,d\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(M(\varepsilon)\) is constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multivariate parametric LCP is a family indexed by a parameter vector, with both the constant vector and defining matrix allowed to vary with the parameter. A scalar affine perturbation of the vector with a fixed matrix is a special case.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left\{\operatorname{LCP}(q(\varepsilon),M(\varepsilon)):\varepsilon\in\Lambda\right\}\text{ is a multivariate parametric LCP family.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Upper Semicontinuity and Local Boundedness of the LCP Solution Map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consequences of boundedness of the reference LCP solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}. If S(\bar q) is bounded, then the LCP solution map S is upper semicontinuous at \bar q. Moreover, there exist c'>0 and a neighborhood V of \bar q such that \lVert z\rVert\le c' for every q\in V and z\in S(q).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the reference LCP solution set is bounded, then the solution map is upper semicontinuous there and all nearby solution sets are uniformly bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is upper semicontinuous at }\bar q,\quad \exists c'>0\;\exists V\ni\bar q\;\forall q\in V\;\forall z\in S(q):\ \lVert z\rVert\le c'

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unique LCP solutions are stable under an interior-Q and R-zero condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient matrix-class and global-uniqueness condition for stability at an LCP solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let M\in\operatorname{int}(\mathbf Q)\cap\mathbf R_0. If \operatorname{LCP}(q,M) has the unique solution z^*, then \operatorname{LCP}(q,M) is stable at z^*.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the LCP matrix belongs to the interior of Q and to R-zero, then a globally unique solution of the LCP is stable at that solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{LCP}(q,M)\text{ is stable at }z^*

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong LCP stability yields a locally unique Lipschitz solution branch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local single-valued Lipschitz dependence on simultaneous perturbations of the LCP vector and matrix data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If z^* is a strongly stable solution of \operatorname{LCP}(q,M), then there exist neighborhoods \bar U of (q,M) and \bar V of z^* and a Lipschitz function z:\bar U\to\bar V such that z(q,M)=z^* and \operatorname{SOL}(\bar q,\bar M)\cap\bar V=\{z(\bar q,\bar M)\} for every (\bar q,\bar M)\in\bar U.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strongly stable LCP solution extends locally to a Lipschitz function of the perturbed vector and matrix data, and this function gives the unique perturbed solution lying in a fixed neighborhood of the reference solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\,\bar U\ni(q,M),\ \bar V\ni z^*,\ z:\bar U\to\bar V\text{ Lipschitz such that }z(q,M)=z^*\text{ and }\operatorname{SOL}(\bar q,\bar M)\cap\bar V=\{z(\bar q,\bar M)\}\ \forall(\bar q,\bar M)\in\bar U

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stable and strongly stable LCP solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Localized solution-set behavior under simultaneous perturbations of the vector and matrix data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let q\in\mathbb R^n, M\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}, and z^*\in\operatorname{SOL}(q,M). The solution z^* is stable if there exist neighborhoods V of z^* and U of (q,M) such that S_V(\bar q,\bar M):=\operatorname{SOL}(\bar q,\bar M)\cap V is nonempty for every (\bar q,\bar M)\in U and \sup\{\|y-z^*\|:y\in S_V(\bar q,\bar M)\}\to0 as (\bar q,\bar M)\to(q,M). It is strongly stable if, additionally, S_V(\bar q,\bar M) is a singleton for every (\bar q,\bar M)\in U. Stability implies local uniqueness of z^*.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An LCP solution is stable when every sufficiently small simultaneous perturbation of the vector and matrix data has a localized solution and all such localized solutions converge uniformly to the reference solution. It is strongly stable when each localized perturbed solution set is also a singleton. Stability necessarily implies local uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z^*\text{ is stable under the localized nonemptiness and convergence conditions, strongly stable under the additional singleton condition, and stability implies local uniqueness.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Schur-complement characterization of strongly stable LCP solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of strong stability, strong stability of the reduced homogeneous LCP, and the P-matrix property of its Schur complement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let z^*\in\operatorname{SOL}(q,M), let \alpha be the associated index set, and let N be the corresponding reduced Schur complement. Then z^*\text{ is strongly stable for }\operatorname{LCP}(q,M)\iff\bigl(M_{\alpha\alpha}\text{ is nonsingular and }0\text{ is strongly stable for }\operatorname{LCP}(0,N)\bigr)\iff\bigl(M_{\alpha\alpha}\text{ is nonsingular and }N\in\mathbf P\bigr).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong stability of an LCP solution is equivalent to nonsingularity of its associated principal block together with strong stability of zero for the reduced homogeneous LCP; equivalently, that block is nonsingular and the reduced Schur complement is a P-matrix.
assumptions_latex: N\text{ is the reduced Schur complement associated with }z^*
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z^*\text{ strongly stable}\iff\bigl(M_{\alpha\alpha}\text{ nonsingular and }0\text{ strongly stable for }\operatorname{LCP}(0,N)\bigr)\iff\bigl(M_{\alpha\alpha}\text{ nonsingular and }N\in\mathbf P\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: LCP Solutions Transport under Principal Pivot Transformation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible-solution correspondence induced by a principal pivot transformation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((q',M')=\wp_\alpha(q,M)\). If \(\bar z\) is a feasible solution of \(\operatorname{LCP}(q,M)\) and \(\bar w=q+M\bar z\), then \(\bar z'\), defined by \[\bar z'_i=\begin{cases}\bar w_i,&i\in\alpha,\\\bar z_i,&i\in\bar\alpha,\end{cases}\] is a feasible solution of \(\operatorname{LCP}(q',M')\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a principal pivot transformation, a feasible LCP solution is transported by replacing its pivot-index components with the corresponding slack components and retaining its complementary-index components.
assumptions_latex: \bar z\text{ is a feasible solution of }\operatorname{LCP}(q,M)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar z'_i=\begin{cases}\bar w_i,&i\in\alpha,\\\bar z_i,&i\in\bar\alpha\end{cases}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \bar z'\text{ is a feasible solution of }\operatorname{LCP}(q',M')

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\deg(H(t,\cdot),\Omega,0)\) is constant; a nonzero value guarantees an interior solution throughout the perturbation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States persistence under boundary-safe LCP residual homotopies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be bounded and open, and let \(H:[0,1]\times\overline\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^n\) continuously deform one LCP residual map into another. If \(0\notin H(t,\partial\Omega)\) for every \(t\in[0,1]\), then homotopy invariance gives \(\deg(H(t,\cdot),\Omega,0)=\deg(H(0,\cdot),\Omega,0)\) for every \(t\). If this common degree is nonzero, each perturbed residual has at least one zero in \(\Omega\). This regime ensures existence stability, not uniqueness or Lipschitz sensitivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero LCP degree persists under perturbations that keep the boundary solution-free and guarantees an interior solution, but not uniqueness.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Modified sequential linear complementarity algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A globally convergent parametric-LCP method for a linear bilevel problem without coupling constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Introduce \(\lambda\) and replace the upper-level objective by \(c_1x+d_1y\le\lambda\), while expressing lower-level primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and complementary slackness as \(\operatorname{LCP}(\lambda)\). If the lower-level feasible polyhedron \(S\) is bounded and the uncoupled bilevel problem has an optimal solution, its global minimum is obtained from \(\operatorname{LCP}(\lambda^*)\), where \(\lambda^*=\inf\{\lambda:\operatorname{LCP}(\lambda)\text{ is solvable}\}\). The modified SLCP method decreases \(\lambda\) along the current complementary basis and changes basis when feasibility is lost; unlike the original SLCP scheme, the modified version is convergent under these assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bound the upper-level objective by a parameter lambda and encode lower-level optimality as a parametric LCP. For a bounded lower-level feasible set and an existing optimum in the uncoupled bilevel problem, the smallest feasible lambda equals the global bilevel objective value. The convergent modified SLCP method decreases lambda while tracking and changing complementary bases; the original SLCP is not convergent in general.
assumptions_latex: \text{The linear bilevel problem has no coupling constraints.}
\text{The bilevel problem has an optimal solution.}
\operatorname{LCP}(\lambda)\text{ encodes lower-level primal-dual feasibility, complementarity, and }c_1x+d_1y\le\lambda.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda^*=\min\{\lambda:\operatorname{LCP}(\lambda)\text{ has a solution}\}\text{ is the global bilevel optimum value, and the modified SLCP method finds a corresponding global minimizer.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(M\) and \(q\), write \(w-Mz=q\) and choose a complementary basis containing at most one variable from each pair \((z_i,w_i)\). Compute its basic solution. If all basic variables are nonnegative, output \(z\). Otherwise select an infeasible basic variable by the fixed rule, exchange it with its complement through an admissible principal pivot, and recompute. Repeat until a feasible complementary basis is obtained; stop with failure if the required pivot is zero, the rule detects cycling, or another rule-specific termination certificate occurs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Principal pivoting repeatedly exchanges complementary basic variables until it obtains a nonnegative complementary basic solution or encounters a certified pivot failure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Leading-principal-subproblem reduction for an LCP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LCP reduction and extension property used in simple principal pivoting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\alpha=\{1,\ldots,n-1\}\). If \(\bar z\) solves \(\operatorname{LCP}(q,M)\) and \(\bar z_n=0\), then \(\bar z_\alpha\) solves the leading principal subproblem \(\operatorname{LCP}(q_\alpha,M_{\alpha\alpha})\). Conversely, if \(\bar z_\alpha\) solves this subproblem and \(\bar w_n=q_n+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}m_{ni}\bar z_i\ge0\), then \(\bar z=(\bar z_\alpha,0)\) solves \(\operatorname{LCP}(q,M)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An LCP solution whose final component is zero restricts to a solution of the leading principal subproblem. Conversely, such a subproblem solution extends by a zero final component when the resulting final residual is nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[\bar z\in\operatorname{SOL}(q,M),\ \bar z_n=0\bigr]\Rightarrow\bar z_\alpha\in\operatorname{SOL}(q_\alpha,M_{\alpha\alpha});\quad\bigl[\bar z_\alpha\in\operatorname{SOL}(q_\alpha,M_{\alpha\alpha}),\ q_n+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}m_{ni}\bar z_i\ge0\bigr]\Rightarrow(\bar z_\alpha,0)\in\operatorname{SOL}(q,M).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Van der Heyden Variable-Dimension LCP Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pivoting procedure for a nondegenerate LCP with a strictly semimonotone matrix; the extract states the procedure but no termination theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a nondegenerate LCP \((q,M)\) with strictly semimonotone \(M\), first order the positive components of \(q\) before the others. If the current \(w\ge0\), stop with a solution. Otherwise set \(k=\min\{i:w_i<0\}\), drive \(z_k\), and allow \(w_k\) and the other basic variables of the \(k\)-subproblem to block. After pivoting the blocking variable \(v_j\) against the driving variable: if \(j<k\), increase the complement of \(v_j\) and continue pivoting; if \(j=k\) and \(v_k=w_k\), regard the \(k\)-subproblem as solved and repeat the feasibility test; if \(j=k\) and \(v_k=z_k\), set \(k=\max\{i:z_i>0\}\), use \(-w_k\) as the new driving variable, and continue pivoting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nondegenerate LCP with strictly semimonotone M, order positive q-components first. Stop when w is nonnegative. Otherwise select the first negative w-index, drive its complementary z-variable, pivot against eligible blockers from the current leading subproblem, and update either within that subproblem, to the feasibility test after solving it, or to a smaller-subproblem solution whose largest positive z-index determines the new driving variable -w_k.
assumptions_latex: q\text{ is preprocessed so its positive components occur first}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: w\ge0\Rightarrow\text{stop with an LCP solution; otherwise perform the stated variable-dimension pivot transitions}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Principal-minor determinant identity under principal pivoting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transformation rule for principal minors of a principal pivot transform.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be a square matrix, let \(A_{\alpha\alpha}\) be nonsingular, and let \(C=\wp_\alpha(A)\). For any index set \(\beta\), define \(\gamma=\alpha\triangle\beta\). Then \[\det C_{\beta\beta}=\frac{\det A_{\gamma\gamma}}{\det A_{\alpha\alpha}}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a principal pivot transform of a square matrix, the principal minor indexed by beta equals the original principal minor indexed by the symmetric difference of alpha and beta, divided by the pivot principal minor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \det C_{\beta\beta}=\frac{\det A_{\gamma\gamma}}{\det A_{\alpha\alpha}}

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Removal of the artificial variable yields an LCP solution; a secondary ray is a failure certificate for that run.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the classical covering-vector Lemke path procedure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(M\), \(q\), and \(d\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\), augment the system to \(w=Mz+q+dz_0\) with \(z\geq0\), \(w\geq0\), and \(z_0\geq0\). Start from \(z=0\) and the least \(z_0\) making \(w\geq0\), then pivot along almost-complementary bases, using the complement of the leaving variable as the next entering variable. If \(z_0\) leaves the basis, output the resulting \(z\), which solves \(\operatorname{LCP}(M,q)\). If the path reaches a secondary ray, terminate with that ray certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lemke's method follows an augmented almost-complementary path; eliminating the artificial variable gives a solution, while a secondary ray signals failure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Negative entry after a block pivotal transform
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block-matrix lemma used to establish a blocking-direction property in Lemke's method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widehat M=\begin{bmatrix}a^{\mathsf T}&\delta\\B&c\end{bmatrix}\) be square, where \(a\le 0\), \(\delta<0\), and \(B\) is nonsingular. The pivotal transform of \(\widehat M\) obtained using \(B\) as the pivot block has at least one negative entry in its last column.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the stated square block matrix, componentwise nonpositivity of a, strict negativity of delta, and nonsingularity of B imply that the last column after pivoting on B contains a negative entry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The pivotal transform using }B\text{ as pivot block has at least one negative entry in its last column.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lexicographically feasible basis and initial ratio rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lexicographic perturbation convention used to resolve degeneracy in Lemke's method; the symbols refer to the source's associated system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Relative to the associated system, a basis \(B\) is lexicographically feasible precisely when \(B^{-1}\mathcal Q\succ0\), meaning that every row of \(B^{-1}\mathcal Q\) is lexicographically positive. An initial almost-complementary lexicographically feasible basis is selected using \[r=\arg\operatorname{lexico}\max\left\{-\frac{1}{d_i}\mathcal Q_i:\mathcal Q_{i0}<0\right\},\] the lexicographic analogue of Lemke's initial ratio test.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basis is lexicographically feasible when every row of its transformed perturbation matrix is lexicographically positive. The displayed lexicographic maximum ratio rule selects the index used to form an initial almost-complementary lexicographically feasible basis.
assumptions_latex: B\text{ is a basis for the associated system}
\mathcal Q_{i0}<0\text{ for each index participating in the ratio rule}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B\text{ is lexicographically feasible}\iff B^{-1}\mathcal Q\succ0,\qquad r=\arg\operatorname{lexico}\max\left\{-d_i^{-1}\mathcal Q_i:\mathcal Q_{i0}<0\right\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lemke Scheme II for an unaugmented LCP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complementary-pivoting algorithm with its initialization, blocking test, termination conditions, and driving-variable update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given $\operatorname{LCP}(q,M)$, return $z=0$ if $q\ge0$. Otherwise assume that some $k$ satisfies $q+M_{\cdot k}z_k\ge0$ for every $z_k\ge\bar z_k$, and, under nondegeneracy, let $w_r$ be the unique component vanishing at $z_k=\bar z_k$. Pivot $\langle w_r,z_k\rangle$ and drive $z_r$. Repeatedly apply the minimum-ratio test: if no basic variable blocks the driving variable, stop; otherwise pivot the blocking variable with the driving variable. If $z_k$ or $w_k$ blocks, an LCP solution has been obtained; otherwise drive the complement of the latest blocking variable and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lemke Scheme II first returns the trivial solution when q is nonnegative. Otherwise, under its ray and nondegeneracy assumptions, it performs an initial complementary pivot and repeatedly uses a minimum-ratio blocking test. It stops without a solution if no blocker exists, stops with a solution when z_k or w_k blocks, and otherwise continues with the complement of the latest blocking variable.
assumptions_latex: q\not\ge0\implies \exists k\;\forall z_k\ge\bar z_k:\ q+M_{\cdot k}z_k\ge0.
\text{The pivot configuration is nondegenerate, so }w_r\text{ is uniquely determined.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure either returns }z=0,\text{ reaches an LCP solution, or stops when the driving variable has no blocking basic variable.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Index and Facet Control of the Geometric Lemke Path
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Method-specific evolution of the covering parameter through full complementary cones and proper, reflecting, or absorbing facets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Process \(\operatorname{LCP}(q,M)\) by Algorithm 6.3.1 using \(d\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\) satisfying its Step 0 nondegeneracy condition, and suppose the full cone \(\operatorname{pos}C(\alpha)\) is distinguished at the beginning of Step 1. Then Step 1 decreases \(z_0\) if \(\operatorname{ind}(\operatorname{pos}C(\alpha))=1\) and increases \(z_0\) if the index is \(-1\). If the new value satisfies \(0<\bar z_0<\infty\), the next distinguished facet is proper, reflecting, or absorbing around \(q+d\bar z_0\). An absorbing facet fixes \(z_0=\bar z_0\) for the remainder of the algorithm and eventually leads to a strongly degenerate cone and secondary-ray termination. At a proper facet, \(z_0\) is changed again in the same direction as its preceding change; at a reflecting facet, it is changed again in the opposite direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The index of a full complementary cone determines whether the covering parameter rises or falls. A proper next facet preserves the direction of its next change, a reflecting facet reverses it, and an absorbing facet freezes the parameter and eventually causes secondary-ray termination through a strongly degenerate cone.
assumptions_latex: \operatorname{pos}C(\alpha)\text{ is a full distinguished complementary cone at the beginning of Step 1}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{ind}(\operatorname{pos}C(\alpha))=1\Rightarrow z_0\text{ decreases},\qquad \operatorname{ind}(\operatorname{pos}C(\alpha))=-1\Rightarrow z_0\text{ increases},\quad\text{with later behavior determined by the proper, reflecting, or absorbing facet type.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lemke–Howson complementary-pivoting algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complementary-pivoting scheme for the structured LCP associated with a bimatrix game.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the order-$(m+n)$ LCP $(q,M)$ given by (17), choose $k\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$, select $s\in\arg\min_{1\le j\le n}b_{kj}$, and pivot $\langle v_s,x_k\rangle$. Next select $r\in\arg\min_{1\le i\le m}a_{is}$ and pivot $\langle u_r,y_s\rangle$. If $r=k$, stop with a solution; otherwise drive $x_r$. Thereafter use the minimum-ratio test and pivot each blocking variable with the driving variable. Stop if no blocker exists; if the blocker belongs to the basic pair, return the LCP solution; otherwise drive the complement of the latest blocker and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Lemke–Howson algorithm makes two prescribed initial pivots based on row and column minima. It immediately returns a solution if the resulting indices coincide; otherwise it repeatedly applies a minimum-ratio blocking test and complementary pivots, returning a solution when the blocker belongs to the basic pair and stopping if no blocker exists.
assumptions_latex: (q,M)\text{ is the order-}(m+n)\text{ LCP specified by (17).}
s\in\arg\min_{1\le j\le n}b_{kj},\qquad r\in\arg\min_{1\le i\le m}a_{is}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The pivot sequence either reaches an LCP solution or stops when the driving variable has no blocking basic variable.}

children.title: Pivoting-Framework Comparison
children.top_down_role: Structural distinctions between the two pivoting frameworks.

assumptions_latex: The same finite-dimensional LCP \((M,q)\) is considered
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Principal pivoting searches complementary bases directly, whereas Lemke follows an augmented path; neither framework is universally finite without matrix-class assumptions.

notation.meaning: artificial variable used by Lemke's augmentation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares pivot state spaces and termination outcomes without asserting universal convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Principal pivoting methods operate directly on complementary bases of \(w-Mz=q\) and may require admissibility, finiteness, or matrix-class hypotheses to guarantee success. Lemke methods instead introduce \(z_0\) and \(d\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\), then trace an almost-complementary path in the augmented system. Their successful terminal events differ: principal pivoting reaches a feasible complementary basis, whereas Lemke removes \(z_0\). Their failure modes also differ, including unavailable pivots or cycling for general principal schemes and secondary rays for Lemke. Neither framework is universally finite for arbitrary \(M\) without additional assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Principal methods pivot directly among complementary bases; Lemke follows an augmented path. Their success and failure events differ, and neither is universally finite for arbitrary matrices.
knowledge_statements.title: Pivoting-Framework Comparison

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The comparison fits the exact leaf and carefully avoids universal convergence, but the family-wide termination and failure-mode comparison has no cited source or inspectable locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(z^0\in\mathbb{R}_+^n\), generate \[z^{k+1}=\bigl[z^k-\tau_k(Mz^k+q)\bigr]_+.\] Stop when \(\|z^{k+1}-z^k\|\le\varepsilon\), and return \(z^{k+1}\). For any \(\tau>0\), a vector \(z\) is a fixed point of this update exactly when \(z\ge0\), \(Mz+q\ge0\), and \(z^{\mathsf T}(Mz+q)=0\). Convergence requires additional conditions on \(M\) and the step sizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Iterate a projected residual step. Every fixed point solves the LCP, although convergence of the iteration requires additional matrix and step-size conditions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotone convergence of block-diagonal Z-matrix LCP splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block-diagonal splitting convergence using least-element subproblem solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let M be a \mathbf Z-matrix partitioned into blocks M_{ij}, with each diagonal block M_{ii} square, and let B=\operatorname{diag}(M_{11},\ldots,M_{kk}). If \operatorname{LCP}(q,M) is feasible and z^0\in\operatorname{FEA}(q,M), then the iteration in which z^{\nu+1} is the least-element solution of \operatorname{LCP}(q^\nu,B) is well defined and converges monotonically to a solution of \operatorname{LCP}(q,M).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a block-partitioned Z-matrix, using the diagonal blocks as the splitting matrix and choosing the least subproblem solution at every step produces a well-defined monotone sequence converging to an LCP solution, provided the original LCP and the initial point are feasible.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spectral-radius criteria for a positive-definite LCP splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence criteria for a matrix splitting M=B+C.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let M and B be positive definite, let M=B+C, and suppose B is symmetric. If \widetilde B^{\mathsf T}\widetilde B=B, then \rho(\widetilde B,C)<1 if and only if 2M-M^{\mathsf T}B^{-1}M is positive definite. Moreover, if G is symmetric positive definite, B=\lambda G, and \lambda>\|M\|_2^2/(2\mu\gamma), where \mu=\lambda_{\min}((M+M^{\mathsf T})/2) and \gamma=\lambda_{\min}(G), then \rho(\widetilde B,C)<1.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a positive-definite splitting M=B+C with symmetric B and a factor B=tilde B transpose times tilde B, the splitting spectral radius is below one exactly when 2M−M transpose B inverse M is positive definite. A sufficient condition is B=lambda G with G symmetric positive definite and lambda exceeding the stated eigenvalue bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho(\widetilde B,C)<1\iff 2M-M^{\mathsf T}B^{-1}M\succ0;\quad B=\lambda G,\ G\succ0,\ \lambda>\frac{\|M\|_2^2}{2\mu\gamma}\implies\rho(\widetilde B,C)<1

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter-range specialization of LCP splitting convergence to projected successive overrelaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let M be an \mathbf H-matrix with positive diagonal and write M=D+L+U, where D, L, and U are respectively its diagonal, strictly lower-triangular, and strictly upper-triangular parts. For B=L+\omega^{-1}D with \omega>0, there exists \bar\omega\in(1,2] such that, for every \omega\in(0,\bar\omega), the PSOR splitting (B,C), with C=M-B, has the convergence conclusion of the H-matrix splitting theorem: for arbitrary q and any z^0\geq0, its iterates converge to the unique solution of \operatorname{LCP}(q,M).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an H-matrix M with positive diagonal, projected SOR converges throughout a nontrivial relaxation interval (0, omega-bar), where omega-bar lies above one and at most two. The convergence is to the unique LCP solution from every nonnegative start.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: LCP Matrix Splitting and Fixed-Point Formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a matrix splitting for an LCP and the associated set-valued fixed-point mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=B+C\), where \(B,C\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\). The pair \((B,C)\) is called a splitting of \(M\). For each \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\), define \(q^z=q+Cz\) and \(T(z)=\operatorname{SOL}(q^z,B)\). Then \(z\) solves \(\operatorname{LCP}(q,M)\) if and only if \(z\in T(z)\), that is, if and only if \(z\) solves \(\operatorname{LCP}(q+Cz,B)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A splitting of M is a representation M = B + C by real matrices of the same order. Mapping each vector z to the solution set of LCP(q + Cz, B) gives a set-valued map whose fixed points are exactly the solutions of LCP(q, M).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z\in\operatorname{SOL}(q,M)\iff z\in\operatorname{SOL}(q+Cz,B)

knowledge_statements.title: LCP Newton Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semismooth Newton iteration applied to the Fischer–Burmeister reformulation of a finite-dimensional LCP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\phi(a,b)=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}-a-b\) and \(\Phi_i(z)=\phi(z_i,(Mz+q)_i)\). From \(z^0\in\mathbb{R}^n\), choose \(V_k\in\partial_C\Phi(z^k)\), solve \[V_kd^k=-\Phi(z^k),\] select \(\alpha_k\in(0,1]\) by a merit-function globalization rule, and set \(z^{k+1}=z^k+\alpha_kd^k\). Stop when \(\|\Phi(z^k)\|\le\varepsilon\). A zero of \(\Phi\) satisfies exactly \(0\le z\perp Mz+q\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Apply a generalized Newton step to the Fischer–Burmeister residual, with merit-function globalization. A zero of that residual is exactly an LCP solution.
assumptions_latex: \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(\varepsilon>0\), and each selected Newton matrix \(V_k\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi(z)=0\) holds exactly when \(0\le z\perp Mz+q\ge0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes LCP solutions as zeros of a componentwise nonlinear residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q\in\mathbb R^n\), \(M\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), and let \(\theta:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be strictly increasing with \(\theta(0)=0\). Define \(H:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) by \[H_i(z)=\theta\!\left(\left|(q+Mz)_i-z_i\right|\right)-\theta((q+Mz)_i)-\theta(z_i),\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.\] Then \(z^*\) solves \(\operatorname{LCP}(q,M)\) if and only if \(H(z^*)=0\).

knowledge_statements.title: LCP Interior Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual central-path iteration for a finite-dimensional LCP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(k\), linearize \[w-Mz-q=0,\qquad z\circ w=\mu_k e\] at a strictly positive pair \((z^k,w^k)\), solve the resulting Newton system for \((\Delta z^k,\Delta w^k)\), and choose a damped step preserving strict positivity and the prescribed central-path neighborhood. Reduce \(\mu_k>0\), stop when the feasibility and complementarity residuals are at most \(\varepsilon\), and return the current pair. If \(\mu_k\to0\), the feasibility residuals and \(z^k\circ w^k\) converge to zero, and \((z^{k_j},w^{k_j})\to(\bar z,\bar w)\), then \(\bar w=M\bar z+q\), \(\bar z\ge0\), \(\bar w\ge0\), and \(\bar z\circ\bar w=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Follow the positive central path by damped Newton steps while reducing the barrier parameter. Every accumulation point obtained with vanishing feasibility and complementarity residuals solves the LCP.
assumptions_latex: \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(\varepsilon>0\), and an initial pair satisfies \(z^0>0\) and \(w^0=Mz^0+q>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\mu_k\to0\) and the feasibility and complementarity residuals vanish, every accumulation point is an LCP solution.

knowledge_statements.title: Secondary-Ray Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbounded-path failure of Lemke's complementary pivoting method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In Lemke's augmented system \[w=Mz+q+z_0d,\qquad z\ge0,\quad w\ge0,\quad z_0\ge0,\qquad z_iw_i=0\ \text{for }i=1,\ldots,n,\] a secondary ray is an unbounded edge of the complementary feasible set reached before the artificial variable has been eliminated. If the pivot path enters such a ray, no leaving variable exists for the prescribed entering variable. The method then terminates on the ray rather than at a point with \(z_0=0\), and therefore returns no solution of the original LCP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lemke's method fails on a secondary ray when its augmented complementary path becomes unbounded before the artificial variable is removed.
assumptions_latex: Lemke's augmented system uses a covering vector \(d\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\) and an artificial variable \(z_0\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Entering a secondary ray terminates the pivot search without producing a solution of the original LCP.

assumptions_latex: The task is to solve \(0\le z\perp Mz+q\ge0\) by complementary pivoting.

source_refs.locator: 4.3 General Principal Pivoting Methods p. 251

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Complementary pivoting has no unconditional finite-solution guarantee for arbitrary \((M,q)\). Degenerate basic solutions can make pivot choices nonunique or permit cycling, and an augmented Lemke path can terminate on a secondary ray. Solvability itself is also necessary: for \(n=1\), \(M=0\), and \(q=-1\), the constraint \(Mz+q\ge0\) is impossible, so no pivoting method can terminate with an LCP solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: General LCP pivoting can fail through degeneracy, cycling, a secondary ray, or simple infeasibility; finite successful termination needs additional structure and pivot rules.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized derivatives of E-type complementarity functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Piecewise-affine regions and exact generalized-derivative formulas for the unbounded and interval E-functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(\phi^E:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\) is piecewise affine and affine on \(\{x:x_1<x_2\}\) and \(\{x:x_1>x_2\}\). Moreover,
\[
\partial\phi^E(x)=\partial_B\phi^E(x)=\{(1,0)\}\quad\text{if }x_1<x_2,
\]
\[
\partial\phi^E(x)=\partial_B\phi^E(x)=\{(0,1)\}\quad\text{if }x_1>x_2,
\]
and if \(x_1=x_2\),
\[
\partial_B\phi^E(x)=\{(1,0),(0,1)\},\qquad \partial\phi^E(x)=\{(t,1-t):0\le t\le1\}.
\]
For \(\alpha<\beta\), \(\phi^E_{[\alpha,\beta]}\) is piecewise affine and affine on each connected component of \(\{x:x_1-x_2\ne\alpha,\ x_1-x_2\ne\beta\}\). Its generalized derivatives are
\[
\partial\phi^E_{[\alpha,\beta]}(x)=\partial_B\phi^E_{[\alpha,\beta]}(x)=\{(1,0)\}
\quad\text{if }x_1-x_2\notin[\alpha,\beta],
\]
\[
\partial\phi^E_{[\alpha,\beta]}(x)=\partial_B\phi^E_{[\alpha,\beta]}(x)=\{(0,1)\}
\quad\text{if }x_1-x_2\in(\alpha,\beta),
\]
and, if \(x_1-x_2\in\{\alpha,\beta\}\),
\[
\partial_B\phi^E_{[\alpha,\beta]}(x)=\{(1,0),(0,1)\},\qquad \partial\phi^E_{[\alpha,\beta]}(x)=\{(t,1-t):0\le t\le1\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The E-type NCP function and its interval MCP extension are piecewise affine. Away from switching boundaries, both generalized derivatives equal the relevant singleton slope; on a switching boundary, the B-subdifferential contains the two adjacent slopes and the convex generalized differential is their line segment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The displayed piecewise-affine regions and formulas for the B-subdifferentials and convex generalized differentials hold.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: NCP Functions and Infinite-Interval MCP Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines NCP functions, their componentwise equation reformulation, and canonical functions for lower-bounded, upper-bounded, and free variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A map \(\phi:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\) is an NCP function if and only if \[\phi(x_1,x_2)=0\iff x_1\ge0,\quad x_2\ge0,\quad x_1x_2=0.\] Thus the NCP for \(F:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^m\) is equivalent to \(\Phi(u)=0\), where \(\Phi_i(u)=\phi(u_i,F_i(u))\). The projection-based example is \(\phi^E(x_1,x_2)=\min\{x_1,x_2\}\). For \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R\), canonical MCP functions derived from \(\phi\) are \[\phi_{[\alpha,\infty)}(x)=\phi(x_1-\alpha,x_2),\quad \phi_{(-\infty,\beta]}(x)=-\phi(\beta-x_1,-x_2),\quad \phi_{\mathbb R}(x)=x_2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An NCP function vanishes exactly on nonnegative complementary pairs, so applying it componentwise converts an NCP into equations. Shifting, reflecting, or taking the residual component gives canonical functions for lower-bounded, upper-bounded, and free variables.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(\phi:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\) is an NCP-function if, for every \((x_1,x_2)\in\mathbb{R}^2\), \[\phi(x_1,x_2)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x_1\ge 0,\;x_2\ge 0,\;x_1x_2=0.\] In particular, \(\phi_{\min}(x_1,x_2)=\min\{x_1,x_2\}\) is an NCP-function. knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\) is pointwise FB-regular precisely when every matrix in \(\partial_B\Phi(\bar x)\) is nonsingular.

source_refs.locator: 9.1.2 Pointwise FB regularity p. 809
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), define \(\Phi_i(x)=\sqrt{x_i^2+F_i(x)^2}-x_i-F_i(x)\). A solution \(\bar x\) of \(\Phi(x)=0\) is pointwise Fischer–Burmeister regular if
\[
\det V\ne0\qquad\text{for every }V\in\partial_B\Phi(\bar x).
\]
Equivalently, because \(\partial_B\Phi(\bar x)\) is compact, there exists \(\kappa<\infty\) such that \(\|V^{-1}\|\le\kappa\) for every \(V\in\partial_B\Phi(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the solution, every limiting Jacobian of the Fischer–Burmeister residual is nonsingular, equivalently their inverses are uniformly bounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Fischer–Burmeister Regularity

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The solution \(\bar x\) is sequentially Fischer–Burmeister regular if, for every sequence \(x^k\to\bar x\) at differentiability points of \(\Phi\), the matrices \(V_k=\nabla\Phi(x^k)\) are nonsingular for all sufficiently large \(k\) and
\[
\sup_{k\ge k_0}\|V_k^{-1}\|<\infty.
\]
Equivalently, the same requirement may be imposed on arbitrary selections \(V_k\in\partial_B\Phi(x^k)\) with \(x^k\to\bar x\), provided the generalized Jacobian convention is fixed accordingly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All limiting Jacobians along every sequence approaching the solution eventually remain nonsingular with uniformly bounded inverses.
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Fischer–Burmeister Regularity

source_refs.locator: 9.1.2 Pointwise FB regularity p. 809; 9.1.3 Sequential FB regularity p. 816
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\partial_B\Phi\) be nonempty, locally bounded, compact-valued, and outer semicontinuous at \(\bar x\). If every \(V\in\partial_B\Phi(\bar x)\) is nonsingular, then there exist \(r>0\) and \(\kappa<\infty\) such that
\[
\|V^{-1}\|\le\kappa
\quad\text{whenever}\quad
\|x-\bar x\|<r,\;V\in\partial_B\Phi(x).
\]
Consequently, pointwise FB regularity implies sequential FB regularity. Conversely, sequential regularity applied to the constant sequence \(x^k=\bar x\) implies pointwise regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under compactness and outer semicontinuity, pointwise FB regularity yields uniform nearby nonsingularity and hence sequential regularity; the converse follows from constant sequences.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise-to-Sequential Regularity Relations

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonnegative NCP merit function \(\Psi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) and initial point \(x^0\), define
\[
L_0=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\Psi(x)\le\Psi(x^0)\}.
\]
The level-set boundedness condition holds at \(x^0\) when \(L_0\) is bounded. If \(\Psi\) is continuous, this condition makes \(L_0\) compact. For the residual merit function, one takes \(\Psi(x)=\tfrac12\|\Phi(x)\|^2\).

knowledge_statements.title: Regularity–Boundedness Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative coupling of merit-level confinement and uniformly nonsingular Newton models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Phi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(\Psi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be a merit function, and fix \(x^0\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Define
\[
L_0=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\Psi(x)\le\Psi(x^0)\}.
\]
Suppose \(L_0\) is compact and \(\mathcal J\Phi(x)\) is a nonempty family of \(n\times n\) matrices such that
\[
\|V^{-1}\|\le\kappa<\infty
\quad\text{for every }x\in L_0\text{ and }V\in\mathcal J\Phi(x).
\]
Then, for every admissible pair \((x,V)\), the Newton equation
\[
Vd=-\Phi(x)
\]
has a unique solution satisfying \(\|d\|\le\kappa\|\Phi(x)\|\). Moreover, every sequence \((x^k)\) with \(x^0\) as its initial point and \(\Psi(x^{k+1})\le\Psi(x^k)\) remains in \(L_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform invertibility on the compact initial merit level set uniquely defines each Newton step and bounds it by the residual. Any merit-nonincreasing iteration remains in that level set.
assumptions_latex: \(\Phi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\Psi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) are given, with initial point \(x^0\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
\(\mathcal J\Phi(x)\) is nonempty and \(\|V^{-1}\|\le\kappa<\infty\) for every \(x\in L_0\) and \(V\in\mathcal J\Phi(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every equation \(Vd=-\Phi(x)\) with \(x\in L_0\) and \(V\in\mathcal J\Phi(x)\) has a unique solution satisfying \(\|d\|\le\kappa\|\Phi(x)\|\), and every merit-nonincreasing iteration remains in \(L_0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise inequality representation of a bound-constrained variational inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the conventions required where lower or upper bounds are absent and records the nonlinear-complementarity special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(u\in L^2(\Omega)\) solves the stated variational inequality with lower bound \(a\) on \(\Omega_a\) and upper bound \(b\) on \(\Omega_b\) if and only if, almost everywhere on \(\Omega\), \[a\le u\le b,\qquad (u-a)F(u)\le0,\qquad (u-b)F(u)\le0.\] Here \(a=-\infty\) on \(\Omega\setminus\Omega_a\) and \(b=+\infty\) on \(\Omega\setminus\Omega_b\); on these respective sets the second and third conditions mean \(F(u)\le0\) and \(F(u)\ge0\). If \(a\equiv0\), \(b\equiv+\infty\), \(\Omega_a=\Omega\), and \(\Omega_b=\varnothing\), the system reduces to \(u\ge0\), \(uF(u)\le0\), and \(F(u)\ge0\), equivalently the corresponding NCP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function u solves the bound-constrained variational inequality exactly when it satisfies the lower and upper bounds together with the two stated pointwise product inequalities. Where a lower or upper bound is absent, the corresponding product condition is interpreted directly as F(u) ≤ 0 or F(u) ≥ 0. With only the lower bound zero, this becomes the nonlinear complementarity system.
assumptions_latex: a\text{ is imposed on }\Omega_a\text{ and }b\text{ is imposed on }\Omega_b
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u\text{ solves the variational inequality}\iff a\le u\le b,\ (u-a)F(u)\le0,\ (u-b)F(u)\le0\quad\text{a.e. on }\Omega.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global FB Error Bound from Regional Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines asymptotic FB regularity on a region with an exterior residual error bound to obtain a global error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n be continuously differentiable, and suppose S=\operatorname{SOL}(\operatorname{NCP}(F))\ne\varnothing. Suppose there exist W\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n and c>0 such that F is asymptotically FB regular on W and \operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le c^{-1}\|\mathbf F_{\mathrm{FB}}(x)\| for every x\notin W. Then there exists c'>0 such that \operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le c'\|\mathbf F_{\mathrm{FB}}(x)\| for every x\in\mathbb{R}^n.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an NCP has a solution, its map is asymptotically FB regular on a set, and an FB residual error bound holds outside that set, then an FB residual error bound holds globally.
assumptions_latex: F\text{ is asymptotically FB regular on }W
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists c'>0\ \forall x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\ \operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le c'\|\mathbf F_{\mathrm{FB}}(x)\|

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convergence properties of a modified interior-point NCP algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accumulation-point correctness, residual convergence under feasibility, and iterate boundedness under strict feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable and monotone on \(\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\), and let \(\{(x^k,y^k)\}\) be an infinite sequence generated by the modified interior-point algorithm. Every accumulation point \((x^\infty,y^\infty)\) has \(x^\infty\) solving \(\operatorname{NCP}(F)\). If \(\operatorname{NCP}(F)\) is feasible, then \(x^k\circ y^k\to0\), \(y^k-F(x^k)\to0\), and \(\min(x^k,F(x^k))\to0\). If \(\operatorname{NCP}(F)\) is strictly feasible, then \(\{(x^k,y^k)\}\) is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every accumulation point produced by the modified interior-point algorithm solves the monotone NCP in its x-component. Feasibility gives convergence of the complementarity and equation residuals to zero, while strict feasibility makes the full iterate sequence bounded.
assumptions_latex: F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is continuously differentiable and monotone on }\mathbb{R}_{++}^n
\{(x^k,y^k)\}_{k\ge0}\text{ is an infinite sequence generated by the modified interior-point algorithm}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every player \(v\) and every \(x^{-v}\), suppose \(\theta_v(\cdot,x^{-v})\) is convex and differentiable, and \(\Xi^v(x^{-v})\) has the representation in (12.5), with \(g_i^v(\cdot,x^{-v})\) convex and differentiable for every \(i=1,\ldots,m_v\). knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iteration applies a semismooth Newton step to \(\Phi(x)=0\) and globalizes it through the merit function \(\Psi(x)=\tfrac12\|\Phi(x)\|^2\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x^0\), tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), and \(\Psi(x)=\tfrac12\|\Phi(x)\|^2\), repeat while \(\|\Phi(x^k)\|>\varepsilon\): choose \(V_k\in\partial_B\Phi(x^k)\), solve
\[
V_kd^k=-\Phi(x^k),
\]
and choose \(\alpha_k\in(0,1]\) by backtracking until \(\Psi(x^k+\alpha_kd^k)\) satisfies a prescribed sufficient-decrease test. Set \(x^{k+1}=x^k+\alpha_kd^k\). Output the first iterate satisfying \(\|\Phi(x^k)\|\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve generalized Newton systems for the Fischer–Burmeister residual, globalize by merit-function backtracking, and stop when the residual meets tolerance.

children.title: NCP-Map Algorithm Comparison
children.top_down_role: Structural comparison of algorithms induced by the two NCP maps.

knowledge_statements.title: NCP-Map Algorithm Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares solution equivalence and local structure of the minimum and Fischer–Burmeister NCP maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable, and define
\[
M_i(x)=\min\{x_i,F_i(x)\},
\qquad
\Phi_i(x)=\sqrt{x_i^2+F_i(x)^2}-x_i-F_i(x).
\]
For every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
M(x)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\Phi(x)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x\ge0,\;F(x)\ge0,\;x^{\mathsf T}F(x)=0.
\]
Thus algorithms based on the two maps target the same NCP solution set. The minimum map directly exposes branch-dependent active sets, whereas the Fischer–Burmeister map is symmetric in each complementary pair and is smooth wherever \((x_i,F_i(x))\ne(0,0)\) for every \(i\). Their generalized Newton matrices and globalization behavior need not coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum and Fischer–Burmeister maps have exactly the same zeros as the nonlinear complementarity problem, although their local generalized derivatives, active-set structures, and resulting algorithms can differ.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the conditions \(M(x)=0\), \(\Phi(x)=0\), and \(x\ge0,\;F(x)\ge0,\;x^{\mathsf T}F(x)=0\) are equivalent.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x^0\), \(\Delta_0>0\), and \(\Psi(x)=\tfrac12\|\Phi(x)\|^2\), choose \(V_k\in\partial_B\Phi(x^k)\) and approximately solve
\[
\min_{\|d\|\le\Delta_k}m_k(d),
\qquad m_k(d)=\tfrac12\|\Phi(x^k)+V_kd\|^2.
\]
Compute \(\rho_k=[\Psi(x^k)-\Psi(x^k+d^k)]/[m_k(0)-m_k(d^k)]\). Accept \(x^{k+1}=x^k+d^k\) when \(\rho_k\) exceeds a prescribed threshold; otherwise set \(x^{k+1}=x^k\). Update \(\Delta_k\) according to \(\rho_k\), and stop at the specified residual tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize a linearized residual model inside a radius, then accept the step and update the radius using actual versus predicted reduction.

Given \(x^0\in C\), construct at iteration \(k\) a local model \(q_k(d)\) of \(\Psi(x^k+d)\) and compute an approximate solution of
\[
\min_d q_k(d)\qquad\text{subject to}\qquad x^k+d\in C.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exceptional sequence with respect to an NCP mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition using positive identity regularizations of a nonlinear complementarity mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An unbounded sequence $\{x^k\}$ is exceptional with respect to $F$ if there exists a sequence $\{\tau_k\}$ with $\tau_k>0$ for every $k$ such that $x^k$ solves $\operatorname{NCP}(F+\tau_k\mathbf I)$ for every $k$.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At a feasible iterate \(x^k\in C\), the trust-region constrained regime computes a trial step from
\[
\min_d q_k(d)
\qquad\text{subject to}
\qquad x^k+d\in C,
\quad \|d\|\le\Delta_k.
\]
The feasibility constraint encodes the admissible NCP reformulation, while the radius limits reliance on the local model. A trial step is accepted only when its actual merit reduction is adequate relative to its predicted reduction; this ratio also determines contraction, retention, or enlargement of \(\Delta_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The step must be both feasible and inside the trust region; actual-versus-predicted merit reduction controls acceptance and radius changes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vertical LCP and piecewise-affine minimum equation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the vertical LCP, records its standard-LCP boundary case, and gives its equivalent zero-function representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let M=[M_1^T\ \cdots\ M_n^T]^T\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}, q=[q_1^T\ \cdots\ q_n^T]^T\in\mathbb R^m, where M_i\in\mathbb R^{m_i\times n}, q_i\in\mathbb R^{m_i}, \sum_{i=1}^n m_i=m, and m\ge n. The vertical LCP seeks z\in\mathbb R^n satisfying q+Mz\ge0, z\ge0, and z_i\prod_{j=1}^{m_i}(q_i+M_i z)_j=0 for i=1,\ldots,n. Define H_i(z)=\min\{z_i,(q_i+M_i z)_1,\ldots,(q_i+M_i z)_{m_i}\}. Then H is piecewise affine and z solves the vertical LCP if and only if H(z)=0. If every m_i=1, the problem is the standard LCP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertical LCP assigns each nonnegative variable a block of nonnegative affine residuals and requires that the variable or at least one residual in its block vanish. It reduces to the standard LCP for singleton blocks and is equivalent to a piecewise-affine system formed by taking the minimum within each block.
assumptions_latex: M\in\mathbb R^{m\times n},\ q\in\mathbb R^m,\ m\ge n
M_i\in\mathbb R^{m_i\times n},\ q_i\in\mathbb R^{m_i},\ \sum_{i=1}^n m_i=m
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z\text{ solves the vertical LCP}\iff H(z)=0,\qquad H_i(z)=\min\{z_i,(q_i+M_i z)_1,\ldots,(q_i+M_i z)_{m_i}\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: MPEC formulation with parametric mixed complementarity constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Here x is the upper-level variable and (y,w,z) are lower-level variables. The PIPA and implicit-programming approaches discussed by the source do not permit an additional general joint constraint (x,y,w,z)\in Z.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(y,w\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(z\in\mathbb{R}^{\ell}\). The MPEC is represented as
\[
\min_{x,y,w,z} f(x,y,w,z)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad x\in X,\quad F(x,y,w,z)=0,\quad y\ge 0,\quad w\ge 0,\quad y^Tw=0,
\]
where \(X=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Gx\le a\}\) is a nonempty polyhedron. For every fixed \(x\), the variables \((y,w,z)\) satisfy a mixed nonlinear complementarity system; it is mixed because \(z\) is free.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The MPEC minimizes an objective over an upper-level variable x and lower-level variables (y,w,z), subject to x belonging to a nonempty polyhedron, an equation system F=0, and complementarity between the nonnegative vectors y and w. For each fixed x, these lower-level conditions form a mixed nonlinear complementarity system because z is unrestricted.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb{R}^{n+2m+\ell}\to\mathbb{R}\text{ is continuously differentiable on an open set containing }X\times\mathbb{R}_+^{2m}\times\mathbb{R}^{\ell}.
F:\mathbb{R}^{n+2m+\ell}\to\mathbb{R}^{m+\ell}\text{ is twice continuously differentiable on an open set containing }X\times\mathbb{R}_+^{2m}\times\mathbb{R}^{\ell}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min f(x,y,w,z)\ \text{s.t.}\ x\in X,\ F(x,y,w,z)=0,\ y,w\ge0,\ y^Tw=0,\quad\text{and for fixed }x\text{ the lower-level system is a mixed NCP because }z\text{ is free.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mixed LCP and its reduction to a standard LCP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the mixed linear complementarity problem, its nonsingular-block reduction, and its representation of quadratic-program KKT conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}, B\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}, C\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}, D\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}, a\in\mathbb R^n, and b\in\mathbb R^m, the mixed LCP seeks u\in\mathbb R^n and v\in\mathbb R^m such that a+Au+Cv=0,\ b+Du+Bv\ge0,\ v\ge0, and v^T(b+Du+Bv)=0; u is unrestricted in sign. If A is nonsingular, eliminating u gives the equivalent standard LCP with q=b-DA^{-1}a and M=B-DA^{-1}C. The KKT conditions of a quadratic program with linear equality and inequality constraints have this mixed-LCP form, with primal and equality-multiplier variables free and inequality multipliers nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed LCP combines unrestricted linear equations with complementarity conditions. When the equation block A is nonsingular, eliminating the unrestricted variables produces an equivalent standard LCP through a Schur complement. KKT systems for quadratic programs with linear equalities and inequalities are mixed LCPs. Although the reduction is theoretically valid, explicitly forming it need not be computationally advisable.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n},\ B\in\mathbb R^{m\times m},\ C\in\mathbb R^{n\times m},\ D\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}
A\text{ is nonsingular for the standard-LCP reduction}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u=-A^{-1}(a+Cv),\qquad 0\le v\perp (b-DA^{-1}a)+(B-DA^{-1}C)v\ge0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Dimensional Mixed Complementarity Problem with Box Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an MCP with finite, one-sided-infinite, or free component bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(a\in(\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\})^m\), \(b\in(\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\})^m\), and \(F:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^m\), the mixed complementarity problem is to find \(u\in\mathbb R^m\) such that, for every \(i=1,\ldots,m\), \[a_i\le u_i\le b_i,\qquad (u_i-a_i)F_i(u)\le0,\qquad (u_i-b_i)F_i(u)\le0.\] When \(a_i=-\infty\), the second condition means \(F_i(u)\le0\); when \(b_i=+\infty\), the third condition means \(F_i(u)\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An MCP solution satisfies the component bounds and their complementarity sign conditions. A missing lower bound yields F_i(u) ≤ 0, while a missing upper bound yields F_i(u) ≥ 0.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall i,\quad a_i\le u_i\le b_i,\quad (u_i-a_i)F_i(u)\le0,\quad (u_i-b_i)F_i(u)\le0

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the generalized box \([l,u]\), the inclusion \(0\in F(x)+N_{[l,u]}(x)\) gives every coordinate regime. Two finite endpoints give bounded-variable complementarity; replacing \(u_i\) by \(+\infty\) removes the upper-bound case; replacing \(l_i\) by \(-\infty\) removes the lower-bound case; and \((l_i,u_i)=(-\infty,+\infty)\) forces \(F_i(x)=0\). Thus changing an endpoint between a finite value and infinity effects the corresponding bound-regime transition without changing the normal-cone formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extended-real bounds unify bounded, one-sided, and free variables; moving an endpoint to infinity deletes its associated boundary condition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global Accumulation-Point Guarantee for an Implicit-MiCP Interior-Point Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundedness and KKT accumulation-point conclusions for the specified infinite sequence generated by Algorithm 11.3.2.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuously differentiable and \((g,h):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^{m+\ell}\) be twice continuously differentiable. Suppose \(\mathrm{(LI)}\) and \(\mathrm{(PD)}\) hold. From any \((\lambda^0,w^0,x^0,\mu^0)\in\mathbb R_{++}^{2m}\times\mathbb R^{n+\ell}\), let \(\{(\lambda^k,w^k,x^k,\mu^k)\}\subset\mathbb R_{++}^{2m}\times\mathbb R^{n+\ell}\) be an infinite sequence generated by Algorithm 11.3.2 with the stated specifications and \(\sup_k\sigma_k<\bar\sigma\). Then (a) \(\{\lambda^k\circ w^k\}\) and \(\{H(\lambda^k,w^k,x^k,\mu^k)\}\) are bounded; (b) every accumulation point of the iterate sequence is a KKT tuple of \(\operatorname{VI}(K,F)\); and (c) if \(\mathrm{(BD)}\) also holds, then \(\{(x^k,w^k)\}\) is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For continuously differentiable F and twice continuously differentiable constraint mappings, under (LI), (PD), the stated algorithmic specifications, and a uniform upper bound on sigma_k, the complementarity products and residuals are bounded and every iterate accumulation point is a KKT tuple of VI(K,F). Under the additional condition (BD), the primal-slack sequence is bounded.
assumptions_latex: \{(\lambda^k,w^k,x^k,\mu^k)\}\text{ is an infinite sequence generated by Algorithm 11.3.2 with the stated specifications}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{\lambda^k\circ w^k\}\text{ and }\{H(\lambda^k,w^k,x^k,\mu^k)\}\text{ are bounded, every accumulation point is a KKT tuple of }\operatorname{VI}(K,F),\text{ and }\mathrm{(BD)}\Rightarrow\{(x^k,w^k)\}\text{ is bounded.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Column-representative kernel condition versus horizontal-LCP boundedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between a kernel implication for every column representative of (A,B) and boundedness of every right-hand-side solution set, with empty sets explicitly permitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The implication \[\forall E\in\operatorname{ColRep}(A,B),\qquad Eu+Cv=0,\ u\ge0\Longrightarrow (u,v)=0\] holds if and only if, for every \(p\in\mathbb R^{n+m}\), the mixed horizontal LCP \[p+Ax+By+Cz=0,\qquad 0\le x\perp y\ge0\] has a bounded solution set, possibly empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The kernel implication for every column representative of (A,B) is equivalent to boundedness of the mixed horizontal-LCP solution set for every right-hand side p; existence is not asserted, because the solution set may be empty.
assumptions_latex: A,B,C\text{ have compatible dimensions for the displayed mixed horizontal LCP}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[\forall E\in\operatorname{ColRep}(A,B),\ Eu+Cv=0,\ u\ge0\Longrightarrow(u,v)=0\right]\iff\left[\forall p\in\mathbb R^{n+m},\ \operatorname{Sol}(p+Ax+By+Cz=0,\ 0\le x\perp y\ge0)\text{ is bounded, possibly empty}\right].

children.title: Differentiable Implicit MCPs
children.top_down_role: Smoothness structure of mappings that generate implicit mixed complementarity problems.

assumptions_latex: \(F:U\times V\to\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(H:U\times V\to\mathbb{R}^m\) are continuously differentiable on open sets.
For every \(x\in U\), \(H(x,s(x))=0\), and \(D_yH(x,s(x))\) is nonsingular.
The MCP feasible set is a box \(C\subset U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(DG(x)=D_xF-D_yF(D_yH)^{-1}D_xH\), evaluated at \((x,s(x))\).

notation.meaning: Derivative with respect to the second argument.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite-dimensional implicit-function theorem and chain rule
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Locally single-valued smooth elimination in a finite-dimensional implicit MCP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The implicit-function theorem makes \(s\) continuously differentiable locally, with \[Ds(x)=-D_yH(x,s(x))^{-1}D_xH(x,s(x)).\] Hence the implicit MCP is the ordinary box MCP \(0\in G(x)+N_C(x)\), where \(G(x)=F(x,s(x))\), and its reduced Jacobian is \[DG(x)=D_xF(x,s(x))-D_yF(x,s(x))D_yH(x,s(x))^{-1}D_xH(x,s(x)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsingular smooth implicit equation yields a smooth reduced MCP map whose Jacobian is given by implicit differentiation.
knowledge_statements.title: Differentiable Implicit MCPs

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Accumulation-Point Convergence and Conditional Boundedness of RWIPA
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence and conditional boundedness of an infinite Ralph–Wright interior-point sequence for an implicit mixed complementarity problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H:\mathbb R^{2n+m}\to\mathbb R^{n+m}\) be continuous on \(\mathbb R_+^{2n}\times\mathbb R^m\) and continuously differentiable on \(\mathbb R_{++}^{2n}\times\mathbb R^m\). Suppose \(JH(x,y,z)\) has the mixed \(P_0\) property for every \((x,y,z)\in\Omega\). If \(\{(x^k,y^k,z^k)\}\) is an infinite sequence generated by Algorithm 11.6.3, then every accumulation point of the sequence solves the implicit mixed complementarity problem. If, additionally, \(\Omega\cap\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^{2n+m}:x^Ty\leq(x^0)^Ty^0\}\) is bounded, then the generated sequence is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under continuity, differentiability on the strictly positive region, and the mixed-P0 Jacobian property throughout Ω, every accumulation point of an infinite RWIPA sequence solves the implicit mixed complementarity problem. The sequence is bounded if the portion of Ω with complementarity product no larger than its initial value is bounded.
assumptions_latex: \(H:\mathbb R^{2n+m}\to\mathbb R^{n+m}\text{ is continuous on }\mathbb R_+^{2n}\times\mathbb R^m\)
\(H\text{ is continuously differentiable on }\mathbb R_{++}^{2n}\times\mathbb R^m\)
\(JH(x,y,z)\text{ has the mixed }P_0\text{ property for every }(x,y,z)\in\Omega\)
\(\{(x^k,y^k,z^k)\}\text{ is an infinite sequence generated by Algorithm 11.6.3}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{acc}\{(x^k,y^k,z^k)\}\subseteq\operatorname{Sol}(\mathrm{implicit\ MiCP});\quad \Omega\cap\{(x,y,z):x^Ty\leq(x^0)^Ty^0\}\text{ bounded}\implies\{(x^k,y^k,z^k)\}\text{ bounded}

children.title: Monotone Implicit MCPs
children.top_down_role: Monotonicity structure within implicit mixed complementarity problem mappings.

assumptions_latex: The implicit relation determines a single-valued map \(s:C\tobR^m\).
\(F:C\times\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is defined on the graph of \(s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle G(x)-G(z),x-z\rangle\ge0\) for all \(x,zbin C\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard monotonicity predicate applied to the reduced operator
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonicity is imposed on the reduced operator after implicit elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The implicit MCP determined by \(s\) and \(F\) is monotone on \(C\) precisely when its reduced map \(G(x)=F(x,s(x))\) satisfies \[\langle G(x)-G(z),x-z\rangle\ge0\qquad\text{for all }x,z\in C.\] The associated problem is to find \(x\in C\) such that \(0\in G(x)+N_C(x)\). Monotonicity of either \(F\) or the implicit relation separately does not replace the displayed condition on their composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An implicit MCP is monotone when the residual obtained after solving the implicit relation is a monotone map on the feasible box.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Implicit MCPs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement_latex gives the standard monotonicity condition for the reduced operator, but the assumptions contain the undefined command \tobR and the conclusion contains the malformed text x,zbin C. No inspectable source is supplied. The notation defects and source gap must be corrected together.

children.title: Differentiability–Monotonicity Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Interaction between smoothness structure and monotone geometry in implicit MCPs.

assumptions_latex: \(U\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is open and convex, and \(G:U\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is continuously differentiable.
\(G(x)=F(x,s(x))\), where the differentiable implicit map \(s\) satisfies the nonsingularity assumptions of the implicit-function theorem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) is monotone on \(U\) if and only if \(\tfrac12(DG(x)+DG(x)^{\mathsf T})\succeq0\) for every \(x\in U\).

notation.meaning: Symmetric part of the reduced Jacobian.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Jacobian characterization of continuously differentiable monotone maps
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Jacobian test for compatibility of smooth implicit elimination and monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The differentiable reduced map \(G\) is monotone on \(U\) if and only if \[\operatorname{sym}DG(x):=\tfrac12\bigl(DG(x)+DG(x)^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\succeq0\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.\] When \(s\) is defined by \(H(x,s(x))=0\), the Jacobian tested here is \[DG=D_xF-D_yF(D_yH)^{-1}D_xH,\] with all derivatives evaluated at \((x,s(x))\). Thus smoothness and monotonicity are compatible exactly when the symmetric part of this reduced Jacobian is positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth implicit MCP is monotone exactly when the symmetric part of its reduced Jacobian is positive semidefinite everywhere.
knowledge_statements.title: Differentiability–Monotonicity Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Jacobian characterization is standard on an open convex domain, but the second displayed formula introduces F, H, and their partial derivatives without fully specifying their domains in this record. No citation is provided for either the characterization or the reduced-Jacobian formula.

children.top_down_role: Regimes where one or both organizing properties cease to support the paired classification.

assumptions_latex: Scalar implicit equations and residuals are considered on neighborhoods of \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Smooth implicit data need not yield a smooth reduced map without regularity, and smooth reduction need not preserve monotonicity.

notation.meaning: Implicit solution of the first example.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit scalar counterexamples verify both failure mechanisms
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two scalar examples isolate loss of smoothness and loss of monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Loss of smoothness occurs even for smooth implicit data: let \(H(x,y)=y^3-x\) and \(F(x,y)=y\). The unique solution is \(s(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}\), so \(G(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}\) is not differentiable at \(0\); here \(D_yH(0,0)=0\). Loss of monotonicity can occur without loss of smoothness: let \(H(x,y)=y-x\) and \(F(x,y)=-y\). Then \(s(x)=x\) and \(G(x)=-x\), for which \((G(x)-G(z))(x-z)=-(x-z)^2<0\) whenever \(x\ne z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular implicit equation can destroy differentiability, while a smooth implicit substitution can produce an antimonotone reduced residual.
knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Smooth or Monotone Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two scalar examples correctly exhibit loss of differentiability under singular implicit elimination and loss of monotonicity under smooth elimination. Failure_boundary is the correct content kind, but the record has no inspectable citation as required by the statement-review contract.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each parameter \(x\in C\), let \(s(x)=(y(x),\lambda(x))\) satisfy the lower-level KKT system \[\nabla_yL(x,y,\lambda)=0,\qquad g(x,y)\le0,\qquad \lambda\ge0,\qquad \lambda_jg_j(x,y)=0\ \text{for every }j.\] Given an outer residual \(F(x,y,\lambda)\), define \(G(x)=F(x,s(x))\). The KKT-map implicit MCP is to find \(x\in C\) satisfying \(0\in G(x)+N_C(x)\), equivalently the coordinate complementarity conditions determined by the bounds of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve a parametric KKT system, substitute its selected primal-dual solution into the outer residual, and impose the resulting box MCP.
knowledge_statements.title: KKT-Map Implicit MCPs
